His proofs stay geometric, but his aim is human: to free us from slavery to passion. Part Four is Spinoza's moral psychology at its most practical, and it repays slow, careful reading.
9753-night-and-morning-volume-4:
Volume four of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Night and Morning opens with a microscope moral: monsters in a drop of water shock us, yet we drink on, forgetting the unseen strife. Lytton likens human blindness to that draught, as hidden cruelties teem beneath calm surfaces. Book four then follows the novel's tangled fates through that lens.

The volume weighs what men ignore in themselves and others, with polished, grave prose. Lytton's image of the teeming globule frames the plot's secret wars. A reader gets the fourth book of a Victorian novel, where science lends a moral mirror to ambition.
a-book-of-old-ballads-volume-4:
Volume 4 closes Beverley Nichols's A Book of Old Ballads, still drawn chiefly from Percy's Reliques and the Child collection. It opens with 'Edward, Edward,' the terrible dialogue in which a mother draws her son, line by line, to confess that the blood on his sword is his father's. to name the curse he lays on her.

Later pieces range wider in time. 'King Leir and His Three Daughters,' 'Hynd Horn,' and 'The Wife of Usher's Well' stand beside the marching song 'John Brown's Body' and 'It's a Long Way to Tipperary. ' 'The Three Ravens,' 'The Bailiff's Daughter of Islington,' and 'The Gaberlunzie Man' keep the old company. Oscar Wilde's 'Ballad of Reading Gaol' ends the volume, and the set, in a modern voice.
a-collection-of-old-english-plays-volume: Delayed for many months, the fourth and final volume of Arthur Henry Bullen's old plays at last appeared. It includes the unpublished Heywood play from a British Museum manuscript, transcribed with care by Mr. Jeaves. Bullen closes a series that rescued rare English drama from obscurity. The four volumes together form a lasting resource for students of the stage.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co:
Part 4 of Mark Twain's A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court stays at Morgan le Fay's court for a royal banquet, then descends into the queen's dungeons. Where Hank counts prisoners kept for years on suspicion and hears what long confinement has done to them. One prisoner, accused of murdering his brother, tells a story that would clear him to any hearer except his jailers.

Hank then tries knight-errantry as a trade, riding out with sandwich-board advertising like a drummer on tour, before the party joins pilgrims bound for the Valley of Holiness. There a famous holy fountain has run dry, and the monks wait for a miracle to restore it. The part sets up the contest between Hank's pumps and plumbing and Merlin's spells that opens the next.
a-doctor-of-the-old-school-volume-4: Volume four of Ian Maclaren's Doctor of the Old School recalls a winter when Dr. MacLure lay two months with a broken leg. The glen then depended on the dubious care of the Kildrummie doctor. MacLure, who rode through the snow of forty winters, never complained of suffering. The volume honors a hardworking country doctor and his people.
a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-volume-4:
William Dean Howells opens the fourth part not long after Lent, with Fulkerson laying before old Dryfoos his scheme for a celebration dinner for Every Other Week. Dryfoos, the natural-gas millionaire who owns the magazine, has never meddled in its conduct, but he is proud of the connection and likes to drop in on lucky days in stocks.

March, the editor, watches the old man's pride and his distance from his own son with growing unease. The dinner that follows brings the novel's worlds — money, art, labor, and society — to one table, with results no one planned. Howells builds toward his climax through manners and talk, his realism at its most patient.
a-history-of-science-volume-4:
Henry Smith Williams turns to chemistry and biology in the fourth volume of his history, covering much the same years as the third volume but in different fields. His opening pages link the new chemistry back to Greek guesses about atoms and breath. Dalton's atom stands near the center of the early chapters.

The contents move from the beginnings of modern chemistry through anatomy and physiology in two centuries, theories of organic evolution, and medicine old and new. A final chapter treats the new science of experimental psychology. Williams and his brother Edward write for the general reader, keeping terms plain and the story moving. The volume shows life science taking modern shape.
a-popular-history-of-france-from-the-ear: François Guizot takes his history of France into the sixteenth century, opening with Francis the First against Charles the Fifth. The volume treats Francis and the Renaissance, Francis and the Reformation, then Henry the Second, Francis the Second, and the religious wars under Charles the Ninth and Henry the Third. Engravings of Chambord, Diana of Poitiers, Mary Stuart, and the Duke of Guise accompany a century of rivalry, faith, and court intrigue.
a-romance-of-youth-volume-4:
Francois Coppee closes his Paris tale in A Romance of Youth, Volume 4 of the English edition. Amedee, the boy of the earlier volumes, now faces manhood. The Gerard household, where he played at marriage as a child, still anchors his affections. Youth's romance, the title promises, must survive contact with real life and real loss.

Childhood games have ripened into feeling between Amedee and the Gerard daughters. Work, money, and family duty press on every tender plan the young people make. Coppee keeps the scale small: rooms, streets, visits, and letters carry the emotion. Paris of clerks, artists, and small tradespeople fills the background in warm detail. Kindnesses from neighbors return to shape the ending. Readers finishing the set get a gentle, regretful close, true to Coppee's manner: first love remembered as the purest chapter of a life, however the life itself turns out afterward.
ancient-records-egypt-breasted-1906-vol-:
Volume four of Ancient Records of Egypt, published in 1906, carries the corpus from the twentieth to the twenty-sixth dynasties. Ramesses III's wars against the Sea Peoples open the volume in the great Medinet Habu inscriptions. Breasted then follows Egypt through division, Libyan and Nubian kings, Assyrian invasion, and the Saite revival.

The tone of the records changes with the centuries: boasts give way to donations, oracles, and careful priestly accounts. Together the texts document a civilization adapting to a smaller place in its world. Breasted's fourth volume completes the historical sequence of the set. Volume five, the indices, makes the whole corpus searchable. Few translation projects of its age match its lasting use.
andersonville-a-story-of-rebel-military-:
Volume 4 of John McElroy's Andersonville opens at chapter sixty-two with another man's story inside his own. Sergeant Leroy L. Key, of Company M, 16th Illinois Cavalry, led the Regulators who hanged the six Raiders on July 11th, 1864. At the author's request Key tells his career afterward: parole work in the cook-house, escape attempts, recapture and Macon, another escape, a compelled return, and final exchange at Savannah. The prison governed itself for one summer week, and its president lived to narrate it.

The volume then follows the great transfers: Andersonville emptied to Millen, Savannah, Blackshear, and Florence as Sherman's march remade the map. Sickness, exchange rumors, and the war's end close the fifteen months. Readers finishing McElroy get the whole arc, from capture to freedom. He measures that freedom against the thousands who did not come out. Their names fill his closing pages like a muster of ghosts.
ante-nicene-fathers-vol-4:
Volume four of the Ante-Nicene Fathers, from the Roberts and Donaldson set of 1885, holds the third-century fathers in mixed company. Tertullian's fourth part leads, with his later and sterner writings. Minucius Felix and Commodian follow, and Origen's first two parts close the volume.

Minucius Felix's Octavius is a graceful dialogue defending Christians on a seaside walk. Commodian thunders in rough verse against pagans and lax believers. Origen, the giant of Alexandria, then begins: his case against the pagan Celsus and his first thoughts on first principles. The volume runs from street-level apology to the deepest mind of the early church.
arabian-nights-payne-1883-vol-4:
Payne's fourth volume of the Thousand Nights and One Night appeared in 1883, mid-set in the nine-volume run. The Calcutta Arabic text supplies more nights of marvels, told by Shahrazad to hold death at bay. John Payne Englished them all without the cuts that marked earlier versions for family reading.

Story opens inside story like nested boxes, an art the Nights taught the whole world. Kings in disguise walk night streets, slaves outwit masters, and fortune turns on a word. Volume IV keeps the cycle's spell unbroken for readers following Payne's complete design from the first volume onward.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-4:
Michael L. Rodkinson's fourth volume of the Babylonian Talmud joins two tractates: Shekalim and Rosh Hashana. Shekalim treats the half-shekel tax every Israelite once paid toward the Temple service. Rosh Hashana, the New Year tractate, treats the calendar of festivals and the year itself.

In Shekalim, the rabbis run the Temple's money: collection, exchange, and the care of funds. Rosh Hashana fixes how witnesses prove the new moon, and when the shofar, the ram's horn, must be blown. It also weighs the four new years of the Jewish calendar. The pairing shows the Talmud moving from Temple finance to the order of time.
bancroft-history-us-vol-4:
Crisis years fill the fourth volume of Bancroft's History of the United States, from 1860. Taxes levied without consent stir protest across the colonies in the 1760s and early 1770s. Petitions give way to boycotts, and boycotts to open defiance.

Bancroft's pace quickens as protest hardens into rebellion. He believed he was tracing the hand of providence in these events. Crowds, congresses, and pamphleteers share his stage with ministers in London. Readers watch a people argue itself into revolution. The volume forms the hinge of his great work, where colonial grievance turns into a cause worth a war.
beauchamp-s-career-volume-4:
The fourth volume of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career runs from chapter twenty-six to chapter thirty-three. Nevil Beauchamp has returned lame to his canvass at Bevisham, and rumours follow him. Cecilia Halkett, the heiress he courts, finds only his card after a missed visit. A short sidelook at the election frames the personal drama.

Dr. Shrapnel writes Nevil a long epistle of radical counsel. Chapters probe a young lady's heart and her intellect, meaning Cecilia's divided feelings. Blackburn Tuckham embodies the hard commercial interest against Nevil. An effort to conquer Cecilia in Beauchamp's blunt fashion leads to the first encounter at Steynham. Meredith studies love conducted like a campaign, by a man who charges drawing rooms as he charged in war.
bill-s-lapse-odd-craft-part-4:
W. W. Jacobs tells this tale in the voice of his night watchman, as part four of Odd Craft. Strength and good-nature always go together, the watchman muses, feeling his biceps. The strongest and kindest-hearted man he ever knew was Bill Burton, a shipmate of Ginger Dick, Peter Russet, and Sam Small. Bill was no taller than the watchman, but his arms were like another man's legs and his chest might have been made for a giant.

Bill's lapse is drink, and his mates hold the inquest in dialect. Why doesn't he go away and leave them alone, they demand. Because I've got a heart, says Bill; he can't chuck up pals in that free-and-easy way. Peter urges him to take the pledge again. Bill smiles kindly: it's just a weakness. Jacobs lets the comedy sit on real ruin, one round at a time.
carlyle-friedrich-vol-4:
Rossbach and Leuthen blaze in the fourth volume of Carlyle's History of Friedrich, from 1865. The Seven Years' War reaches its pitch of danger and glory. Carlyle calls such victories the miracles of the House of Brandenburg.

His prose hits a kind of battle frenzy in these pages. Swift marches, oblique attacks, and a king calm in smoke fill the tale. He writes as if possessed by the poetry of war itself. Readers who love military history in grand style will find few equals. The volume forms the blazing center of his six-book epic of Prussian endurance.
casanova-memoirs-vol-4:
Volume Four of Casanova's memoirs, in Arthur Machen's unabridged translation, carries the adventurer through southern Europe. Giacomo Casanova wrote his memoirs in French late in life, while serving as a librarian in Bohemia. He claimed every word was true.

The adventures here run through Italy and the Mediterranean world of courts, theaters, and convents. Casanova gambles, schemes, loves, and escapes, always talking his way forward. His eye for the fashions and morals of the age is sharp and amused. Volume Four is subtitled Adventures in the South, and it shows the legendary lover at the height of his powers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100050012-4:
Research paper titled Analysis of Criticisms of Validity Generalization Research and Selection Programs is by Frank Schmidt, John Hunter, and Kenneth Pearlman. Their affiliations are given as the Office of Personnel Management, George Washington University, and Michigan State University. It answers doubts raised against their line of testing research.

Evidence that the validity of employment tests carries across settings had been well accepted in science and the profession, the authors state. Some criticisms were good faith requests for clarification, they allow, while others were not. Many questions concerned whether selection programs built on cumulative findings could hold up in court. Only one decision, the Pegues case, had given such findings a major role, they note, and its judge accepted and stressed them. No defense yet rested wholly on studies done by others, the paper states. Work applying the method to LSAT scores reached the same general finding.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100070001-4:
Memorandum to the Director of Central Intelligence gives comments on the Inspector General's survey of the Junior Officer Training Program. The typewriting is heavily garbled in this scan, but its argument is legible. The writer concurs in the survey's findings and recommendations, with a few points of exception noted.

Development of the program had been a significant accomplishment, the memo states, and its success pointed to gradual expansion, which the writer would act to achieve. His main disagreement was with a proposed Phase II: an eventual joining of the Office of Personnel and the Office of Training, to centralize career management. Close cooperation on the training program was needed, he allows. But that work was only a small part of both offices' totals, and would not justify merging many unlike functions into one central office. He proposed the closest cooperation instead. Specific replies to numbered recommendations follow.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100110006-4:
Standards for Quality and Fairness of the Educational Testing Service were adopted by its Board of Trustees in October 1981, at Princeton, New Jersey. The board resolution adopts, as ETS policy, the principles management had set out in its guidelines publication. It also endorses the working rules built to carry those principles out.

Two further resolutions shape how the standards would run. Management must keep monitoring how well programs and services follow the rules, the board directs. It must revise the rules as needed and report to the board each year. Management may also allow other procedures that reach the same ends, it states, with room for small or new programs. A numbered standards passage turns to tests in running programs. Their specifications should be reviewed for relevance before each new form is built, it says. Big changes should prompt thought about score comparability and renaming.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100130004-4:
Memorandum of 4 February 1980 from Charles A. Briggs, Inspector General, forwards a draft chapter for comment. Chapter IX, Professional Applicant Test Battery, belonged to the Inspector General's report on the agency's recruitment system. The consultants' report behind it, with summary and appendices, is included.

Neither draft was being shown elsewhere in the agency while comments were awaited, Briggs writes. He asked for them by 29 February 1980. The chapter states the test battery was an eight-hour series of written tests, used for over twenty years to select new professional staff. The inspection covered two sides: its role in processing and selection, and evidence for its reliability and validity. A later finding faults how psychologists wrote up results. Their reports varied in unpredictable ways, reflecting personal habits more than applicant performance, it states. Writing assessments used shifting criteria and vague terms.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100020051-4:
Two letters of February 1981 exchange a research request and a refusal. George A. Shaughnessy wrote on 19 February to the agency's Historical Division in Virginia. He was researching a book on planning for the invasion of Japan, set to begin 1 November 1945. The plan was codenamed Downfall, he notes, with Olympic against Kyushu and Coronet against Honshu.

His questions concern wartime deception. An archivist had told him of a conduit that passed misinformation to Japan through the Spanish Embassy, he writes. He also held a newly declassified deception plan called Pastel, and puzzled over its mention of bunsen burners dropped as decoys. Roberta S. Knapp, Acting Chief of the History Staff, replied on 26 February. Her office could not help, she regrets: the CIA was established in 1947, and its records do not cover World War II. Names in the file are partly masked.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100060011-4:
A December 1983 cover note sends along an account of a meeting held the month before on historical access. Chief Historian J. Kenneth McDonald writes on 12 December 1983 to the Information Review Officer. He notes that his own account is largely overtaken by a 23 November memorandum on historical access, a copy of which he had been sent.

The attached record covers a meeting on 22 November 1983, held from 10 to 11:30 in the morning. Talk turned on a Senate-passed bill, the Intelligence Information Act of 1983, and on letters exchanged between Senator Durenberger and Director Casey. The Senate committee report on the bill was shared, and a proposed program of selective review of records of historical interest was weighed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100060110-4:
State Department historians seek to read a classified CIA history in a secret memorandum dated 10 August 1983. Chief Historian J. Kenneth McDonald writes to the Deputy Director for Administration, whose office controls access to the study. The request came in a July letter from the Historian of the Department of State.

McDonald explains that the History Staff holds a copy and can let cleared State historians read it on site, under supervision, if permission is granted. Any facts they wished to publish, in the Foreign Relations of the United States series or elsewhere, would first go to the CIA for a release review. The memo asks for a yes or no on those terms.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100070029-4:
Four items are set for the first meeting of the History Advisory Board in a memorandum dated 13 December 1982. Chief Historian J. Kenneth McDonald, as the board's executive secretary, lists the business for the morning of 15 December. The memo cites the January 1982 notice that set up the CIA History Staff.

The board would weigh a study of Congress and the CIA, and judge whether a history of the Agency role in overhead reconnaissance up to about 1970 could be done. Progress on director studies for Helms, Schlesinger, and Colby is listed, plus Director Casey's wish for studies of McCone, Raborn, Bush, and Turner. Staff access to records across the directorates closes the agenda. A prospectus for the Congress study is attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100090072-4:
Press dealings over OSS records are reported in a memorandum dated 22 June 1984 to George Lauder, the Director of Public Affairs. Chief Historian J. Kenneth McDonald sends records of his three phone talks with John Sherwood, a reporter for The Washington Times. The talks concerned wartime OSS records then drawing press interest.

McDonald notes that Sherwood's piece in that day's paper looked harmless enough. He was glad the reporter had dropped a line about missing war diaries, but sorry the story gave no credit to the Director for releasing the records. With two stories now out, he expects more press queries to follow. The attached records give the talks in detail.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100100025-4:
Material on the Klaus Fuchs case changes hands in an October 1984 exchange kept in this file. Chief Historian J. Kenneth McDonald writes on 19 October to Robert Williams, Dean of University College at Washington University in St. Louis. He thanks Williams for a letter and the attached material on the Fuchs case.

Williams had written on 4 October asking for help after trouble gaining access to Agency records on the case. He explains that the main case file is the FBI's, and that the Atomic Energy Commission and Los Alamos also hold much material. His own letter and copies passed to Agency staff make up the rest of the file, which records a scholar's route into closed records.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04b01991r000100020001-4:
Guidelines from the Attorney General govern prosecutions that involve classified information, in a Justice Department paper held in Agency files. The opening sets the general rule for federal cases. Where a person is believed to have broken federal law and the evidence can sustain a conviction, prosecution should be sought.

Two exceptions frame the rest of the guidance. A case may be dropped where no real federal interest would be served, or where other strong federal interests point the other way. The text ties this rule to the recently published Principles of Federal Prosecution, and quotes the part of those principles that covers the decision to decline. The classified setting gives that balance extra weight.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100080001-4:
South America's debt burden is the subject of a secret intelligence assessment dated April 1984, carrying two report numbers, ALA 84-10036 and GI 84-10065. Analysts from Latin American and global issues offices shared the work. It rests on information available as of 30 March 1984.

Key judgments say the region faces a hard task this year. The countries need 62 billion dollars, the paper reckons, to meet foreign financing duties. Without strong cooperation among lenders, payment suspensions could spread. Pressure for bolder steps is also tracked. The Declaration of Quito sought a cap on debt service tied to export earnings. Former central banker Carlos Langoni proposed longer terms and lower rates.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100350001-4:
A June 1984 meeting of Latin American debtor nations at Cartagena, Colombia, is analyzed in a memorandum dated 12 July 1984. The Secretary of State requested the paper, and South America analysts wrote it with a contribution from the global issues office. It rests on information available as of 5 July 1984.

Eleven debtor countries met to seek a shared approach to their debts. Reporting before, during, and after the meeting points to little real agreement beyond broad statements of concern, the paper says. Most firm proposals were watered down. Still, a debtors' secretariat was left in place. Argentine leaders called the meeting a political win for their diplomacy, without giving details.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000302400001-4:
China's National Day parade is read for signs of military progress in a memorandum dated 23 November 1984. The Defense Issues Branch of the China Division prepared the paper. The 1 October parade in Beijing drew unusually heavy media coverage at home, the paper notes.

The parade showcased recent gains in conventional and nuclear weapons and underlined progress in defense modernization since the mid-1970s, the paper reports. Foreign technology was plainly present in many conventional weapons on show, despite official stress on self-reliance. If the new weapons are produced and fielded in quantity, they would fix some, but not all, of the critical gaps in China's defenses, the paper judges.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000100360001-4:
Peru under its incoming president is assessed in a paper dated 15 July 1985, with a praise note from Director William Casey dated 17 July on the file. Casey calls the response to a National Security Council tasker a good piece of work. The paper's subject pairs the Garcia administration with prospects for communist inroads.

Alan Garcia, 36, takes office on 28 July after winning on charm, energy, and a promise of a fairer society, the summary says. His party holds a congressional majority. Hard tests wait: a weak economy, lethal leftist terrorism, and a fast-growing drug trade. On the communist question, the body reports no firm evidence of Soviet-directed activity in the military.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000100540001-4:
Japan and South Korea, past and present, are traced in a secret research paper dated January 1985, EA 85-10012. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it for a regional analysis staff. Its title promises a look at yesterday, today, and tomorrow in the two countries' dealings.

The factors shaping the relationship have stayed fairly constant since 1945, the paper argues. Closeness on the map, economic ties that matter to both in different ways, and the weight each sets on ties with the United States all push toward stability. Friction also has a pattern: press and public anger over perceived insults from Japan, and suspicion about Japanese security links with South Korea, recur in the account.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000100630001-4:
China's foreign trade is laid out in tables in a reference aid dated March 1985, EA 85-10055. Titled China: International Trade Annual Statistical Supplement, the aid came from the East Asian analysis office. A front note says the publication is made for American government officials, with copies available through Agency channels.

Method notes explain how gaps in the figures were filled. For countries that never reported commodity detail between 1970 and 1983, the small remainder was spread in proportion over values built by other steps. Long runs of numbers then give trade totals by year and partner. The aid is a working data book, meant to sit beside the narrative China assessments of the same period.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000200800001-4:
Vietnam ten years after unification is assessed in a secret paper dated June 1985, EA 85-10106. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it, using information available as of 10 May 1985. Its title asks whether change is ahead in the second decade.

Key judgments say Hanoi's leaders have launched foreign and domestic economic steps aimed at guarding national security and speeding growth. New appointees include cadres with technical skill and younger cadres. Party propaganda has grown less contentious, and a pragmatic line won endorsement at a party plenum the previous July, the paper reports. Shifts and partial reversals since then leave the course unsettled, and the body tracks that wavering.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201340001-4:
Changing opposition views on security in Japan are covered in a confidential memorandum dated 7 March 1985. The Japan Branch prepared the paper, using information available that day. Deep splits over defense policy were once the rule between the ruling party and its rivals.

In recent years, the summary reports, opposition members have moved closer to ruling party ground. Most now back the security treaty with the United States and support the Self-Defense Forces in general terms. The Democratic Socialist Party led the way, endorsing the treaty in 1976. Opposition parties will still fight the government on single defense issues in the Diet, the paper adds, and will use themes such as disarmament to win voters.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201700001-4:
China's year in review is summed up in a memorandum dated 6 June 1985. The summary reports that the economic and political state kept improving over the past year, though signs of overheating showed early in 1985. Deng Xiaoping still dominates the system and pushes it toward more reform.

Ties with the United States stayed stable, and links with the Soviet Union improved a little, though deep differences remain. China still tilts toward the West for both strategic and economic reasons, the paper says, despite its claim to an independent foreign policy. Leaders have used Washington as a counterweight to Moscow and as a source of help for modernization, while also making friendly overtures to the new Soviet leader.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000301790001-4:
Japan news from 1 May to mid-June 1985 is rounded up in a memorandum dated 17 June 1985. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it, using information available that day. It carries the number EA M 85-10115 and a duplicate file note.

The Japanese media play up Prime Minister Nakasone's strong showing at the Bonn Summit, the summary reports. The summit serves as a prelude to his work for the Tokyo economic summit the next year. At home, talk centers on the Tanaka faction. Former prime minister Tanaka is home from hospital, but reporters who cover him guess he will stay incapacitated a year or more. Comment now holds that his time as faction leader and kingmaker is over.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000301970001-4:
Japan news for July 1985 is gathered in a memorandum dated 24 July 1985. The Japan Branch prepared the roundup. Market opening dominates the month: the government is building a program to open its markets to foreign goods.

A tariff cut package announced in late June won only mixed press reviews, the summary reports. With protectionist feeling rising in the United States and Europe, Japanese journalists urge Tokyo to deliver a fuller program. The public backs Prime Minister Nakasone's market steps, and he calls that support his only weapon. Reporters who cover the ministries still note stiff resistance from officials and powerful interest groups.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01506r000300880001-4:
Poland is the subject of an alert memorandum dated 25 November 1980, sent to the National Security Council. Two near-identical versions sit in the file, one signed by Deputy Director Frank Carlucci. The series number is NI-IAM-80-10010, and a footnote explains that alert memoranda flag grave possible developments without predicting them.

Warsaw leaders of the Solidarity trade unions have issued six political demands, the memo reports. They threaten a large strike in Warsaw factories unless talks begin by Thursday noon. The demands include freeing jailed dissidents and a joint commission to probe police powers. Railway strikes were already reported that day. The memo warns that the Kania regime may use limited force, and that Soviet military intervention is possible.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000100040009-4:
The intelligence directorate drafts answers to a Bar Association questionnaire in a memorandum dated 14 February 1984. The Deputy Director for Intelligence writes to the Associate General Counsel for Intelligence Community Affairs. A document control sheet for the General Counsel's office heads the file, dated the same day.

The writer apologizes for missing the deadline and offers answers to the questions fitting his directorate. One answer lists the ways sensitive collection is kept focused on targets of real weight. At the top level, the Senior Interdepartmental Group for Intelligence brings together the main consumers of intelligence and community representatives on a regular basis. The questionnaire itself concerns oversight of the intelligence community.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200480004-4:
Stansfield Turner sends Naval Reserve material to Professor Vincent Davis in a letter dated 6 July 1977. The attached paper had been circulated by the Chief of Naval Operations. Turner also corrects a mix-up over a speaking date in Lexington.

He had the months confused: it is 11 November that he will be at DePauw and Wabash, not a date that frees the Lexington slot. That timing clashes with a speaker Davis already has for a November exercise, so another time must be found. The enclosure is a statement on the United States Naval Reserve. It opens with a letter from Senators Dole, Mathias, and Nunn asking Turner's view, as former naval chief, on reserve missions and mobilization needs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200480022-4:
Vincent Davis congratulates Stansfield Turner on his confirmation in a letter dated 28 February 1977. Writing from the University of Kentucky, Davis jokes that the result was a lead-pipe cinch. He encloses an article from that day's Business Week.

The article raises what Davis calls one of the hardest questions in intelligence: how to avoid locking into assumptions that harden into conventional wisdom. In Washington's competitive policy process, he argues, sounding unsure is often to lose. Egos and careers push people to sound more certain than the evidence allows. Over years, that certainty turns into belief. The file's later pages carry the article's matter on Soviet military spending estimates and the burden calculation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200500001-4:
Two letters between Stansfield Turner and Vincent Davis sit in a September 1979 file. Turner's letter of 7 September 1979 finds Davis back from vacation and in the fray again. Turner asks how the Reserve Intelligence Seminar at the end of the month turns out.

A speaker on the faculty is well suited to discuss the role planned for military intelligence within the national effort, Turner writes. He thanks Davis for letting him name-drop when talking to academic people. Davis's own letter of 28 August 1979 follows, thanking Turner for a warm letter of 23 August and for a phone call that tracked him down at a camping retreat. One page in the document is withheld.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200600055-4:
Prospective guests for a two-day seminar are listed in a letter from Paul Fay Jr. dated 24 March 1978. Fay heads the Fay Improvement Company, a financial consulting firm in San Francisco. His letter goes to press with the names for a seminar on 5 and 6 April.

The table pairs each attendee with an organization and a lodging mark for the nights of 4 and 5 April, most at the Jefferson Hotel. Names come from government, banking, insurance, and business: Bankers Trust, Chemical Bank, Connecticut General, Fidelity Management, General Electric, and Putnam Management appear among them. An economist, Walter Heller, is listed without a firm. The list is a planning tool, not a report of the event.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000300830013-4:
Former Director Richard Helms testifies on charter legislation in a hearing reported on 30 May 1978, OLC 78-0399/84. Helms appeared before the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence on 16 May 1978. The bill before the committee was S. 2525. Senators Bayh, Moynihan, Goldwater, Chafee, and Garn attended.

Helms made no formal statement and offered observations instead. S. 2525 would create more difficulties than it resolves, he held. It would build a legal structure that cuts the President's flexibility in national security. Congress keeps an oversight role, he allowed, but guidelines and restrictions for intelligence should come from the President. The memorandum lists his points in order, as the Agency observers recorded them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000501190039-4:
Remarks by Admiral Stansfield Turner, USN, Bryant College, 21 May 1977 is a second copy of a speech text. The text is the Director's commencement address. It opens by honoring the graduates and their families. It notes their pride in work completed. Then it turns to the greater opportunity of the present day. It contrasts a mid-1970s education with the campus years that came before. Those years were polarized.

The remarks go on that few things in life are entirely one way. Governments, they say, are no more all-evil than people are. The American government has shown a marvelous resiliency over two hundred years. The address then moves toward its appeal for public service. The text tracks the companion copy closely. It is set out in clean paragraph form.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601410006-4:
Long-range schedules for the Director of Central Intelligence run month by month here. They cover December 1977 through November 1978. April 1978 alone is full. A Washington Press Club dinner leads it. Trips to the University of Kentucky come next. Detroit and Ohio State stops follow. A White House Correspondents Dinner ends the month.

Later months add a Far East trip. A Yale panel is listed. A Golden Plate award event sits in Kentucky. Weeks at Aspen appear too. Some dates carry a mark of doubt. The file maps a year of public duty. Talks, awards and travel were planned far ahead. All sit in one running list.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601450057-4:
Oxford hosts this conference file for September 7 to 10, 1978. The International Institute for Strategic Studies held its 20th annual conference there. A letter dated 9 May 1978 writes to members who had said they hoped to come. It asks them to confirm that they still wish to attend.

Christ Church is named as the site of the meeting. A form goes with the letter, to be filled in and sent back fast. The institute needed the facts for planning, it says. The file is the advance paper for a set-piece meet of defense thinkers, kept among the Director of Central Intelligence's records for that autumn.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601470019-4:
Executive order text on national security information fills this White House file. The order was held back until after a briefing on June 29, 1978. It sets out to balance two goods: public access to state papers, and the need to guard some facts from disclosure. A long table of heads maps the scheme.

Original and derived grading of papers each get a part. So do the rules for marking, guarding and review. Downgrading and release of old papers close the scheme. Time limits on secrecy run through the order. For the Central Intelligence Agency and the wider spy world, the text is a base rule book: what may be kept secret, by whom, and for how long.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601480036-4:
Comparative Guide to American Colleges, eighth edition, supplies this Ohio State entry. James Cass and Max Birnbaum wrote the guide for students, parents and counselors. Harper and Row published it in New York. The entry calls admission to Ohio State selective.

About 75 percent of applicants were taken, it says. Most of those then enrolled. Average freshman test scores are given for men and women. Early decision, early admission and midyear entry all appear as paths in. Transfers are welcomed in set terms. It reports that about 55 percent of entering freshmen graduate in time, and it lists special paths such as study abroad, honors and undergraduate research.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601550001-4:
FBI National Academy graduation exercises for the 113th session fill this program. The date is June 16, 1978. The place is the FBI Academy at Quantico, Virginia. The program speaks first to the class: eleven weeks of hard effort lie behind them.

That effort had one end, the text says: to lift the quality of law work through training. Each graduate wore the badge of a professional on arrival, it adds. The class leaves with that standing raised. The file is the printed program for the rite, kept in the Director of Central Intelligence's papers as a guest of the day.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601560073-4:
Houston Clubber fills this Central Intelligence Agency file as an issue of the Houston Club magazine. Speaker previews lead much of the text sampled here. One talk would lay out what each candidate's election would mean for business planning. The speaker ran a government research firm in Washington.

A second preview treats a noted forecaster on the economy. His firm counsels investment managers and company chiefs at home and abroad. Member and club matter fills the rest of the issue. The file shows the fare a big city club laid on for its members: talks on politics and money, set among the news of the house.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601580017-4:
National Security Act of 1947 fills this committee print. The act's own opening words set out its short title. A note explains that the table of contents from the act of July 26, 1947 is left out here. It is covered by the print's own contents instead. Section two states the policy of Congress.

Congress meant to give the land a full scheme for security, the text says. The act is the base law of the modern spy world. It set up the posts and councils under which the Central Intelligence Agency works. A copy in the director's file served as a ready text of the law that made his office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100090001-4:
CY 78 schedule for small group meetings with the DCI fills this routing sheet. The sheet is dated 24 January 1978. It comes from the Career Management Staff in the administration arm. A routing and record form carries it through the house.

Small group meetings were Turner's way of hearing staff at first hand. Groups from across the agency sat with him in turn. The schedule for the year set out which groups would come and when. Comments columns and initials fill the form's lower half. The file is a plain staff paper, but it marks a set habit of the new director: regular, face-to-face time with working staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100090010-4:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) panels get their paper trail in this file of slips and memos. A routing slip from the Deputy Director for Administration opens it. The file treats the advisory groups that fed views to the director. One memo sets up a management advisory group for the Director of Security.

That group would meet its chief at least once a month for feedback sessions. Its topics would be part self-chosen, part referred by the chief. The memo casts the group as study unit, research arm and sounding board in one. The file shows how the panel system was meant to work inside one directorate of the house.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100170002-4:
Clark M Clifford wrote to President John F Kennedy on October 25, 1961. His letter is marked Exhibit 8 in the file. At the President's request, he encloses a memorandum. An original and two copies go with the letter. The memo is meant for the President's conference with the new Director of Central Intelligence.

Five points fill the memo, Clifford writes. They are the points he judges most important as the new director takes up his duties. The form lets the President hand a copy to the director if he wishes. Clifford offers more help if called on. The file is a crisp piece of counsel from a past defense chief.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200510003-4:
Turner wrote to Richard J Kneeley on 5 June 1980 in warm thanks. Kneeley is Rick in the greeting. Turner thanks him for the privilege of joining his graduating class at Pace the past Sunday. The ceremony was inspiring, he writes, and so was the group.

He praises Kneeley's own achievements and the recognition accorded him that day. That standing will serve him as his career moves forward, Turner adds. If the CIA ever figures in it, the agency would be pleased. Literature on the Graduate Studies Program goes with the letter. The file is a graduation note with a gentle recruiting tail.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200650008-4:
Questions regarding handicapped employees fill this routing and record sheet. It is dated March 1978 and comes from the Director of Central Intelligence of Personnel. The sheet is marked secret in the print. Comments run down the page in the set form. Each comment shows from whom and to whom it moved.

Added responses from the administration arm are noted on the sheet. They treat concerns raised by handicapped employees. Their review had been made in the personnel office. The file is the paper path of a staff welfare matter: queries raised by a group of employees, worked through the house and answered in form.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200660016-4:
Agenda for a meeting of the Director of Central Intelligence and the operations advisory group is set for 5 December 1977. The sitting starts at 1500 hours. It treats the personnel reduction program for fiscal years 1978 and 1979. First comes a sampling of reactions from operations staff to the cuts. Five minutes are allowed for that.

Questions take the next quarter hour. The group seeks clarity on the reasons for the cuts. Job security and tenure policy stand behind the queries. Recommendations and discussion fill the rest of the hour. The agenda shows the clandestine arm facing its chief, weeks after the November cut, with morale and policy on the table.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200690013-4:
Recent writings by Harlan Cleveland get a list dated June 2, 1980. Books, articles and papers are sorted in order. Forthcoming books lead: an edited volume on energy futures of developing countries comes first. It grew from an Aspen workshop in Cairo in January 1979. Praeger would publish it with the Aspen Institute.

A book on the management of sustainable growth follows. It gathers papers from the Third Biennial Woodlands Conference. Cleveland edited it and wrote the opening essay. Parts of that essay had already run in print. The list, kept in Central Intelligence Agency files, is a scholar's record at a move: what was out, what was coming, and what themes held his work together.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200710001-4:
Address by Admiral Stansfield Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, to the United States Coast Guard fills this file. He spoke at Fort McNair in Washington. The time was noon on Wednesday, 19 November 1980. He opens by asking for short remarks and many questions. Two things would fill his brief talk, he says.

First, his sense of the prospect the country faces into the 1980s. Second, how the spy world can better support the Coast Guard. That service faces growing duties, he suggests. The talk is a late-tenure address: a spy chief telling a sea service where he thinks risk and duty are heading.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200770005-4:
Non-fuel minerals study gets a forwarding memo dated 19 September 1980. It goes to Michael Calingaert at the Department of State. He was deputy assistant secretary for international resources and food policy. His memo of 4 September had asked for the work. The study enclosed assesses possible Soviet manipulation of critical metals markets.

Four metals name the scope: chromium, cobalt, manganese and the platinum group. Two questions frame the study. Could the Soviets bend these markets? And how likely were they to try, if exports from southern African producers were halted? The file is a Central Intelligence Agency market study with a cold war edge, sent across the river to State.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200780004-4:
Herbert E Hetu heads this public affairs file for the director. Hetu directed public affairs at the agency. His letterhead and hand notes sit at the front. The body of the file holds a set of questions for 60 Minutes. The questions are the kind a reporter would put to Turner at the end of his term.

What do you feel you have accomplished in four years, the first asks. Which one or two accomplishments count most, the second asks. What was left undone comes third. The list runs on through his views and choices. The file is a press office at work: drafting the grilling its own chief should expect on camera.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000300850014-4:
Speaking invitations from three universities are weighed in this staff memo of 10 May 1978. Harvard and Fletcher School invitations came together. A Duke invitation came with them. The memo to the Director of Central Intelligence gives a clear recommendation. Harvard and Fletcher should be tied to the New York address of 13 November 1978.

Fall would then be full, with Chicago already set for October. Duke could be put to February 1979 instead. A winter trip south could carry it then. Hand marks on the memo show the calls made. The file is a small, complete piece of scheduling judgment, kept with the invitations that prompted it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000300890001-4:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) trip plans fill this office note dated 25 April 1978. The note treats a phone call from Andrew Sides that day. Sides had written on 31 May 1977 with an invitation. The Forging Industry Association wanted Turner to address its meeting. The meeting ran 12 to 16 November 1978 at Palm Springs, California.

One snag stands out: Turner had already accepted a Navy League address in New York on 13 November. He could offer to speak later in the session, the note suggests. Grouping several stops in one trip was his normal aim. The file is a diary note on the Phoenix and Denver circuit of asks that reached the director that spring.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000300960003-4:
Guest list for October 1979 fills this Business Council file. Each guest gets a sketch of a life and a post. Clement E Conger leads the sampled pages. Conger curated the Diplomatic Reception Rooms at the Department of State. He had curated the White House since March 1970.

He joined the State Department in 1947, the sketch says. Two tours as deputy chief of protocol stand in his record. He started the program of stocking the rooms with fine pieces by gift and loan. The list served the council's Homestead meeting. It told members who their guests were before the weekend began, in a pack kept for the Central Intelligence Agency director.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000301030004-4:
Purpose, the alumni magazine of The Principia, fills this file for spring 1980. The Principia Alumni Association publishes it from St. Louis, Missouri. A cover note treats the River Road at Elsah. On weekends more bikes than cars use it, the note says. Tower bells open the magazine's own essay.

Principia's tower bells form part of student life on campus, the piece says. They live in the memory of graduates long after. The issue came out the spring of the Director of Central Intelligence's visit to the college. Its presence in the file marks the school as his hosts knew it: a small college on the river bluffs, proud of its sounds and scenes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000301090017-4:
Amherst alumni holiday and reunion weekend gets a welcome booklet in this file. Welcome back to Amherst, it opens. The booklet gives the information a guest needs to enjoy the stay. The Reception Center at the Alumni House is the hub. Light refreshments and morning papers wait there.

Good company and answers to questions are promised too. The weekend was the 1980 reunion round at the college. Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence,'s class marked 35 years in that round. The booklet served all returning classes at once. Its place in the file is simple: the guide the director carried, or was sent, for his own return to Amherst that spring.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401130020-4:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) scheduling item 79-321 logs a National Prayer Breakfast in this file. The item was received on 30 November 1979. The source was a telephone call and letter from Senator Mark Hatfield. The event was set for 0800 hours on Thursday 7 February 1980. The Washington Hilton Hotel is the place.

A formal invitation would follow, the form notes. Mrs Turner was invited as well. Spaces on the form route the item to deputies for action. The file is the staff record of a standing Washington rite: a breakfast of officials and faith, entered in the director's diary by form and number.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401130039-4: Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) scheduling item logs an invitation for George A Bariscillo Jr in this single-page form. The item was received on 20 November 1979. The New Jersey State Bar Association sought a key speaker for its annual dinner. The date was Saturday 17 May 1980, at Atlantic City, New Jersey. A formal invitation route by letter and phone stands on the form.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401140029-4:
A scheduling item for the Director of Central Intelligence scheduling item 80-50 logs a speaking engagement request with no fixed date. Robert Barensfeld relayed the request, received on 29 February 1980. The event was an annual business and industry dinner. Baldwin-Wallace College sponsored it. The ask was for an address by the DCI on any date in the future.

Berea, in the Cleveland area of Ohio, is the place named. A suspense date of 14 March 1980 is marked on the form. Open-ended asks like this one tested a diary: a college dinner, a willing host, and no day yet set. The file is the staff record of the request, kept while the office weighed its spring.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401140038-4: Card to Godfrey Sperling Jr carries a short letter from Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, dated 31 January 1980. Budge is the greeting used. Turner thanks him for a nice note on the Gridiron dinner. He accepts with alacrity, he writes. The card is brief and warm, a press man's dinner answered in a friend's hand, on the director's own letterhead.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401150046-4:
President's Commission on Executive Exchange supplies the letter in this file, dated March 21, 1980. Jan Zeszatek's name heads the record in the catalog. The commission sat at the White House. Its letter invites Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, to speak informally and off the record. His audience would be the Presidential Exchange Executives based in Washington that year.

The exchange program moved business men into government posts for a season. A talk from the spy chief fit its aim: to show executives how the state truly works. The file holds the invitation and its staff routing marks. It shows a White House program drawing on the director as a teacher for a term.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401310011-4:
A concept of education for the intelligence profession gets a covering memorandum dated 23 June 1980. It goes to the four deputy directors of the agency. A special assistant to the deputy director signs it. Attached is Don Smith's concept paper on the subject. The paper had been discussed with them already.

That discussion took place at the meeting of the DCI and his deputies on 11 June. The memo's mark is an NFAC registry number. The file is the routing piece for a reform paper. It asks how to school a whole profession. It went to the four men who ran its branches. A June talk lay behind it, and decisions lay ahead.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501400001-4:
Press clippings for July 1980 carry a file head naming Libya and Billy Carter. A New York Times essay by William Safire, dated July 23, leads the sampled pages. Safire asks why the national security adviser insisted he had not discussed Libya with Billy Carter. The President's brother had taken money from Libya, the story ran.

Questions of influence and truth fill the month around that tale. The file gathers a scandal summer in print: a brother, a foreign state and a White House denial, all weighed day by day. The agency kept the bundle as it kept the rest: the whole month of news that touched its world.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601690009-4:
Executive Order 11905 of 18 February 1976 appears here as a full Federal Register printing. Headed United States Foreign Intelligence Activities, the order sets policy for the whole intelligence field. It states three aims: better intelligence, clear duties for each body, and oversight to keep work within the law.

A contents list maps eight sections before the text begins. Early sections define terms and place control with the National Security Council and named committees. Middle sections assign tasks to each department and agency in turn. Final sections cover limits on activity, oversight boards, and protection of secrets.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601730004-4:
Personnel policy work by the Executive Advisory Group is reported in a memo dated 1 July 1977. E. H. Knoche, Deputy Director, wrote to the Director for information only. Much of the work grew from an August 1976 survey of staff views.

The survey sampled a quarter of staff and gauged how they saw the personnel system. In reply the group reviewed promotion rules, grievance steps, rotation, morale, and the role of women, among many topics. Rules on promotion, grievances, separation, and marriage to foreign nationals were revised as a result. Later pages take up staff rated in the lowest three percent and staff promoted above their post grade.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t02051r000200370005-4:
H.R. 4836, a House bill on satellite data use, is printed in full as introduced on 9 February 1984. The bill is cited as the Land Remote-Sensing Commercialization Act of 1984. Mr. Fuqua led a group of members in bringing it to the House.

It went to the Committee on Science and Technology for review. Early titles state findings, aims, and policy for the field. Policy calls for open access to civil satellite data for all users on fair terms. Policy also backs private running of systems that suit it, while the state keeps tasks of a public kind.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000100070001-4:
Tables and charts comparing bloc and NATO economies fill the 1960 handbook, dated June 1960. The volume is research aid A.ERA 60-4 from the Office of Research and Reports. Its stated scope is stocks, output, and national income for key goods.

Data cover 1950 and 1955 to 1959, with 1965 plan or forecast figures where found. Charts use both bar form and half-log scales for major goods. Summary tables set the United States against the USSR and China against India. One table tracks sheep counts at the start of each year by country, with footnotes on count dates.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000100160001-4:
New tables and charts mark the 1969 handbook, marked ER H 69-1 and dated July 1969. The Directorate of Intelligence states its scope as Communist and NATO economies, France included. Data in most tables cover 1955, 1960, and 1963 to 1968. Charts are shaped for use as visual aids, the preface states.

Summary tables give one page each to major states and blocs, the preface states. Mongolia gets a summary table only, since its data are thin. One table tracks natural rubber output from 1955 to 1968 by growing land. Malaysia leads that table, rising past one million metric tons in 1968. A paired table tracks man-made rubber, with NATO output rising from 1,100 to 2,640 thousand metric tons across the span.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10-01569r000100030004-4:
Board procedure for the Intelligence Advisory Board is proposed in a paper dated 13 May 1947. The Central Intelligence Group sent it out as C.I.G. 24 for board review. J. S. Barman signs as Acting Secretary of the National Intelligence Authority.

No set procedure yet exists for the board's work, the paper states. Facts are drawn from the President's letter of 22 January 1946 and past authority rulings. The paper holds that not all Director's reports need board review before they go up. A formal set of steps is urged as fit and proper. Voting slips would ride with each item sent for board views.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10-01569r000100040003-4:
Tentative structure for the Central Intelligence Group is proposed in N.I.A. 2, dated 5 February 1946. The report comes from the Director with board concurrence. It rests on the President's letter of 22 January 1946 calling for staff from State, War, and Navy.

First tasks named are daily and weekly sums of top intelligence for the President and the Authority. A survey of current foreign intelligence collection is also named as an early task. The enclosed draft directive sets an Administrative Section, a Central Reports Staff, and a Central Planning Staff. Assistant directors would be drawn one each from the State, Army, Navy, and Air contingents.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10m02313r000703910007-4:
Fate of old security memos is settled in a White House memo dated 7 December 1977. The memo, control TS 770253, carries the subject line PD/NSC 14 Follow Up. Zbigniew Brzezinski signs for the President at the close.

Review of the old action and decision memos is now done, the memo states. Six decision memos still wait, numbered 3, 7, 8, 50, 132, and 207. Memos listed at Tab A stay in force until further notice. Memos listed at Tab B are ended by the memo itself. Front sheets show the Agency routing slip and the Top Secret cover form for the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10t01930r000100090006-4:
Records held by one Agency office are counted in an annual report dated 18 October 1983. The routing sheet comes from room 7D18 at Headquarters and goes to the DDA records office. The report covers registry, mail, and support files of the office.

Total volume on hand is given as 400.30 cubic feet on the form. That marks a drop of 63.70 cubic feet from the past fiscal year figure of 464.00. Office files of letters and cases make up 243.45 cubic feet of the total. Reference books and manuals add 140.40 cubic feet more. The form also counts tapes, film, and 51 reels of 16mm microform stock.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100070003-4:
Wartime correspondence of the Coordinator of Information fills a large file catalogued under several heads. Catalogued heads include the setting up of the Coordinator's office and the naming of Allen W. Dulles to Berne. A plan for bombing oil sites in Axis-held lands is also listed.

One legible letter dated 7 August 1941 comes from the Pacific Coast Borax Company in San Francisco. It writes to Colonel William Donovan on a British borax group and its grip on boron ore trade. Later pages hold a staff work history from the Interior Department and press work in Washington. Much of the scan is rough, though the file's scope is clear from its parts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100090001-4:
Correspondence tied to William J. Donovan fills a 1941 file whose scan is rough throughout. Catalogued heads name Donovan letters and a proposal to give shelter to Jewish refugees. Only parts of the pages can be read with confidence in the copy held here.

One readable letter tells of ill health, a bout of flu, and a hope to return to work soon. An office memo takes up a confidential matter the writer wishes to raise in person. A note from James P. Baxter III treats hiring of economists, naming Calvin Hoover and Edward S. Mason in that work. The file shows the wide range of mail reaching the Coordinator's office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100120007-4:
Mixed correspondence from 1941 fills a large file catalogued under three heads. Heads listed name letters on would-be OSS recruits, a match of Hitler's speeches against his acts, and the war balance between the Allies and the Axis. A War Department letter opens the readable text.

That letter, dated 2 January 1942 as printed, tells Colonel Donovan of approval for two projects. The projects are named as the Azores and the Cape Verdes with North Africa, one to be tied to the British. A later office memo rules on Americans joining armed forces in Canada. It holds that enlistment must occur in Canada, not on United States soil, to stay within the law.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100230005-4:
Victory for China, a radio broadcast, anchors a file catalogued with mixed letters and a study of French strength. A letter dated 24 January 1942 from William J. Donovan opens the readable text. It goes to the Secretary of the Navy with a script copy enclosed.

The script was written for Senator George to broadcast to China, Donovan states. Far from clashing with Secretary Knox, the script quotes him at length with approval, the letter argues. Press tales of the broadcast got the facts wrong, Donovan adds. Later pages hold staff notes on two men weighed as contacts, with a warning against one Sardinian link. A Boston address and family names are given for that man.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100250003-4:
Basic Estimate on Psychological Warfare is set out in a long 1942 study with a clear summary. The summary states the present state of such warfare, its drive, its aims, and its task. Means at hand and means opposed are then weighed in turn.

Factors span politics, trade, minds, and news flow for four powers. The United States, Germany, Italy, and Japan each get a past and current review. Skill of the Axis three is judged in light of what each hopes to gain. Courses open to the United States are tested for fit, ease, and public acceptance. One course is picked for swift action, with steps to put it in place.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100270001-4:
Zionism and staff matters share a 1942 file catalogued under four heads. Heads listed name staff letters, Zionism aims and prospects, the Emergency Committee for Zionist Affairs, and Palestinian Jews in the British army. A study of the Zionist case fills much of the readable text.

On 29 August 1939 Zionist leaders in Geneva put a plan to Prime Minister Chamberlain, the study states. They sought Jewish units in the British army to guard Palestine and the Middle East. The reply was polite but bound the British to nothing, the study reports. When war came, 136,000 men and women in Palestine signed up for war service, it states. Use of that offer stayed small in the years that followed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100070026-4:
High level talks on Project AQUATONE are set up in a memo dated 3 May 1957. The memo goes to the Director ahead of a 6 May meeting with the President. A brief status paper for that meeting is attached as Tab A.

Four topics left out of the paper are listed for oral raising. They cover lower-grade targets, the RAINBOW program, and keeping a non-military flight capacity. The fourth treats a shift in how flights are run. The third topic is flagged as the sore one, since Air Force and Agency views split there. The split turns on what political chiefs would prefer, the memo argues, so their views should be asked outright.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100080025-4:
Use of AQUATONE photos is planned in a Top Secret memo dated October 1956. The memo goes to the Director and sets terms for a new office to handle the yield. That office would sit within the Deputy Director (Intelligence) area, the memo states.

Photo flow starts in April and climbs fast to a peak in October 1956, it projects. The new office must screen, read, and file the new material in order. The ORR photo reading division forms its core, with a machine register for files. First work is coverage plots for each flight, shared with IAC agencies. Fast scanning and spot reports follow, then deep reading of each frame.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100430008-4:
Approval of the AQUATONE plan is sought in a paper whose scan is badly garbled. Enough text reads through to show the same CL-282 proposal as the project's founding case. Twenty aircraft at 70,000 feet over the Soviet Bloc form its core claim.

A list of aims follows: firmer counts of Soviet nuclear strength and guided missile work among them. The paper then asks that the project be approved as set out. The Special Assistant for Planning and Coordination would lead it as approving officer. Buying of airframes and gear would be cleared under set provisos, it states. Contract papers would pass the General Counsel, and large sums need the Director's own approval.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200020002-4:
Cuba overflights from 29 August to 12 October 1962 are logged in a mission history file. Mission 3088, flown 29 August 1962, closed the month's approved set, the file states. SA-2 sites were first noted on that flight, it records.

Weather grades run from Category I, clear, to Category V, full overcast. With clear or light cloud, at least three quarters of targets photograph well, the file states. Daily sheets then track each planned flight against forecast and real weather. Aircraft numbers 343, 352, and 342 stand at Del Rio, Texas, in one mid-September sheet. Mission 3090 was set for 16 September to cover Guantanamo and Banes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200200002-4:
Project Dragon Lady, the Air Force U-2 effort, is laid out in briefing pages marked Secret. One page warns that the SAC program name is Secret as to mission and gear. The squadron itself, as a weather unit, stays unclassified, it states.

Aircraft facts match the type's known form: 80 foot wing, bicycle gear, pogos, and tip skids. The support office stood up in January 1956, with go-ahead to the contractor that month. First article came in September 1956, with training through June 1957. The 4028th SRS flies the U-2 from June 1957, the pages state. Contract sums run to a final settlement of 15,475,000 dollars in March 1958.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200300047-4:
Depot work from 1 August to 9 October 1969 fills a bimonthly report dated 21 October 1969. The report goes to the Director, OSA from the supply depot staff. A plan to split the report in two parts was dropped, it states.

A new receptionist began on 15 September 1969 with cover phone lines in hand. She guides callers away from the local personnel office, the report states. A fresh post office was picked for sterile mail after checks for security. A wired cage for large classified goods was judged unfit for overnight storage. Photo work for new badges drags on, held up by staff absence.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400040008-4:
R and D test results are reported to Project Headquarters in a paper dated 23 January 1957. Three parts structure the report: a master schedule, tests past the research phase, and open problems. Sources are flagged where the writer thought it wise.

One C camera flight is complete, with 1,900 exposures made at high altitude. The shutter failed to work on that flight, the report states. Nitrogen housing now guards the camera bay against frost and dirt. Total camera and housing weight stands near 750 pounds in the report. Mk II drift sight trials are set to close by 1 February 1957.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400050052-4:
Memorandum dated 29 November 1961, from Eugene P. Kiefer, Special Assistant for Technical Analysis, to the Deputy Director for Plans, transmits a draft paper on division of responsibility in the National Reconnaissance Office. Kiefer suggests the addressee argue from that paper. The reference cited is a 24 November 1961 memo about a letter to Dr Charyk on the same tangle of questions.

Recent staff talks are summarised: Air Force officers and CIA men met over past weeks to seek agreement, or at least define disagreement, on NRO organisation and procedure. One product was a 17 November memo describing the Air Force side's internal setup and its methods of communication. A security office memo of 22 November records early staff agreement on a standard security system for NRO matters.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500120008-4:
Minutes of the 11 July 1968 meeting of the Committee on Imagery Requirements and Exploitation, document COMIREX-M-43, open with an index that maps the whole session. A special briefing on a new dry film processing concept leads, followed by approval of past minutes and an operational briefing on satellites. Reports on aircraft activities in the Far East and over Cuba come next, then an NPIC report of mission highlights.

Later sections take up subcommittee reports, action items, and the status of recent committee papers. Action items include revised needs for satellite photography in mapping and charting, and a requirement for coverage of Santiago, Cuba, with the H camera. The meeting ran from 1000 to 1300 hours in the auditorium, chaired by Mr L. A. Moyer Jr, with members drawn from State, the services, NSA, DIA, and CIA.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500190010-4:
Verbatim English translation of a Soviet article from the top secret version of Military Thought, the USSR Ministry of Defense journal, forms the bulk of the record. Dated December 1961 and printed in the journal's first 1962 issue, the piece by Major General P. Vysotskiy surveys American military means for combat in space.

Vysotskiy traces United States work since 1946 on photo and radio reconnaissance satellites and on satellite missiles for nuclear strikes. Coverage extends to early warning systems such as Midas, long range radar detection, and space bombing projects including Dyna-Soar. He closes by reporting that most bombing projects remain at an early study stage, though some already draw government funding.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500390054-4:
Memorandum for the record GUS-0087/A, dated 25 May 1959, sets out how a follow-on reconnaissance vehicle should be judged. Survival comes first. The memo ties survival to avoiding detection, flying high, moving fast, and using tactics that exploit gaps in an opposing air defense system.

Further sections weigh availability, growth in power plant and load, and range needs for the 1963 to 1965 period. One passage treats a Mach 3 vehicle at 90,000 feet, where radar tracking is taken as certain. The closing pages argue that airborne electronics collection gives unique data, and that the vehicle could be the sole source if ground sites were lost for political reasons.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500390063-4:
Summary GUS-0258, current as of 15 May 1959, reports progress in the GUSTO program, an effort to design a new high altitude reconnaissance aircraft. Two teams are at work: Lockheed with Pratt and Whitney, and Convair with a second engine partner whose name is redacted. Both teams are building wind tunnel models and running structural and design studies through 30 June 1959.

Lockheed's design is judged too early to assess, though its approach is called straightforward, with a large, heavy, radar visible aircraft as the drawback. Convair's tests, by contrast, show real cuts in radar return and lift figures near estimates. Ramjet burner tests close the summary, with a larger model showing lower burn efficiency than expected.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600050032-4:
Local buying for the 1130th group at Edwards Air Force Base is governed by ATTG Reg 67-2, dated 13 March 1972. The Chief of Supply, the Director of Support, and each person who starts a request share charge of the fund. Its stated aim is tight accounting, with local buying used only when normal supply channels or in-house shops cannot meet a need.

A Purchase Request covers goods only, while a Service Request covers repair work done outside the group. Service requests go on a set form, in three copies, through the requestor's director and then to Support for final approval. Sample forms at the end show cost lines, the reason for the work, and the firm picked to do it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600050050-4:
Reporting accidents and incidents for the 1130th group is set by ATTG Reg 127-1, dated 1 June 1970, under group commander R. A. Schamber. Any accident or incident must reach the commander, deputy, or acting commander as soon as it can. The first supervisor who learns of it judges whether it is reportable, then the proper director reviews that call. If doubt remains, the commander is told at once, day or night.

Fast notice to the commander must not slow word to higher headquarters by phone or message. Duty hour calls go to the Headquarters Control Center. An attached format, drawn from AFR 127-4, lists the fields for a flash message: type of gear, cause factors, damage, injuries, and action taken.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600070012-4:
Runway choice for takeoffs and landings is fixed in standing operating procedure 50-3060-11, dated 3 May 1966. It binds all pilots using the airfield and all controllers in its tower. Landings and takeoffs are normally made on the runway lined up with the wind, as the tower advises, though a pilot may choose otherwise for safety when the tower clears it.

Jet aircraft make power checks and start their takeoff roll on the concrete part of the runway, using the turnaround pads described. Lighter aircraft may use part of the runway from side taxiways if enough length remains. Emergency landings may be made on the lakebed. An attached sketch shows touchdown areas and overrun space.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000700050022-4:
File opens with a sample IDEALIST message form, marked top secret, from the Director to air force and Joint Chiefs staff in Washington. Its Part III fields call for a mission number, route legs, and targets to be covered. That form gives the shape for the mission notices the rest of the bundle puts into use.

Project Headquarters directive 50-10-24, dated 7 February 1966, then defines operational hazard reports. A hazard is any state or act that may affect the safety of project aircraft or people. Detachment commanders must report hazards at once, look into them, and send a summary to headquarters, which directs the fix. Later pages list in-flight faults, from oil pressure to the primary camera, by mission phase.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000700050031-4:
Development Projects Division directive 50-14, dated 23 October 1961, sets the mission of its Weather Staff. The staff is made up of Air Weather Service officers attached to DPD headquarters. Its chief reports to the Acting Chief, DPD, and the staff acts as the central point for weather support needs and for all contact with the Air Weather Service.

Weather factors must be weighed in every operational plan the headquarters makes, and support must reach all DPD projects. Duties listed run from supervising the section to advising project staff. Papers bound later in the file turn to board practice: agendas sent out before meetings, written records of each session, and membership lists for an OXCART board.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800050003-4:
Progress report for 1 January to 31 March 1971 is forwarded to the Director, CIA Reconnaissance Programs, with distribution dated 6 April 1971. Its development section opens with aircraft 058, sent from Detachment H to Lockheed at Palmdale on 5 February 1971 for an exploratory IRAN inspection. Findings showed other U-2R aircraft would not need that inspection until at least 2,500 hours of total time.

Life support testing of a six-line release for parachute control ran into poor early pull test results, with more work planned at El Centro. Other flying in the quarter was varied: one sortie photographed Sierra snowfields for the Department of Commerce, and four sorties surveyed damage from the Los Angeles earthquake.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800290007-4:
Cables from Kelly Johnson of Lockheed to John Parangosky carry urgent OXCART questions. In the first, Johnson reports that aircraft 122 has flown its one allowed functional check flight before phasedown. He asks whether to proceed with phasedown, or switch to the shakedown and validation program set out in a second reference. Lockheed planning would move most OXCART flight test staff into TAGBOARD by 1 July 1967.

A second cable turns to people. Recent BLACK SHIELD activity has left crew shortages, and Johnson wants two willing backup crews for each crew out on assignment. Vendor staff in radio, air inlet control, processing, and other key areas face cuts of up to fifty percent in July under the phasedown plan, so updated guidance is needed fast.
