cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800290025-4:
Statement of significant OSA activities answers a request of 21 August 1964 from the Deputy Director for Science and Technology. The attachment describes the Office of Special Activities as formed to conceive, develop, produce, and operate covert photographic and electronic collection systems. Its staff is small: scientists and engineers working with support specialists and with industry, for speed and efficiency in the work assigned to the office.

Achievements named include the development of the U-2 and the A-12 aircraft. Praise from Dr. Edwin Land and Dr. James Killian is quoted on the office's design and sensing work. A later passage describes a project tracking objects drifting toward Soviet territory under a weather observation cover, which added knowledge of Soviet air defense deployment and capability.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800340029-4:
Draft history outline, undated in its legible pages, maps the OSA story in twenty-two chapters. Early chapters cover the Land Panel recommendation, presidential approval, a joint CIA and air force program, and funding from the Director's reserve with Bureau of the Budget review. Contracting chapters list airframe, engine, optics, cameras, and electronics, plus procurement for the air force and navy.

Detachment chapters follow, with build-up, training, deployment, and operations for each unit named. One detachment section runs from Middle East coverage in 1956 to 1958, through the May Day period and after. Closing chapters treat reorganizations from the autonomous AQUATONE project to OSA, intelligence gained from overhead reconnaissance between 1955 and 1962, and its effect on national policy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02416a000300040001-4:
Briefing slides set out a new phased deployment concept effective 31 August 1967 for IDEALIST detachments. Phase I sends a forward detachment covertly to a crisis area as fast as possible, for a single mission. Phase II adds people and gear for three to five more missions if the situation requires. Phase III places a detachment where sustained operations will run for months.

Camera comparison charts follow, giving lens, aperture, scale, and swath figures for the B camera, Delta, and optical bar cameras at 70,000 feet. Detachment G duties at Edwards Air Force Base are listed: worldwide staging, flight testing of new gear, and pilot training. The file ends with the mission approval chain, from 303 Committee approval through alert, plan, and go or no-go messages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030005-4:
Office memorandum dated 1 May 1947 sends a redraft of travel procedure material for the CIG Administrative Manual. The sending chief notes insertions his office made: a section on temporary duty in the United States, an information for the traveler section, and added material under motor transportation. The Transportation Section chief is asked to review, correct, and return the draft.

The manual text follows the traveler through each step. Initiation, clearance, and approval come first, then the preliminary interview, travel order, clearance certificate, notice of departure, and confirmation of arrival. Rules cover advances of funds, granted on a bond of indemnity, and the traveler's duties on the road. Later pages treat vehicle accident investigation, storage and repair of official vehicles, and records of dispatch and service.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050058-4:
National Security Council order dated 1 December 1950 delegates a wide list of powers to the Deputy Director for Administration, CIA, and his assistant. The delegation is made by the council's Executive Secretary, under a council resolution approved 26 September 1947 and section 101 of Public Law 253. Personnel actions lead the list: appointment, termination, direction, and general administration of staff.

Allowances for civilian staff abroad and transfers between stations follow, with travel and shipment of household goods, cars, effects, and dependents covered. Other delegated powers reach tort claims under the Federal Tort Claims Act, execution of contracts, publication of notices, property rules for council staff, and certification of vouchers. Walter B. Smith, Director of Central Intelligence, concurs on the same date. The order takes effect the day it is signed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050148-4:
National Security Council resolution, certified as approved on 26 September 1947, authorizes the council's Executive Secretary to control, supervise, and administer council funds. The powers match those a department head holds over his own funds, including the right to delegate. Delegation may run to staff of the Executive Secretary's office. It may also run to officials of the Central Intelligence Agency. Control of spending stays with the council throughout.

An order of 1 October 1947 then delegates in detail. Fourteen numbered powers cover personnel, allowances abroad, and transfers. Travel advances up to 1,000 dollars, emergency travel, and bonds of certifying officers are also covered. Some powers may also be used by the Chief, Budget and Finance Branch, or the Chief, Fiscal Division, CIA. The order takes effect 26 September 1947, with concurrence by the Director of Central Intelligence.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050184-4:
Exchange of letters in August 1946 settles where the Central Intelligence Group's job classification sheets will be kept. The group's letter of 14 August 1946 argues that its work demands the utmost security. Classification sheets and documents on members' positions should therefore rest in a place with more than usual safeguards. Control over who may enter the area holding them is also required.

The United States Civil Service Commission replies on 28 August 1946. Its executive director, L. A. Moyer, states that the arrangement in the group's letter meets with the commission's approval. The group also asks that facilities provided for the Strategic Services Unit pass to it. The request names locked safes and office space in Room C2C2 of the New War Department Building. The transfer would follow that unit's liquidation, as its selected staff join the group.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200100007-4:
Report dated 2 April 1953 covers March operations of the Records Management and Distribution Branch. Leave stays low this month: one in Records Management, three in Mail Control, one at the Records Center. Nine new applicants were interviewed, eight recruited by Personnel. The analyst detailed to the Jackson Commission and the courier in Transportation both serve the full month, as before. A new system is being built to account weekly for couriers' free time, for inclusion in the weekly statistics.

Free time results for two weeks are given: one percent in the first, four and a half percent in the second. The lower second figure is tied to couriers assigned to OCI jobs. Project 1-53, rearranging and indexing distribution material, is complete. Project 2-53 remains at ninety-eight percent for want of folders. Project 3-53 stands at ninety-five percent.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00355a000100020036-4:
Course outline for Section II, National Security, National Policy and Strategic Planning, plans thirty lectures on how policy is made and carried out. Scope runs from the meaning of national security to the instruments of national policy. It takes in the government's security organization, and the making and execution of policy. Strategic planning follows, with the role of intelligence in support of all of it. A survey of settled policies, objectives, and measures closes the scope list.

Named lectures include a six part run on psychological instruments of national policy. The run ends with content analysis, and its use in judging enemy intent from propaganda. The armed forces as an instrument of policy are treated by the Department of Defense. The final lectures survey the work of the National Security Council. They also cover the security measures in force, their objectives, and how far they have succeeded.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100040008-4:
Essay on how national estimates relate to national action argues that a report is not an end in itself. It is a tool, a resource for the forming, carrying out, and review of government action. Material is needed in forms and amounts that vary with the action in hand. The central problem is therefore a flow problem: matching the product against the current needs of action, short and long range.

Knowing what action officials will face begins with policy papers, the essay argues. Those papers state the nation's aims abroad in concrete form, as policies, decisions, and pledges. Staff must know NSC papers in detail, not casually. A worked case closes the visible argument. If a revolt is found likely to succeed in a named country, a review of past action on the Tito case would serve the first phase of action well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100150033-4:
Transcript, made in April 1952, of the Ford Motor Company's management development film strip and record, Coaching the Management Team. The narration builds its whole case on one comparison: a manager is a football coach. The president's phrase management team is no idle figure of speech, the script argues. A manager, like a coach, is judged not by what he does himself. He is judged by what his people do under his direction. The game is won or lost on the field.

The program's first steps follow the coach's. Personal histories are gathered, as a coach studies his material at the season's start. Appraisals of each man's performance are then reviewed with the superior. The review teaches much about personnel problems. Practice at the right things, planned by the coach, is the only road to a winning team. The script ends ready for the development work itself, player by player.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00037a000200010001-4:
Bound file of TR(G) Weekly Summary Reports runs from May 1952 to October 1953, fronted by an index of the series. The index lists eighteen numbered groups of memos from the Deputy Director of Training (General) to the Director of Training, with dates week by week. Two early memos set the form: a deadline time for the weekly reports, and suggested terms of reference for them.

A sample report of 27 February 1953 tells of training bulletins to carry remarks from the Ninth Agency Orientation Course. The speakers named are the Vice President and General Walter B. Smith. Undersecretary of State William H. Jackson is also named. Later pages note forty-seven new staff at one week's indoctrination program, a low trend against a former one hundred a week. As of 23 May, 691 staff were enrolled in Office of Training courses.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100030008-4:
Message from General Walter Bedell Smith, Director of Central Intelligence, dated January 1952, speaks to the whole Agency. The past year left no chance to meet the staff, he says, after a year spent on reorganization. That work, directed by the National Security Council on the Dulles committee report, is called annoying and painful, above all for those moved, transferred, and renamed. Most of it is over, and the benefits should be good.

Weaknesses found in the Agency are then named in plain terms. Staff are scattered over almost thirty buildings in Washington, many in temporary buildings called rabbit wards: hot in summer, cold in winter, dingy, and bad for morale. Funds and staff limits on the sister services are noted. The close sets the standard for hiring: talent is limited, and beyond a point the Agency cannot get people of the knowledge, ability, character, and integrity it demands.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100070013-4:
Memorandum dated 16 November 1953 from the Chief, Management Training Division, sent through the Director of Training to the Assistant Deputy Director for Intelligence, on building sound human relations in CIA. Good relations at work are presented as the product of sound management. The training effort behind the note had run for twelve months with supervisors across most of the Agency.

A long list gives the management problems raised again and again in training groups. They include poor communication up, down, and across, weak personnel work, no clear statement of basic policy for supervisors, and unclear duties for units and for single staff. Senior staff who bypass set lines of duty, and supervisors too busy doing work themselves to direct others, also figure in the list.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100080003-4:
Course description for the Intelligence Staff Officer Course run by the Intelligence Division, Air Command and Staff School, at Maxwell Air Force Base, Alabama. The course lasts twenty-two weeks, runs twice a year, and takes seventy students a class. It serves field grade officers with seven or more years of service and picked civilian staff at GS-11 or above, all holding Top Secret clearance.

Its mission is to build skill in the command and staff tasks met at wing level and above, and in solving staff problems tied to intelligence work. About fifty-eight percent of set time goes to committee work or single assignments on real staff problems. Field trips, guest talks, and a block on air weapons, covering atomic, biological, and chemical weapons, are also described.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000200040006-4:
Office of Training regulation setting up policy, program, duties, and procedures for training evaluation across the Agency. All teaching run or backed by CIA, in groups or one to one, inside or outside the Agency, is to carry an evaluation method matching the rules set here. Only the CIA Orientation Course is left out of that reach.

The Training Evaluation Branch of the Assessment and Evaluation Staff owns the program. Its work covers building a testing program, watching and measuring traits of character in class, and reporting student results, conduct, and special gifts or problems to the right people. Material further in covers interest testing, and the weak link found between what a person likes and how well that person later performs at work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100030001-4:
Handbook of operations dated January 1952 for the Allowance Branch of the Division of Foreign Service Personnel, Department of State. The book serves as a working reference for branch staff and as training material for Foreign Service and departmental staff sent to the branch. It covers allowances, post differentials, and linked gains for American civilian staff serving in foreign areas.

Contents run from the law behind the payments, through the Foreign Service Act of 1946 and the orders and government-wide rules that govern them, to the branch and how it is run. Quarters, cost-of-living, and representation payments are each defined and worked through. One section explains how post rates are set from reports on quarters costs sent in by posts at least twice a year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100080024-4:
Extract from volume one of a Defense commission report. The pages run from fifty-five to sixty. Findings and recommendations are given on special pays. The full title names incentive and hazardous duty pays. One theme runs through the summary. High effectiveness in the armed forces is the goal. Terms of service should not change without warning.

Changes should take effect only after notice. Members hurt by a change should be shielded. Saving clauses can do that shielding. Medical and dental care should be wide. Base pay should track a cost-of-living index. All extra pays should be shares of base pay. Congress should pass a law for that formula. Insurance advice follows in the extract. Survivors of members killed in service gain more. Double indemnity of twenty thousand dollars is urged. Flying, submarine, and parachute pays are then weighed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100020012-4:
Brief for the Basic Intelligence Course, dated 10 December 1952. The Office of Training offered the course. It formed the first stage of post-entry training. New Agency professional staff were its students. Three subjects made up the course. The first covered principles, methods, and practices. The second covered intelligence and national security. The third covered the world situation. Communism and the USSR got special weight there.

Teaching used several methods in turn. Staff lectures and guest speakers both featured. Guided discussion periods were built in. Assigned readings supported the lectures. Problems and projects gave practice in methods. Each trainee prepared a country estimate. That project trained research and analysis skills. Map work and clear writing were stressed too. A reading improvement course ran alongside. Clarity and accuracy were demanded throughout.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100020076-4:
Summary of external training for fiscal 1953. The Programs Division compiled the survey. Courses run by other bodies fill the pages. A Western Europe seminar leads the list. The Foreign Service Institute hosted it. State, aid, and defense staff attended together. United States aims in Europe were studied first. German and French aims were compared with them.

A special program on Central Asia follows. Chinese Central Asia filled the summer session. Russian Central Asia filled the fall term. Climate, farming, and industry were covered. Languages and religions were covered too. A Near East program ran a full year. Intensive language and area work sat in the United States. Language courses fill the later pages. Chinese courses are set out in stages. A beginner course led to an intermediate one. Polish reading gets its own entry.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100040010-4:
Set of CIA training regulations, with a contents list. Issued rules cover Agency training facilities under Public Law 110. Requests for non-CIA training are covered. Attendance at Defense colleges is covered too. Detail of officers as students gets a rule. Indoctrination and orientation rules follow. Briefing of military attaches has its own rule.

Draft rules and planned rules are also listed. One issued rule dates from 21 February 1952. It covers non-CIA facilities under the law. The Director of Training gives final approval. Office heads recommend candidates for training. Training must raise a person's capability. Home and foreign schools both qualify as facilities. Trade and labor bodies appear in the list. Later rules cover lecture attendance at Defense schools. Rosters of approved staff must be kept. Liaison with the schools is assigned as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100060009-4:
Memorandum for the record dated 9 July 1953. It covers group meeting two for Agency intelligence directorate liaison officers. The meeting itself sat on 8 July 1953. Officers from many intelligence offices attended. Intermediate intelligence training headed the business. A summary of one course was presented. That course served scientific analysts in June.

The course had three basic parts. Principles and doctrines of intelligence came first. A scientific seminar on the USSR followed. Case work projects from the science office came third. Student critiques praised the course for analysts. Grades seven through fourteen were named as fitting. Similar small courses could run each quarter. Two weeks of full-time study was the pattern. Division chiefs might sit in or join panels. Office training needs close the record. One office needed mainly Russian and German. Economic skill was hard to find there.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000040215-4:
List of position numbers, job titles, and grades. The tables carry an MTS heading and copy markings. A commanding officer heads one visible list. His grade is colonel, with code 0066. An aircraft maintenance technician appears first in one column. Operations officers and pilots follow in the tables. Photo navigators hold lieutenant colonel and major grades.

Intelligence posts appear in several rows. An intelligence officer holds the grade of major. An intelligence operations specialist is a master sergeant. Clerks, typists, and admin staff are listed too. A flight surgeon appears among the posts. A physiological training specialist is a staff sergeant. Later pages repeat the list in fuller form. Agency project leadership posts open that later list. A project director and operations director are named. Weather officers and materiel staff close the visible rows.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000100137-4:
Contract schedule headed Schedule Part I, Contract Work. A table of contents maps the whole schedule. Contract form pages come first in the list. The index of the schedule follows them. Part two covers rates, fixed prices, and reserves. Part three covers anticipated costs in the work. Special instructions form another listed part.

Later parts cover still more contract ground. One part treats a named contract subject in full. General provisions close the contents list. Corporate certification pages open the file itself. An officer certified signing for the contractor company. The contract was duly signed for that corporation. Its governing body gave the authority claimed. Deep in the text, cost rules appear. Approval of a cost does not settle allowability. Notice duties fall on the contractor as well. Suits or claims by subcontractors must be reported. Written notice must reach the Agency Contracting Officer promptly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000130161-4:
General provisions for a supply contract, on Standard Form 32. The form was prescribed by the General Services Administration. Its edition dates from November 1949. Definitions open the provisions text. Secretary and Contracting Officer are defined first. Subcontracts are defined to include purchase orders. Changes form the second numbered provision.

A Contracting Officer may order changes in writing. Drawings, designs, and specifications can be changed. Goods made specially for the government are covered. No notice to sureties is required for changes. Later provisions treat taxes in detail. Price can fall when a tax is removed. Invoices must state such changes as separate items. The tax behind each change must be identified. Refund and drawback terms follow in the text. The set runs to a full standard form. It reads as the boilerplate half of a supply deal.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000160041-4:
Agency letter contract number EC-200 with Hycon Manufacturing Company. The company sat in Pasadena, California. The letter went to its vice-president's attention. An order is placed for equipment and supplies. Services are covered by the order as well. Exhibit A gives the fuller detail. That exhibit is made part of the contract.

On acceptance, the contractor must proceed at once. Materials must be procured without delay. Time schedules in Exhibit A govern delivery. Any need to extend those schedules must be flagged. The government must hear of it immediately. A definitive contract must be negotiated soon. A detailed cost breakdown comes first. All cost elements must be shown in it. Direct costs, indirect costs, and profit are listed. Security restrictions get their own numbered clause. The contractor must conform to those restrictions. Contact with the Contracting Officer is directed on security matters.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000100070001-4:
Memorandum dated 17 July 1953 to the Agency Director of Training. A planning procedure for training films is proposed. Films should use all fitting resources of the office. They should sit fully inside the curricula. Technical effect as teaching aids is the goal. Military and commercial practice was reviewed first. A settled procedure has grown up in those fields.

Set principles underlie that procedure, the memo states. Planning needs deep knowledge of the curriculum. Training methods specialists supply that knowledge. Technical accuracy of content must be secured separately. The principles run from first idea to classroom use. A film team structure is set out later. A script writer and project role are named. Added members come from both training branches. The chief instructor of the course concerned joins. Chiefs of related units may join as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100060018-4:
Office memorandum dated 8 September 1949, an interim survey report. The Liaison Branch of the collection office is its subject. The Agency Management Officer sent it to the Assistant Director. Comparisons reach back to surveys of 1947 and 1948. Substantial improvements were found since those surveys. They are called commendable in the report. Operations had been greatly simplified overall.

Much collection now happens through informal action. Formal directives are no longer needed for it. Inter-library loan service changed the branch's work. Document procurement shrank as that service grew. Record-keeping was greatly simplified as well. Work quality of professional staff had risen. All significant non-IAC agencies were being exploited. Researchers got positive help with outside contacts. Action items close the report text. One transfers an allocation of materials between offices. Another seeks evaluation of information furnished to requesters.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100070008-4:
Memorandum dated 28 February 1950 on the Industrial Register. The Agency Assistant Director for Collection and Dissemination wrote it. Comments are keyed to a management report's headings. The Executive and COAPS received the memo. First product cards have now been prepared. A test run of those cards was made. Isolating faults and correcting them has begun.

The typing backlog has been liquidated, it states. Extra hands were made available temporarily. The Executive supplied those hands for the task. Dissemination of ICF cards still weighs heavily. Avoiding it seems hard under an old commitment. That commitment dates from taking over the Washington Document Center. Army and Air Force both insist on continuation. Soundings on the subject were made several times. Navy takes only some of the cards. About ten of eighty industrial categories interest Navy. Overseas Army commands call the cards vital.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100100004-4:
Notice of a meeting of Agency Area Top Secret Control Officers. The meeting was set for Friday 12 September 1952. It sat in Room 2125, M Building, at two o'clock. Many problems face an efficient control system. Full attendance was requested for the discussion. Installation of a uniform system heads the list. Control cards would carry that uniform system. A sample card is attached as an annex.

Control of documents in draft comes next. Drafts should enter control once readable in form. Multiple numbering of one document is a problem. Outside agencies sometimes send documents straight to areas. Actions on one document may each get numbers. One basic number per document is recommended instead. The originating area would assign that number. Signature records and cover sheets are discussed too. Their effectiveness and refinement were open questions. A dispatch procedure with five card copies follows.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100140019-4:
File built around a memorandum for record dated 20 April 1949. An indorsement of 20 April forms its opening pages. A Rear Admiral signed as collection chief. Disposition of foreign language documents is the issue. His office cannot concur in the study comments. Captured enemy documents drive that non-concurrence. Responsibility of the Foreign Documents Branch is disputed.

The attached memo gives the collection office's comments. A draft survey of the Foreign Documents Branch was examined. Pages seven through fifteen were the part reviewed. Tabs A and B of the draft were included. Wording changes are proposed paragraph by paragraph. One study was conceived and developed by OCD itself. ORE was only one agent in its preparation. Translation requests get a firm view later. They should not route through the Reference Center. Existing directives already govern Agency requesters on that point.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100190023-4:
Memorandum dated 8 September 1953 forwarding a survey report. It went to the Acting Deputy Director, Administration. The Chief of Administration, DD/P, sent it. Personnel type positions in EE Division were re-evaluated. Right location for those functions is one question. Minimum staff for them is the second question. Economic and efficient performance is the test.

Only five days were allotted for the survey. Scope was limited by that short time. Functions, records, and procedures were studied as available. Workload data at hand was used in the study. Technical advice came from Agency personnel specialists. The division situation was abnormal in some respects. A current reduction drove high personnel activity. The division held a table of ten slots. Eight of those slots were filled at the time. Military personnel correspondence fills much of one function. Relay of information to the field is its core.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200070016-4:
Functions statement for a Real Estate and Construction Division. The Office of Procurement and Supply is its parent. The overall program of the Agency is directed. Design and building fall within the program. Appraisal and purchase of property are included. Use, repair, and upkeep are also covered. Utility work is part of the same charge.

Space purchase stays outside its main scope. Building upkeep and utilities stay with General Services there. Field building work receives its staff lead. Technical lead of field work is also its role. Advice to Agency officials is provided by the unit. Proposed programs and projects prompt that advice. Design and engineering needs are set there. Plans and specs are prepared under it. Building work is watched, under cover where needed. A reporting system on projects is developed later. Training of field building staff is covered too.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200080015-4:
Draft management analysis dated 11 July 1951 on field procurement. Personnel field procurement activity is the subject. Findings open, citing an earlier survey report. That report came from the Personnel Studies staff. Its date was 31 May 1951. Its findings were found accurate and applicable. Field recruitment consumed about half the staff effort.

Only about thirteen percent of new employees came through it. The division chief accepted that earlier report fully. Analysis of procurement failure makes up the body. Factors behind the failure are isolated one by one. Agency job requirements were never clearly set. Priorities were not communicated to those needing them. Workload for the next year rests on expressed need. A recruitment total in it is redacted here. Coordination with other field activities was lacking. That gap deprived personnel of possible assistance. Processing of personnel actions was slowed by it. The field activity was also understaffed throughout.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200150008-4:
Part three of the Agency indexing study covers machines for searching recorded information. The IBM Electronic Scanning System, Mark III, is described. A position as of April 1953 opens it. No machine now being made fully suits the task. Searching large recorded counts needs better gear. IBM's Poughkeepsie engineering laboratory studied possible designs. A Mark I model was built in 1950.

That model serves trial purposes at present. A Mark II design followed but was not built. Mark III adds further gains recently made. Punched IBM cards are the searching medium throughout. Tie-in with standard IBM gear marks the design. Ordinary work combines with the scanning system. Types of combination for searches are listed. Conditioning of searches receives detailed treatment later. Stated maximums can rise with minor changes. Need for such increase governs that chance. Security information markings run through these pages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200150017-4:
Journal article on machine searching of recorded facts. Chemical technology problems drive the searching need. Finding needed facts is tedious and time consuming. Matching facts scattered across papers takes labor. Patents and lab notebooks scatter those facts. Reports and private files hold more of them. Punched cards have proved their value there.

Searching and matching both benefit from the cards. A continuing growth program builds on that record. Powerful new means for using facts are its aim. Chemical writings are the article's main concern. Side operations receive briefer treatment alongside. Recording, storing, copying, and circulating information are covered. Microfilm and microcards ease that work greatly. Xerography is named among the helpful ways. Fixed fields on cards get analysis later. Accounting cards served narrow fields well. Infrared absorption spectra files are the example. Assigned fields caused few troubles in such files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200220055-4:
Tab C procedure for obtaining refunds on unused tickets. Flow chart symbols open the tab. A proposed procedure for processing refunds follows. Only Agency Transportation Division tickets run through the division. Finance Division prepares the refund request form. An original and three copies are prepared. The original is perforated for detachment midway. Its bottom half goes forward to the carrier.

Forms are padded one hundred sheets per pad. Every fourth sheet is perforated in the pad. Only the address and signature lines stay blank. The subject shows the ticket type involved. Air, rail, or sea tickets are indicated. The traveler for whom it was set is named. Copies are filed in two places afterwards. One copy joins the master refund file folder. Notations there are written by hand, not typed. A second copy joins the proper case file. The original top half waits for the refund.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00259a000100030002-4:
Minutes of an OTR staff meeting held Tuesday 12 October 1954. Career Service Plans for all training personnel lead the record. A regulation defining that policy is being published. Each employee may state his desired development path. Training, rotation, or reassignment wishes are recorded. Supervisors review each plan for their employees. Modification or approval follows from that review.

The OTR Career Service Board acts on both comments. Benefit to individual and Agency is its test. Division chiefs submit plans on a set timetable. Language and Area Training School submits in January. Plans and Research Staff follows in February. Assessment and Evaluation submits in March. School heads and information files appear later. A central file on school heads is contemplated. Travel vouchers receive procedural attention in the minutes. For security reasons the office keeps preparing travel orders. Each traveler must still submit his own material.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100070002-4:
Senate report number 90 on promoting progress of science. The Labor and Public Welfare Committee submitted it. Its date is 3 March 1949 in the heading. Mr. Thomas of Utah presented the report. Senate bill 247 is the measure accompanied. Seven senators introduced that bill jointly. The committee reports favorably without amendments made. Adoption of the bill is recommended straightforwardly.

A general statement opens the report body. Nationwide demand for a science foundation ran for years. Presidents recognized the need in official statements. Hearings and debates of several Congresses recognized it. Outstanding scientists and educators voiced the same need. Prompt enactment is urged in the statement. Analysis by sections of the bill follows. Section one gives the short title there. That title names a 1949 act in this draft. Section two establishes the Foundation as independent. Its seat in the executive branch is specified. Membership of the Foundation is analyzed next.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100120024-4:
General Counsel memo dated 1 August 1952 on work weeks. Staff at certain training sites are its subject. Courses run by the Agency are also covered. A Training Office memo of 1 July 1952 is cited. Extra hours pay for that staff is the question. Proposed rules could be adopted on terms.

Two findings would support adopting those rules. Laws that apply might allow rather than bind. Or else, the Agency might be exempt from them. Its several organic acts could supply that exemption. Current pay schedules rest on a 1945 act. The Federal Employees Pay Act of 1945 governs. Extra hours pay rides on that same statute. The act applies to all executive branch civilians. Exemptions listed there do not cover the Agency. The Agency was subject from its start date. Rule-making power is analyzed in later pages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100120033-4:
Bureau of the Budget study dated 18 May 1950 on time studies. Law limits in the federal government are examined. The Management Improvement Branch prepared the study. Time and motion methods arise often in planning. Methods studies raise the question repeatedly. A wide opinion holds laws bar them. Somewhere in general law something is said to stand against them.

Research identified the extent of limits. Only two items of law target time studies directly. Both apply only to a limited area. Other enactments swayed the general feeling nonetheless. The two measures are the same lines inserted. Military and naval funding acts carry them annually. Their text bars spending appropriated funds on studies. Past episodes fill the research pages. Recording clocks figure in an 1898 hearing episode. A General Deficiency Appropriation Act was the vehicle. Treasury had bought clocks while the limit was pending. Committee members pressed the timing of that purchase.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100140022-4:
Bundle of topic papers from an overseas Agency administrative activity. Travel data sheets lead the papers in this copy. Effective 1 February, all travel vouchers change handling. Personnel vouchers would be computed in Washington. Travel data sheets would be furnished per traveler. Travelers departing Washington after that date are covered. Computations still rely on discussion meanwhile.

Documentation other than data sheets fills the gap. Forwarding of sheets by the activity is the action. Annual leave forms the next topic paper. Current leave regulations are called very unfair there. Employees arriving from headquarters feel that unfairness most. Cover support systems are weighed in later papers. One system pays bills in a different manner. Security under it is judged not good. Duplication of available facilities would also result. Billeting office facilities are named among those available. Another system is easy to handle instead. Its security is likewise judged not good.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100150085-4:
Notes for public utterances on Agency functions. Preliminary comments divide audiences into three categories. The general public forms the first category. Uncleared groups with intelligence training form the second. Cleared groups with considerable knowledge form the third. Basic thoughts hold the same line throughout all. Speaker problems differ very much by audience.

The public poses purely an information problem here. Ordinary persons have barely heard of the Agency. Intelligence groups want techniques and function distribution. Reserve units exemplify that second audience type. Higher cleared groups know a considerable amount already. Specific problems and operations interest them most. Outlines must be completely flexible in consequence. These notes approach the uninformed public chiefly. An outline rather than a speech results again. Statutory provisos anchor the later discussion sections. Police and subpoena powers are denied the Agency. A second proviso protects departmental intelligence work. Departments continue collecting and evaluating their own intelligence.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100210033-4:
Memorandum dated 14 December 1951 on revenue bureau relations. Problems with the Bureau of Internal Revenue are traced. History of clandestine tax participation is outlined. Discussions reach back as far as 1943. The Commissioner of Internal Revenue was a party. The Director of Strategic Services was the other. Assurances of cooperation were given back then.

A working arrangement joined three offices together. The Agency General Counsel's office was one party to it. The strategic services office and the bureau followed. Letters of early 1945 evidence those arrangements. One is dated 29 January 1945 there. Another is dated 6 February 1945. A letter of 26 December 1946 confirmed adoption onward. Procedures for filing income tax returns were covered. Withholding tax filing was discussed in early 1947. Later talks reached the Assistant Secretary level. A liaison channel was established as a result.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100210114-4:
Directory of liaison officers for pending legislation, dated 29 October 1947. Department heads designated those officers government-wide. Reports on enrolled bills also run through them. The Legislative Reference Division compiled the list. The Bureau of the Budget is that division's home. Departments are listed with their heads named. The officer to contact follows each head.

Agriculture heads the department list in the directory. Clinton P. Anderson is its named Secretary. Carl R. Sapp takes legislative reports there. The Air Force entry names F. Stuart Symington. The Army entry names Kenneth C. Royall. Commerce names William Averell Harriman as Secretary. Its solicitor Adrian Fisher is the attention line. Defense names James Forrestal as its Secretary. Interior, Justice, Labor, and Navy follow in order. Agencies and commissions fill the later pages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100220005-4:
Memo dated 1 October 1953 on easing retirement. A liberalized pension system for Agency employees is proposed. Five questions frame the problem for the Director. Duties variance from average employees is the first. Unusual working conditions might warrant more liberal payments. Whether a pension can work as pay is the second. Law would be required for any change.

Form of that law is the third question. A separate Agency retirement act is one form. Amendment to the Civil Service Retirement Act is another. Factors in computing payments form the fourth question. Weight given those factors forms the fifth. A congressional committee study is noted as a factor. Retirement policy for federal personnel is under study. Elliott Kaplan leads that commissioned study effort. Blocks to easing appear in the later pages. Defining risky duty clearly is the first block. Describing it adequately in law is equally hard.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000200090081-4:
An untitled paper weighs the future of a wartime intelligence service and its standing with other agencies, Congress, and the public. Its opening puzzle is plain: a secret service would seem to have no need of public relations, yet in American government it does. The paper points to the FBI as the clearest case beside it. Under J. Edgar Hoover, well handled publicity lifted the Bureau from obscurity in the gangster years after the First World War.

That public standing, the paper argues, brought steady funding and real power on Capitol Hill. It also gave the Bureau unusual freedom from meddling by other parts of the executive branch. The lesson pressed on readers is that goodwill is a form of protection for a secret agency. Public favour, once won, is treated here as a working asset.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400050001-4:
Presented to the Senate in March 1953, a long report studies hiring and use of staff across the federal government. It grew out of work by the Subcommittee on Federal Manpower Policies under Senate Resolution 53. The stated aim was policy for the best use of civilian staff during a national emergency. Findings, conclusions, and advice fill the report, which was ordered printed with illustrations on 20 March 1953.

Contents run from a summary of findings into parts on hiring, placement, and staff use in the many agencies surveyed. The committee behind it was the Senate Committee on Post Office and Civil Service, chaired by Frank Carlson. For Agency files, the report set the wider manpower rules debate inside which CIA hiring then sat.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400090034-4:
Travel expenses for staff who resign overseas form the gap a Legal Staff memorandum of 14 February 1950 asks the Chief of CSS to close. Reviewing contract forms had shown that Agency rules left parts of the overseas travel problem uncovered. Administrative Instruction 30-1 of 6 January 1950 said nothing on paying travel home for an employee who quits abroad. It also ignored any debt owed back where the person left before a set term of service.

The legal base named runs from Public Law 600 to Public Law 110 and the Foreign Service Regulations. Under the older law, new appointees had to promise twelve months of service before travel costs were paid. The memorandum presses for rules matching that bargain when service ends early.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400160072-4:
Regulations in this untitled text govern payment, from the funds named in the order directing travel, for moving staff between stations on permanent duty. Covered costs include transport of the employee's immediate family and of household goods and personal effects. Travel must follow the order of the head of the office or an official he names. The employee's own travel costs are tied to the Subsistence Expense Act of 1926, as amended.

Family is defined in detail: spouse, children under twenty-one, stepchildren, adopted children, and dependent parents of the worker are counted in. Standard government travel rules govern the parts they cover. Age limits lift where a child cannot support himself through bodily or mental limits. The text reads as a full rule sheet for a transfer move.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400180034-4:
Home leave rights after a move between agencies occupy an untitled General Counsel memorandum of 20 November 1952, answering the Assistant Director for Personnel. It replies to a note of 3 November 1952 and to questions on State Department transfers. The reading offered is that most such staff keep their standing under the governing orders. Keeping certain sets of employment unbroken is treated as vital to that result.

The memorandum works through how leave builds up across a transfer and what a past ruling of the Comptroller General's office contributes. Pay already drawn and leave already earned under the State Department are weighed against a bar on double counting. The scan is rough in the middle pages, yet the legal thread on continuity stays legible throughout.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500050028-4:
Under file number B-106300, a Comptroller General letter of 12 August 1952 replies to the Director of the Central Intelligence Agency. The Director had written on 29 October 1951 seeking a decision on planned hiring of retired Foreign Service officers. A State Department report, awaited before the answer could be given, had now arrived. At issue is both the hiring itself and the officers' right to keep retirement annuities in new government jobs.

The letter quotes the act of 31 July 1894, which bars holding a second paid office where the first pays twenty-five hundred dollars or more. Questions framed by the Director follow that quote, each resting in part on those words. The ruling then takes the questions in order, on facts the file supplies.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500070026-4:
Consultants' travel and pay raise several points that certifying officers put to the Office of General Counsel on 3 December 1951. The finance officers say the rules need clearing up and ask for a ruling on each point. First they quote the rules in force, in brief. A consultant may claim travel between home or place of business and Washington or another duty place. Per diem in place of subsistence runs even over weekends and holidays spent away on Agency duty.

Rules on expenses between duty points are quoted next. The questions that follow grow out of hard cases at the pay desk, where a wrong call meant paying from public funds without cover. The routing runs through the Acting Chief of the Finance Division.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500090006-4:
Printed as Report Number 2162 on Union Calendar Number 789, H.R. 7824 is the bill that became the Performance Rating Act of 1950. Mr. Murray of Tennessee brought it in on 28 March 1950, and it went to the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service. The committee reported it with amendments on 29 May 1950. Struck and italic passages show the changes in the print.

Section 2 first defines department across the executive branch, the courts' offices, and the District of Columbia. Later sections set who is covered, how rating plans run, and how ratings may be challenged. This copy is the bill text itself as the House took it up, distinct from the committee report that argues for it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500100013-4:
A suggested guide for sound dealings with organised employee groups in the federal service was adopted by the Federal Personnel Council on 9 August 1951. A special subcommittee drafted it, and the Council revised it over several meetings. The Civil Service Commission issued the guide from its Washington office on 23 August 1951. Practice in some agencies is reflected in its terms, the foreword notes.

The first policy point is that any arrangement with unions or associations must respect the authority of the federal government under the Constitution. Further sections cover recognition, talks, and the handling of grievances. The guide tries to give managers a shared line: deal with organised staff fairly, while keeping the government's power to manage intact.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500120002-4:
Mixed pages make up a file copy tied to leave legislation: Senate debate from the Congressional Record sits beside the printed text of leave law. The debate passage argues over inflation, with one senator charging that speculators grow rich while wage earners fall behind. Later pages turn to postal and leave provisions in statutory form. Rates for second-class mailing and rules on advertising content appear in one proviso.

The closing sections print the Annual and Sick Leave Act's own terms. Temporary and indefinite postal staff are credited with annual leave at fifteen days a year and sick leave at ten. An effective date of 6 January 1952 is set, and approval on 30 October 1951 is shown. The bundle reads as a lawyer's working file rather than one clean document.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500140019-4:
Civil service retirement and Social Security are compared in a Retirement Division memorandum dated 19 February 1952. A pending plan to give probational indefinite standing to staff hired from a register drives the question. Such staff would naturally ask whether they stay under Social Security or move under civil service retirement, and which leaves them better off. Under present rules, the emergency-indefinite worker sits under Social Security.

His tax is one and a half per cent of wages up to thirty-six hundred dollars a year, with rises already set for later years. Government service counts with outside work toward old-age and survivor benefits. A worker under civil service retirement instead pays a share of his whole salary into the fund. The memorandum weighs the two side by side.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500140082-4:
Disability benefits for injuries in training are set out in a Legal Staff paper of March 1950 for the Chief of Training. It answers questions raised about harm suffered during instruction. First aid on the spot is assumed in every case. Where an injury is grave, whoever is in charge is expected to call a doctor and arrange transport at once.

The legal trouble starts with payment: who pays when care comes from a private source, or when government care goes to someone not plainly entitled to it? Side questions cover long hospital stays, pay lost while hurt, and death payments to survivors. The paper also separates vested rights from courtesies based on a trainee's status. Trainers got a rule sheet for the worst day of a course.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000700060115-4:
Legal Staff comments of 16 March 1950 take a proposed CPFF contract form apart clause by clause. The first note strikes the word adequate from the opening clause as needless. The second clause gets a full rewrite, so it says the government wants research and development work done, plus building of equipment or articles to be named. Qualified personnel and facilities are promised in the third clause, paid on a cost-plus-a-fixed-fee basis.

The fourth preamble clause should simply go, the writer says. A fresh fifth clause covers how the planned work will call for secrecy and special handling. Later notes reach the articles on cost, inspection, and ending the contract. Two copies of this comment letter sit in the file; this one carries the fuller set of numbered points.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000700100020-4:
A memorandum of agreement between the United States and a contractor, whose name is redacted, buys the rights in an author's manuscript. The government seeks all right, title, and interest, including full publication rights across the world. Added chapters and separate but related monographs travel with the main work. Article I records the contractor's transfer of those rights to the United States Government.

The term all right, title, and interest is then spelled out at length. Later articles deal with payment, the handling of the text, and what the author may still do with the material. Book-length works bought outright were one quiet tool of the period's information work. The blank name fields in this copy keep the author and the title out of the record.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000700120019-4:
June 1950 dates an untitled career agent agreement between the United States, acting through the Central Intelligence Agency, and an unnamed employee. Recitals say the government wants his services in conditions requiring an operational cover. He will be sent overseas for intelligence operations. Unlike its near twins in the file, this copy places him under the Office of Special Operations rather than the policy office.

His part of the bargain is to serve abroad and to furnish a suitable cover himself. Article I ties that cover to his real professional background, so the story holds up. He must conduct himself outwardly to match the cover job. Pay, orders, secrecy, and separation terms fill the articles that follow. The name and day fields stand blank in this copy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000700120037-4:
A letter of 20 June 1951 from the General Counsel's office offers contract work to a man who has just resigned, with his name redacted. He is returning home to Durham, North Carolina. Two named scholars, Dr. William L. Danger as the name is printed and Mr. Max Millikan, want to keep drawing on his knowledge. The Agency therefore proposes an agreement for his services as his own affairs allow.

The work in view includes advice on Agency problems in his field of special knowledge. Reports and estimates would go to him for critical appraisal. Special reports on economic problems, and help with planning in economic intelligence, are also named. Proposed pay stands at twelve hundred dollars a month in the legible text. The letter keeps a departing expert within reach.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000020089-4:
Recommendation I, in an untitled paper on espionage law, urges an amendment to Title 50, Section 31. Clauses (d) and (e) of that section, it argues, should not be read to require proof of harmful intent. The risk named is that a court might carry the intent test from clauses (a), (b), and (c) across the whole section. A short amendment would head off that reading.

The paper then quotes what each clause punishes. Entering, flying over, or probing a vessel, aircraft, or defence work to gather national defence information is the first offence. Copying or taking sketches and photographic negatives with like intent is the second. Receiving such material is the third. The close parsing shows lawyers hunting for gaps in the main spy statute before a case exposed them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040005-4:
S. 2020, reported on 8 June 1949 with Report Number 475, is the bill that became the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949. Mr. McClellan reported it from the Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments. Its purpose is to simplify how government property is bought, used, and disposed of, and to reorganise certain agencies. The contents list starts with a declaration of policy and definitions.

Title I then builds a General Services Agency. The Bureau of Federal Supply is abolished and its contract settlement work moved. Affairs of the Federal Works Agency are transferred next. Records management and the National Archives follow in the same title. This is the full Senate bill text, the machine that created the General Services Administration in draft.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040014-4:
House Report Number 2747, filed 26 July 1950, backs H.R. 9129 to amend the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949. Mr. Dawson reported for the Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments, in favour with amendments. Small printing fixes lead the list, then a wording change on page 7. A longer change on page 8 adds a proviso after the word security.

That proviso requires a showing of total cost to the government, counting rentals, repairs, alterations, and improvements. The amendment wave a year after passage shows Congress tuning the young supply system. Property deals that hid their full cost were the target of the page 8 change. The report's bulk prints the amended act so members could judge the whole effect.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040023-4:
A draft General Services Administration regulation, circulated 30 April 1951 for comment by 31 May, governs abandonment, destruction, or donation of property to public bodies. Silence by that date would count as agreement. The draft is marked for discussion only. Its authority is the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949. That act was amended by Public Laws 152 and 754.

The opening purpose clause sets policies and methods for executive agencies. It covers disposal of certain property in those three ways. Two classes sit outside it. The first is excess property held beyond the continental United States and the named island areas. The second is surplus already donated to schools or public health bodies under a named section. The rules matter where an agency held goods no longer worth shipping or selling.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000060003-4:
Salary Table Number 26, issued by the General Accounting Office on 31 May 1946, sets executive branch pay from 1 July 1946. It replaces the tables in force after 30 June 1946. Staff paid by the year are its subject, and a forty-hour week underlies the figures. Each rate is broken into the amount due for a full two-week pay period.

The sums follow the Federal Employees Pay Act of 1945 as supplemented by the Act of 1946. Hourly and daily unit rates appear beside the period figures. Tax deductions shown rest on the Revenue Act of 1945. A third part explains what payrolls and vouchers must show so that examination, certification, and audit can proceed. Post-war pay rises run through every line of the table.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000070101-4:
United States Censorship Regulations in the edition of 30 January 1943 replace all the wartime censorship rulebooks issued before them. Cable and radio rules of 19 February 1942 are revoked. So are the telephone rules and the postal rules of May and April 1942. Authority traces to the Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917, the First War Powers Act of 1941, Executive Order 8985, and a Treasury decision.

Scope is set at once: all communications passing between the United States, its territories or possessions, and any foreign country. Traffic carried by any vessel touching a United States port on a foreign run also falls inside. The regulations then grade what may pass, what is cut, and what is held. This was the working law of wartime censorship.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100050030-4:
A Foreign Service despatch of 3 March 1950, sent from Frankfurt under a priority marking, forwards a German request touching the German-American Convention of 1892. That convention covers reciprocal recognition of copyrights between the two countries. The Federal Chancellor's office had written to the Chairman of the Allied Commission on the subject. The Allied General Secretariat passed the matter along, judging it fit for bilateral handling at least in its early stages.

The despatch quotes the German correspondence in full, in the original and in rendering. Washington is asked to take note of the contents and of Bonn's wish to raise the question. Copyright between the two states still rested on a treaty older than either world war, and the new German government wanted its standing made clear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200020069-4:
Insurance coverage for covert personnel is thrashed out in a memorandum of conversation dated 11 January 1949, marked secret. Many sides of the problem were aired: security, who pays the premiums, and the chance that false statements in applications could void commercial policies. The Agency going into insurance itself, with no actuarial tables of its own, was also weighed. A shared view emerged from the talk.

No promise that amounts to cover should be given to covert staff until normal commercial and government insurance routes are used up. Covert staff should normally pay for their own cover, just as overt staff do. Cover granted by CIA would in effect be a bonus or a rise in pay. Such a promise, the group held, normally goes beyond what the government owes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200020078-4:
War Department Circular Number 257, issued in Washington on 23 August 1946, explains the loosening of the National Service Life Insurance Act of 1940. It stands effective until 23 February 1948 unless sooner replaced. The circular works from the Insurance Act of 1946, Public Law 589, approved 1 August 1946. Only changes of immediate weight to the field are included; full detail would follow in AR 600-110.

Heads run from beneficiary liberalisations and optional settlements to plans of insurance and disability income benefit. Reinstatement, eligibility, and longer time to seek waiver of premiums follow. Disability claims close the list. Section II starts the detail: wider freedom in naming who receives the money. Soldiers leaving service needed these rules in plain form, fast.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001300070009-4:
Military bases in the Philippines are governed by an agreement printed as Treaties and Other International Acts Series 177. The United States and the Republic of the Philippines signed it at Manila on 14 March 1947. It entered into force on 26 March 1947. The State Department issued it as Publication 3257 in 1948, priced at ten cents.

The agreement's opening recital ties the two states' shared interest in defending their territories, a lesson the Pacific war had driven home. Articles then list the bases the United States would keep, the terms of use, and the rights of each side. Notes exchanged with the agreement are printed with it. The text is the legal base of the American military presence in the newly independent republic.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001300070018-4:
Intelligence work gets its own reading list in Bibliography Number 33 of December 1940, on the functions, methods, and techniques of intelligence. The State Department's Division of Library and Reference Services prepared it, and the Office of Intelligence Research distributed it. A preface states the aim: list the more important books and publications on how intelligence work is done. Intelligence is defined first as gathering and weighing confidential information on a foreign power's strength.

Counter-measures against foreign intelligence form the second half of the definition. Entries then run through the literature of spying, codes, propaganda, and staff work as it stood in 1940. Compiled before the United States had a central intelligence service, the list shows what a student of the craft could then read in the open.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00039a000100050030-4:
Weekly Activities Report dated 31 August was sent by the Chief of the Language and External Training School through the Chief of Plans and Policy to the Director of Training. It reports that the Agency's first three pilot area courses have been completed. The courses covered a basic country survey and United States foreign policy in the Far East, in a twenty hour format.

Sixty Agency employees took part, along with staff from the National Security Agency, State, the Air Force, and the Navy, and forty seven completed the courses. The report compares cost and reach with training bought from outside schools, finding the internal program far cheaper per student hour. It argues that area training should not be contracted out until the Agency can use outside places to full effect.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200170002-4:
Report number 408, dated 12 June 1953, titled Outstanding Magazine Articles Relating to International Affairs, is a weekly digest obtained and reproduced for the Central Intelligence Agency. The report presents short digests of current magazine editorials and articles of special bearing on United States foreign relations, with a note that they do not mirror overall opinion.

Magazines digested include The Progressive, Business Week, America, The Nation, Saturday Evening Post, U.S. News and World Report, The Freeman, The New Leader, Barron's, The Commonweal, Newsweek, The Christian Century, Time, Life, Look, and New Republic. A subject index covers Asia, a big power conference, China and Korea, foreign policy, Great Britain, India, the information program, and Italy. One digest takes up neutral feeling in Asia and Europe and the limits of broadcasts and aid in meeting it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130078-4:
Excerpts from Title 18 of the United States Code, kept in a Central Intelligence Agency legal file, print the federal criminal sections on threats and extortion sent across state lines. One section covers sending in interstate commerce a demand or request for ransom or reward for the release of a kidnapped person. The penalty is a fine of up to ten thousand dollars or twenty years in prison, or both.

Further paragraphs cover sending a message with intent to extort money or a thing of value that threatens to kidnap or injure a person. They also cover sending a threat without that intent, with lower fines and terms. Threats to injure property or reputation are treated in a later paragraph. The middle turns to mail fraud, covering use of the post office in a scheme to defraud.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100020007-4:
Memorandum dated 10 May 1956 on intelligence testimony before congressional committees explains which committees hear the Director and on what. The Senate and House Armed Services Committees are the parent committees of the Agency, each with a small subcommittee over Agency activities. Before them the Director appears each year to brief operations, discuss problems, and describe major budget items.

Appropriations subcommittees of both houses hear the Director in detail on the annual budget and are also briefed fully on operations. Attendance is larger at hearings on special funds such as the new Agency building. The Director also appears at least once each session before the Joint Committee on Atomic Energy to brief atomic developments in the Soviet Union. A later passage recalls three executive sessions on Soviet air strength before a Senate Armed Services subcommittee.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100020043-4:
Office memorandum dated 5 February 1947, from the Chief of the Legislative Liaison Division to the Deputy Director, is titled Congressional Material of CIG Interest. The memorandum refers to earlier memoranda of 7 August 1946 and 13 January 1947 on a summary of the Congressional Record. The writer judges that the amount of congressional material in which the Central Intelligence Group is interested is not enough to merit a full summary by his office.

All pertinent material will instead be brought to the attention of the Director, the Deputy Director, and proper offices whenever it appears, best done verbally or by memoranda as the occasion warrants. No action is recommended on the proposal at present, and the Executive for Personnel and Administration concurs. Routing slips of the Central Intelligence Group, revised 10 September 1946, follow the memorandum in the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100050040-4:
Newspaper series on Soviet radio propaganda, first article by Robert S. Bird, reports that propaganda in thirty languages pours from Soviet transmitters as exposures, lectures, distortions, anecdotes, and even Morse code. The article states that it rests on a study of Soviet world broadcasts over three months as monitored in London. Later articles would cover the Soviet radio picture of the United States and its language devices.

A hundred Soviet transmitters are said to send a stream of doubt, suspicion, and fear of the United States around the clock, depicting the country as the menace of the world. Broadcasts to the Soviet home audience go further, tying the menace theme to an enemy theme. Later passages in the file quote broadcast treatment of Poland, with Soviet help praised as great and disinterested. Satellite peoples are urged to liberate themselves from capitalist regimes, in the broadcasts' own framing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100070156-4:
Memorandum dated 23 January 1951, for the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence and the Deputy Director for Plans, marked secret, confirms a talk that day on a publicity question. A named journalist of the New York Times, Mr. James Reston, proposed to write an article or series on the government effort in psychological warfare, with reference to its covert side.

Reston's view, as reported, was that public and congressional interest was growing and some assurance that something was being done was needed. The writer advised against referring Reston to himself and suggested a holding reply that consideration was being given to the inquiry by the appropriate authorities. His own view was that a formula could satisfy public and congressional inquiries without giving the Russians information they did not already have. He also held that the Agency should not be identified as the operative agency.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100190036-4:
Draft executive order, marked copy, would create a President's Communications Policy Board, composed of a chairman and two, with four written in as an alternative, other members designated by the President. The draft is stated in the name of the President, by the authority vested in him as President.

The Board's function would be to study the use made of radio and wire communications facilities by government and non-government users. It would also present evaluations and recommendations in the national interest. Topics listed are policies for the most effective use of radio frequencies and alternative administrative arrangements. They also include policies on international radio and wire communications, the relation of government to non-government communications, and related matters the Board chose to take up. The Board could hear industry and government representatives, Departments were to cooperate and furnish information, with security of classified matter protected.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100230022-4:
Draft bill dated 14 April 1954 would further amend section 1 of the Administrative Expenses Act of 1946. It would also repeal certain provisions on transport and storage of household goods and personal effects of government officers and employees, including members of the uniformed services.

Weight limits are restated: not over seven thousand pounds uncrated, or eight thousand seven hundred fifty pounds crated, for transfers within the continental United States. For transfers to, within, or from the Territories and Possessions or foreign countries, the limits are ten thousand pounds uncrated, or fourteen thousand pounds crated. An equivalent applies where charges rest on cubic measure. Four new subsections follow. One covers shipment of one privately owned automobile where an agency head finds it in the interest of the United States at a duty station outside the continental limits.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200020042-4:
Memorandum for the Director of Central Intelligence dated 27 July 1953, subject S.J. Res. 96, marked as reviewed by the general counsel staff, sets out Agency handling of the resolution. On 3 July Senator Wiley had written the Director asking for Agency comments. The resolution was reported out by Senator Hickenlooper on 18 July, with a copy at Tab A and Senate Report 602 at Tab B.

The commission's makeup and charge are summed up, with particular emphasis on television. The Senate report is quoted as stating the USSR had already set uniform telecasting standards across the Soviet bloc. It was reported to plan transmitters able to deliver television signals to many free nations. Floor objection by Senator Johnson of Colorado is noted, the proposal is traced to Senate Report 406 and the Jackson Committee, and a draft reply for the Director sits at Tab C.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200040004-4:
Copy of the memorandum for the Director dated 16 December 1953, subject Congressional Lunches, recommending that a weekly lunch program with senators and congressmen begin immediately. The reasoning is brief: the lunches would apprise key members of Congress of pertinent matters concerning the Agency, and invitations should go out on the schedule printed below the recommendation.

Notes on individual guests explain why each man mattered. Vorys might have foreign trade questions from his Randall Commission work. Saltonstall, as Senate Armed Services chairman and a member of the Armed Services Appropriations Subcommittee, was responsible for Agency legislation in the Senate. Rees of Kansas is described as a man who had always offered any assistance possible, of great help for the career service program. The note adds that the President comes from his district and that Rees would not desire a detailed briefing, in the closing words shown.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200100025-4:
Joint State and ICA message, dated September 1956, announces CODEL Green, a trip to Europe and Africa by Senator Theodore F. Green, a member of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations. Addressee posts include Accra, Addis Ababa, Cairo, Capetown, Casablanca, Dakar, Johannesburg, Khartoum, Lagos, Leopoldville, Monrovia, Nairobi, Paris, Pretoria, Rabat, Rome, Tripoli, and Tunis.

The Senator expected to depart the United States on 14 September for a trip to Africa. There he would study United States technical assistance and other aid programs and American foreign policies in the various countries. As chairman of the Committee's Subcommittee on Near Eastern and African Affairs, he would be accompanied by Dr. Alwyn V. Freeman, consultant to the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations. Posts are asked to prepare in advance information covered in an outline for a post summary printed at the end of the message, covering aid and local government topics.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100170003-4:
Letter dated 13 March 1956 from the Bureau of the Budget, Executive Office of the President, addressed My dear Mr. Chairman, replies to requests for reports on S. 2365 and S. 2469, similar bills extending the authority of the General Services Administration over warehouses and other storage facilities operated by civilian agencies.

Both bills aim at Recommendation 2(b) of the report on Depot Utilization by the Commission on Organization of the Executive Branch. Each would give the General Services Administration all functions then exercised by civilian agencies for warehouses and storage facilities. The letter compares that grant with the Administrator's existing authority under the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act, starting at section 201(a). A middle passage quotes a requirement for justification, with cost comparisons, for each motor vehicle pool.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100210008-4:
Supplement to Full Committee Hearing number 42, printed as number 47, records a sitting of the House Committee on Armed Services on Tuesday 24 January 1956. Chairman Carl Vinson presided, and the subject was H.R. 8499 (H.R. 8710) to amend the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947. The chairman opens with a brief statement of why the committee met again.

The committee had the week before unanimously recommended H.R. 8499, but staff found language on page 2 did not match the committee's thought, and the bill probably trespassed on other committees' jurisdiction. Vinson had therefore introduced H.R. 8710 the day before, with modified language. Later testimony argues that set asides for surplus labor areas rest only on inferential authority from an Office of Defense Mobilization directive.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670035-4:
Public Law 854 of the 84th Congress, chapter 804, second session, H.R. 7619, is the enacted text, cited at 70 Stat. 736. Title I is the Federal Executive Pay Act of 1956. Section 102 lists the offices paid at its top rate. They are the Secretaries of State, the Treasury, Defense, Interior, Agriculture, Commerce, Labor, and Health, Education, and Welfare, the Attorney General, and the Postmaster General.

Section 103(a) sets the next group at a stated rate. It names the Director of the Bureau of the Budget, the Comptroller General, the Director of the Office of Defense Mobilization, the Under Secretary of State, and the Deputy Secretary of Defense. The service secretaries follow. Title matter deeper in the law reaches civilian staff of Army and Navy disciplinary barracks and of the District of Columbia Department of Corrections, whose duties concern persons in detention.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670044-4:
Congressional Record, Senate, pages from 1956 print a run of enrolled and passed measures at the head of the portion shown. Acts listed include one to improve health by aiding training of nurses and public health staff and developing mental health care. Other acts end federal supervision over the property of the Peoria, Ottawa, and Wyandotte Tribes of Oklahoma and their members.

Other items cover development of the Holden trout hatchery at Pittsford, Vermont. An amendment to section 607 of the Postal Field Service Compensation Act of 1955 would include Motor Vehicle Service employees. In the middle of the pages, the Senate takes up the conference report on H.R. 7619, the executive pay bill: unanimous consent is asked for present consideration, and the legislative clerk reads the report for the Senate's information.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200180001-4:
Notice of Pending Legislation circulates S. Res. 134 for comment, with the form sent by the Legislative Counsel, Office of General Counsel. The comment, dated 14 July 1955, names Mr. Green of Rhode Island and sums the matter up as relative to the United Nations establishing a procedure for collecting and releasing radiological information.

The resolution print, 84th Congress, first session, shows Mr. Green reporting it as an original resolution from the Committee on Foreign Relations on 14 July 1955.
