Matter in the file quotes language asking the President to instruct the United States delegate to the United Nations. The delegate would propose and urge an international scientific commission within the United Nations. The commission would study and determine the effects on living organisms of radioactivity released by nuclear explosions. A passage recalls remarks at the June anniversary meeting of the General Assembly in San Francisco.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200270001-4:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel, reviewed by the Office of General Counsel, comments on H.R. 3332, to amend the Armed Forces Leave Act of 1946 so that members of the Armed Forces shall be granted leave on the critical illness or death of a close relative.

The proposal is recognised as one of interest to individuals in the military service who are detailed to the Agency, but no further action by the Legislative Counsel's office is believed required. The attached notice of pending legislation routes the bill to the Comptroller for comment on whether it touches Agency activities and whether further office action is needed. The bill print in the file is the 84th Congress, first session, print of H.R. 3332. The memorandum is short, and the file is mainly the notice form, distribution marks, and the bill.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200360001-4:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel comments on H.R. 4048, an act making recommendations to the States for laws to permit and assist federal personnel, including members of the Armed Forces, and their families, to exercise their voting franchise.

The bill would affect a limited number of Agency employees, the memorandum finds, by giving them a chance to vote while overseas where that choice may not have existed before. Later state legislation might set requirements that cancel the chance. No objections to the present bill appear from an Agency personnel standpoint, and no further action by the Legislative Counsel's office is thought necessary. The office asks to be kept informed of progress, given the bill's interest to Agency staff. Matter in the file estimates about three million men and women on active duty at the 1956 elections, close to a million of them away from home.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100010021-4:
A CIA memorandum, partly hard to read in the scan, sets out the rules for bonding staff who handle public money. It cites the laws on certifying officers and disbursing officers. It also covers others charged with paying out public funds. The power to require bonds rests with each agency head. That head has wide latitude in applying the law.

Most of the memo weighs a Position Schedule bond. The Office of the Comptroller proposed it. The bond offers two gains. First, the premium costs less. Second, and more important, the Agency need not name or locate each bonded employee for a bonding company. The memo also asks whether a governing board should decide which posts must be bonded.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100010067-4:
A CIA paper reviews shortages of funds at overseas stations. Names and places are heavily redacted. Parts of the scan are hard to read. In each case the Chief of the Finance Division urged that the man concerned be cleared of blame for the missing sum. One shortage is put at $148.47. The periods involved fall in 1948 and 1949.

The facts sections tell how each shortage came to light. One was found on 1 April. It was the first cash count since 1 April 1948. Another appeared when a man could not balance his imprest account. An audit then found a like gap between two sums. Efforts to learn the cause went nowhere. Some deficits were made up out of pocket.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100030001-4:
A CIA legal memorandum of 14 December 1956 explains a court case on loss of nationality. The case is Terada v. Dulles, decided in Hawaii in 1954. First the memo lists the acts that cost a United States national his nationality. They include foreign naturalisation and an oath to a foreign state. They also include foreign military service and voting in a foreign election. Formal renunciation, desertion, and treason are on the list too.

The memo then follows Judge McLaughlin's attacks on the law. In Terada, the plaintiff had been drafted into the Japanese Army. The court found that service forced, not chosen. He had also voted in Japanese elections in 1946 and 1947. On that ground the court struck down section 801(e) as unconstitutional. The government did not appeal. The memo notes the judge stood alone among his colleagues.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100040055-4:
An airline passenger rules tariff, issued by the Air Traffic Conference of America on 27 October 1955 and effective 1 December 1955, sets general rules for ticket refunds. The pages come from Local and Joint Passenger Rules Tariff No. PR-3 and cover the voluntary refund rules used by the member carriers, among them TCA, Northwest, TWA, United, and Western.

The rules fix what a passenger gets back when part of a ticket has been used: the difference between the fare paid and the fare for the travel actually taken. Exceptions follow for named routes, sleeper charges, executive service charges, and tickets bought under travel plans or government transportation requests. A separate rule covers lost tickets. The tariff shows the refund practice a traveller, or an agency arranging travel, faced in the mid-1950s.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100170015-4:
A CIA legal memorandum of 15 February 1955, sent to the Deputy Director (Administration), takes up individual claims against the Agency. It responds to an Inspector General memorandum and a draft procedure meant to ensure full staffing of problems that call for discretionary action. The office had held its reply until two pending applications for discretionary relief were decided, one of them a Hawaii situation.

The discussion turns on mistakes by government representatives that cause loss or injury to officers, employees, or agents, and on when relief is proper. It sets out the rights that exist in federal employment and warns against letting administrative convenience convert an apparently arguable situation into a charge on operations. A companion memorandum on rights in federal employment, sent to the Inspector General, is forwarded with it for later discussion.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100190004-4: A CIA letter of 20 August 1955 to the Speaker of the House, signed by Acting Director C. P. Cabell with Legislative Counsel Walter L. Pforzheimer, is partly garbled in the scan. Its opening concerns the Agency's fiscal year 1955 appropriation and a statutory provision on claims. The pages that follow list property-damage claims one by one, most arising out of vehicle collisions, with small sums such as $50.00 and $90.00 beside them. Names and several dates are redacted or unreadable.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100210038-4:
A CIA legal memorandum gives a brief analysis of the Crypto Security Law. It was written for the Office of Security. The scan renders the law as Public Law 513 of the 81st Congress. It sits at 18 U.S.C. 798, in the espionage chapter of Title 18. Its aim is to stop disclosures about cryptographic systems. It also guards the communication intelligence work of the United States.

The memo quotes the offence and the classes of facts it protects. They run from the nature and use of codes and ciphers. They extend to the content of intercepted foreign messages. The memo stresses that its legal reading is open to argument. Its real offer is practical advice. It lists steps the Agency should take in its own practice. Other agencies should take some of them too. Such steps would strengthen the government's case if a prosecution followed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030109-4:
A CIA memorandum of 2 July 1947 gives notes on statutes cited in a draft bill. The bill is the draft of 9 June 1947. The memo goes through it section by section. It was written for the Legislative Liaison Officer. On section 2(b)(2), it cites 10 U.S.C. 576. An Army officer who accepts a civil office stops being an officer. So a specific exception is needed. No such blanket bar applies to Navy officers.

Section 2(b)(5) would let the Agency employ retired officers. That needs exceptions to several pay laws. One bars two salaries from appropriated funds above $2,000 combined. Others cap retired pay above $3,000 combined, except for combat disability. Another bars appointing a retired officer who draws $2,500 or more. Later notes cover buying under Revised Statutes section 3709. They also cover Foreign Service rules on transport and sick leave.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200160015-4:
A CIA paper is titled 'The Security of a Nation'. It gives special reference to legislation of a security nature. It opens with a chart of the constitutional order. Under the executive, it sets the needs of the state. They are sound information for policy, which is intelligence. They are forces to prevent armed attack, a sound civil service, and laws against subversion. Under the judiciary, a prosecuting group must act against violators.

The paper then lists points any intelligence law must cover. The Agency needs a statutory basis. Its duties should be stated in general terms, spanning overt and covert work. Its place among other intelligence units must be fixed. Civil service, customs, immigration, and budget laws all need study. So do reporting duties and employee benefits. The aim is the flexibility security needs. The paper urges latitude to permit some acts barred by law, above all in immigration.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200180040-4:
A CIA memorandum for the record, dated October 1954, traces the repeal of section 9 of the CIA Act of 1949. When the Act passed, the top government salary was $10,330. The Agency struggled to recruit scientists for its scientific intelligence work. Section 9 let the Director set pay for up to three such posts. The rate ran from $10,000 to $15,000 a year.

Later, general pay scales were revised. Super grade posts were created, up to GS-18 at $14,000. CIA was exempt from the Classification Act but followed its scales. The Comptroller General then ruled that section 9 capped the Agency at three super grade posts in scientific intelligence. Several OSI division chiefs were affected. After talks with the Budget Bureau and others, the Agency decided in May 1952 not to seek repeal in the closing months of the 82nd Congress.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300220017-4:
A CIA file of letters from September 1955 arranges a meeting with the Special Committee on the Federal Loyalty-Security Program. The committee belonged to the Association of the Bar of the City of New York. Its chairman was Dudley B. Bonsal, and its director was Elliott E. Cheatham. On 7 September 1955 Cheatham wrote to General Counsel Lawrence R. Houston. Bonsal was in Europe, so Cheatham wrote for him. He welcomed Houston's word that a meeting on 25 October would suit.

Houston's own letter of 2 September 1955 is in the file. He would be glad to join the committee on 25 October. Director Dulles was also expected, as far as could then be told. Houston had asked that the date reach Dulles as soon as he returned. Later pages return to the polygraph symposium mentioned in other files. The tone throughout is cooperative. The Agency was helping the committee's study of the loyalty-security system.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300240088-4:
A wire news report covers a stormy Senate subcommittee hearing. The witness was a playwright and translator who had served with the OSS. He refused to answer the subcommittee's questions. Time after time he cited the rule that no one can be compelled to be a witness against himself. Counsel Robert Morris pressed him. The witness, named Wuchinich in the report, stormed at the subcommittee and its counsel.

Asked whether he had been an OSS officer, Wuchinich said he had, and was proud of it. Senator Olin Johnston asked whether he considered himself a good American. He said he certainly did. He read from his Distinguished Service Cross citation, dated 8 November 1944. It praised extraordinary heroism in secret operations in the Balkans. He had dropped behind enemy lines by parachute. The subcommittee had testimony that he had been a Communist Party member in the Pittsburgh area.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300320025-4:
A CIA legal memo answers questions on invitational travel expenses for job candidates. It went to the Deputy Assistant Director for Personnel. Two cases are posed. In the first, a candidate is ordered to Washington for medical and polygraph examinations. He is not yet in an employment status. In the second, a candidate has been placed in that status, then rejected for failing the examinations. The office wanted to avoid adverse publicity from applicants who came believing they were accepted.

The governing rule is quoted from volume 31, page 175 of the Comptroller General decisions (1951). Agencies may not pay a man's travel to Washington to test his qualifications for a post under the civil service laws. Judging qualifications belongs to the Civil Service Commission. Two facts cut the other way. Most Agency posts are excepted from those laws. And an applicant may technically become an employee before he has truly qualified.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100010004-4:
An Intelligence Advisory Committee plan, IAC-D-96 (Final), is dated 7 June 1955. It covers IAC participation in Operation Alert 1955. The general purposes are threefold. The plan tests the effectiveness of relocation planning. It tests the ability to carry on essential wartime functions at relocation sites during a sustained alert. It also tests the ability to deal with problems under attack conditions.

The general assumption is mild. Washington is intact, and no attack has taken place. But the situation is critical, and a partial relocation has been ordered. The President had said the National Security Council should be ready to meet on its regular schedule. The IAC may be called to advise the Director in his role as intelligence adviser. A test of interagency coordination is set for 16 June. Member agencies would transact some IAC business at the representatives' level, to test communications between relocation centres.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030008-4:
A statement to a House subcommittee presents the Department of Agriculture's record on manpower use. The speaker is MacHenry Schafer, Director of Personnel. He appeared on 3 November 1955. The subcommittee covers manpower utilization and departmental personnel management. Agriculture, he says, has applied good management principles continuously. Programs are set by Congress, but economies come from better procedures and better use of people.

The figures tell the story. Total employment was 106,108 on 31 December 1941. By 31 December 1954 it was 70,267. A table gives paid employees reported to the Civil Service Commission. The count was 96,238 on 31 August 1946 and 77,000-odd by 1951. New programs in research and education added work. Surplus commodities reached record quantities. Even so, totals stayed below 1946 levels. Later sections describe streamlining in the Rural Electrification Administration and closed field offices.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030044-4:
A CIA memo transmits an analysis of the problems in the manpower survey. The analysis sorts the problems into six groups. They are internal CIA duplication and external CIA duplication. They include services performed for another agency, and services that could be transferred to one. Elements of common concern within the intelligence community form a fifth group. Combination of similar functions is the sixth.

References point to the basic papers of the DD/I, DD/P, and DD/S. Under internal duplication, research and development spans OSI, the Office of Communications, and others. Training tied to the Domestic Operations Base spans OTR and SR Division. The remarks urge study of how efforts could complement each other. Personnel record keeping involves the Office of Personnel and all components. The memo hopes its remarks will help plan task forces.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100040007-4:
A statement of 22 September 1955 opens a government-wide manpower study. The speaker is James C. Davis, chairman of the subcommittee on manpower utilization. He addresses executives from federal departments and agencies. The committee means business, he says. It intends to cut government jobs not by a few thousand but by several hundred thousand. All essential tasks, he argues, can be done with two million or fewer employees.

Every agency should manage at least a ten percent reduction. Reports showing less will face the closest scrutiny. Davis attacks bureaucratic empire building. Hiring to flatter a boss's prestige is a luxury the country cannot afford. Cutting spending is the path to cutting taxes. Marginal activities will not survive critical analysis. He notes his colleague Robert J. Corbett chaired the subcommittee in the last Congress. Their roles are now reversed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100010051-4:
A CIA paper examines whether geographic data on the United States should be denied to the USSR. The government interest, it says, grew from the grave difficulty of getting basic facts on the USSR. Unavailability there is not really a top policy choice. Yet it shows how foreign intelligence can be frustrated by normally unclassified information. The United States feels the matter keenly because of the contrast in intelligence advantage.

CIA has a keen interest in geodetic and gravimetric data. Such data bear on mapping accuracy, missile systems, and satellite research. A task force of the Interdepartmental Advisory Committee on Publications took up maps and charts on 13 April 1956. With stated exceptions, all geographic data on the United States are freely available to the USSR. Army Map Service maps larger than 1:500,000 are restricted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410002-4:
A status table lists Geography Division projects as of 1 March 1957. The format matches the monthly series. Geographic Intelligence Review MR-51 is due in March 1957. MR-52, begun 31 January, is due in April. A Far East section leads with a geography of Sinkiang. Its analyst spent almost all of February on analysis and compilation of map data. Preliminary drafting continued.

Other Far East entries track overlays and area studies. Work concentrated on areas G-6 and G-22. Worksheets for 1:250,000 map overlays were compiled. A USSR section follows with an urban area study and territorial-administrative work. Dates run back to 1953 for some long projects. Status notes are terse: in progress, delayed, open, or in draft review. Analyst names are largely redacted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410011-4:
A status table lists Geography Division projects as of 2 December 1957. MR-53's text went to reproduction on 10 October, its maps approved. MR-54, begun 31 October 1957, has maps initiated. Far East entries repeat the long-running geographies. Ningsia, Suiyuan, Chahar, and Shensi remains delayed. Sinkiang is in progress, due in the first quarter of 1958. Tibet is still delayed.

A Northeast Thailand analysis nears editing; its draft should be ready in December. Several entries are marked ADTIC research at low priority. A Chapter 19 contribution is due to another office by 15 May 1958. USSR entries close the table. One program text went to reproduction in December in revised form. An East Germany traffic flow project has been cancelled.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410020-4:
A Cartography Division project status list is dated 1 September 1957. The USSR-Satellites Branch leads. New Sino-Soviet Bloc charts show technicians in the Free World and trade with the Free World. A Soviet international civil air flights sheet serves the State Department. Airframe plant layouts cover Rostov and Gorkiy. Eight Bloc GNP and economic charts form a set.

A Bulgaria Chapter I cover map is new. The USSR state structure chart reaches its fifth revision. Satellite jammer and monitor maps run to twelve sheets with four charts. Moscow and Leningrad chemical science locations continue. Later sections carry proof deadlines through September. A world foreign service posts sheet appears in second revision.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100490004-4:
The NIS Committee held its 238th meeting on 19 February 1957. 238 of 19 February 1957. Colonel Sam Carnes became the Air Force senior representative effective 24 January 1957. Lieutenant Colonel Hamilton Avery moved to alternate member and Air Force NIS coordinator. The committee thanked Avery for his service. It then approved the revised outline guides for Sections 31, 32, and 33.

The Navy member renewed his Section 56 proposal. Navy still wants more on the internal security of foreign countries than the present guide provides. A working group was agreed to, with a caution. It should not chase passing detail that only operational support could satisfy. The Navy member was asked to arrange the meeting. Other business covers supplement comments on communism. Changes to the production forecast for fiscal 1958-60 were also approved.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100490022-4:
Minutes record NIS Committee Meeting No. 256 of 17 December 1957. The Chapter I Task Group had met on 27 November and 13 December on the NIS Annuals. It submitted a tentative outline guide dated 21 November 1957. The committee approved it. A pilot Annual on Poland was also approved. Its deadline is 1 February 1958.

Contributors must use a uniform intelligence cut-off date of 1 January 1958. The Poland Annual will be formally reviewed by the committee. Drafts of Section 11, Significance of New Developments, go to all members as they are submitted. The Army member raised adding Biographies to future Chapters I. Decision was deferred for study. Map scale definitions from the Chapter IX Subcommittee were also considered.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000200100023-4:
A progress report covers the Geographic Area, ORR, for November 1957. Production and services held at a generally normal level. A larger share than usual was high-priority rush work. Area specialist briefings continued. Two were given in November: Soviet Penetration in the Middle East, and Selection of Guided Missile Launching Sites in the USSR. The Cartography Division completed 54 maps and charts.

The Map Library Division received 5,468 maps and 1,004 related publications from foreign sources. It sent out 18,240 map sheets in answer to 1,199 requests. The Photo Intelligence Division completed 21 reports and memoranda. Fifteen supported the DD/P. Others cover the Taganrog aircraft plant and the Southeast China situation. The Geography Division completed three Geographic Intelligence Reports.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100030070-4:
A CIA legal paper examines dual compensation limits on hiring a government employee for outside-hours work. The Agency plans to use a man already on a government salary. The work would fall outside his normal hours. No conflict between the two jobs is expected. Pay might be salary, per diem, or fee. The question is whether the dual compensation statutes allow it.

The law runs back through statutes to 1839. Sections 58, 62, 69, and 70 of Title 5 govern. They bar pay for extra service, extra allowances, and double office holding. Interpretation has divided jurists for years. The cases form a chain with no clear uniformity. Attorney General opinions are quoted at length. One states the aim of the Act of 1894 plainly: to stop an employee from holding two salaried positions at once.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100070012-4:
A CIA file forwards a legal memorandum on exclusion and deportation of aliens. Cover notes from General Counsel Lawrence R. Houston send copies to Agency chiefs. The memorandum was requested by the Office of Special Operations. It lays out the grounds on which aliens may be excluded or deported. One copy went to the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination, for information.

The memorandum proper begins with grounds for exclusion. Aliens are excluded for stated causes under the immigration laws. Later pages take up totalitarian connections. After a brief free immigration, the Department began to look more carefully at supposed totalitarians. The memo estimates that about 1,500 aliens were admitted on one basis between October 1950 and March 1951. The scan's main text is partly garbled, but its structure and rulings can be read.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100160012-4:
Comments dated May 20, 1955, go to the Chief of the Regulations Control Staff. They concern a proposed travel regulation covering performance of travel. The concurrence sheet is returned unsigned. The reviewers raise objections to the draft as written. Their general comments cover the wider plan behind it. A series of ten regulations under basic category 22, Travel, was meant to form the Agency's travel rules.

Detailed comments follow on the draft's wording. The reviewers question rules on sleeping berths for young children on trains. They object to requiring employees to take upper berths when lower berths are not available. A related provision, they note, has been read to allow roomettes in that situation. Other passages suggest simpler wording for specific subparagraphs. The final regulation would then be easier to apply.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100160030-4:
Legal comments on a proposed regulation titled Travel, Per Diem Allowances take up how the Agency should state its daily allowance rules. A request had been made to gather the per diem instructions scattered through many regulations. Some were written and some unwritten. They would be gathered into a single regulation, so the rules would be clearer and easier to find.

The comments then work through the draft's paragraphs in detail. They question wording and suggest changes. One passage deals with cases where government quarters or meals are provided. Another deals with prior approval for certain travel costs. The scan is partly garbled. Some figures and cross-references cannot be read with confidence. The aim of the draft still comes through: one clear home for the per diem rules.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100210043-4:
A personnel case file from the spring of 1955 concerns travel by the nineteen-year-old son of an Agency employee serving overseas. The son was at school in the United States. A routing note of April 1, 1955, forwards the case for action and notes that one paragraph asks for the matter to be sent to the Office of General Counsel. Cable notice is requested if headquarters reconsiders the case.

The attached memorandum of March 31, 1955, cites earlier messages from May 1954 through March 1955. It weighs the rules for bringing dependents home ahead of the employee's own return, which require a finding that the move serves the organization's interests. The employee, the file states, was prepared to pay the cost of the son's return trip at the end of the tour.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00538a000100020009-4:
A survey of field communications procedures counts the traffic between Agency headquarters and field stations. It asks where the traffic slows down. For February 1954 it lists 336 cables and 697 dispatches sent to the field. Against those stand 358 cables and 867 dispatches received. Much of the flow is finance business. It covers payroll changes, travel accounts, transfer account forms, and audit reports. Funding matters for stations are included too.

Turnaround times differ sharply by channel. Cables move in about one day, while dispatches take ten or more days. The survey blames part of the delay on coordination habits. Finance letters are often sent for review to area desks unfamiliar with the question. The survey calls that step needless for routine technical matters.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100060015-4:
A memorandum dated April 25, 1956, to the Director of Training proposes a new concept for the OTR Bulletin. The bulletin had first appeared in 1953, with Agency-wide distribution at supervisory level. Its content had stayed narrow: an edited version of the featured address from the former National Intelligence Orientation course. Some twelve further issues had followed the same pattern.

The proposal would widen the bulletin to tell supervisors what the Office of Training is doing, what it plans to do, and when its courses and activities are scheduled. Sample contents range from a piece titled Russian is Rough? Nyet!, promoting Slavic language courses, to training directories listing names, phone numbers, and rooms for the training liaison structure across the Agency.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100090012-4:
A draft memorandum for the Director of Central Intelligence, dated in the autumn of 1955, carries the Office of Training's recommendations for area and language training. It notes that the office had sent up several studies on the Agency's training problems over the previous eighteen months, with summaries attached as Tab A. The core finding is blunt about responsibility.

Shortfalls in language skill and area knowledge, the draft says, will not be fixed unless the heads of the major components set minimum standards and make their people meet them. The first recommendation is an Agency policy, expressed in a notice, establishing those minimum standards. The attachments also review an incentive awards plan for language study suggested by another office, and a November 1954 proposal on incentive pay for foreign languages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100100001-4:
A revised report for the Killian Committee, sent to the Special Planning Assistant to the Deputy Director (Support), describes the Office of Training's work in numbers. The curriculum holds more than 120 courses of instruction, run by four schools: the Intelligence School, the Operations School, the Language and Area School, and the School of International Communism. Not all courses run at once, and some are given only as required.

During the period reported, an average of 55 courses were in operation each month, with about 600 students enrolled. The report adds that Agency policy devotes a minimum of five percent of total working hours to training. The picture is of a large standing training effort spread across intelligence, operations, languages, and the study of Communism.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200080003-4:
Comments on Assessment and Evaluation activities at the end of the first quarter of fiscal year 1958 are sent to the Agency's Director of Training on November 24, 1957. The headline is workload: 491 assessments in fiscal 1958 against 379 in fiscal 1957. Of the increase of 112, seventy-seven came from a newly established review of FLATS test reports, meant to ensure the report sent to the consumer is read accurately.

Quality, the chief reports, has so far been kept up and even improved while the higher numbers were absorbed. But a saturation point is nearing, and wider use of FLATS field testing is expected to push the load higher still over the next six months. Some decreases in other lines are listed, with the caution that they may not be meaningful.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200090002-4:
A report dated March 23, 1956, covers a management conference held for the Agency's Office of Research and Reports. The conference ran from Monday, February 27, through Friday, March 2, at a location removed in review. The report is organized under set heads. They are origin and preparation, conduct of the conference, results, the instructor's comments, and recommendations. The idea had been discussed for about nine months. ORR representatives and the management training staff did the discussing.

Dr. Guthe, the Assistant Director for Research and Reports, took the proposal further. He carried it to his own staff and to levels outside the office. Those levels included the DD/I and the Inspector General. He judged it a sound risk worth a major expense. The instructor's main criticism stands out. The agenda's big omission was interpersonal relations, above all between supervisor and analyst.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030025-4:
Weekly Activities Report number 19, dated May 15, 1958, from the Chief of the Language and Area School, leads with a funding question. The school had been asked to develop an Agency opinion on a university's wish for 50,000 dollars to finish dictionary projects, including one for Mongolian. The opinion was to be coordinated with the intelligence and plans directorates and to weigh the views of the interagency roundtable and the reasons an outside scholarly council had refused aid.

Other items record a negative answer to an Air Force inquiry, and talks about reviving language training at an overseas post, with a staff visit planned to survey needs on the spot. A borrowed staff member would take over routine voluntary program duties for about four months.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300050005-4:
Weekly Activity Report number 39, from the Registrar's office, covers September 24 to 30, 1958. Its lead item is the Security Reindoctrination Program. The program is described as solidly established and moving ahead steadily. The Office of Security had registered its satisfaction. It was pleased with the way headquarters components were taking part. The offices and staffs of the Deputy Director (Support) had been particularly responsive. They answered the call to support the program.

The file also holds the Registrar's report number 38, for September 17 to 23. It quotes a letter received by the Processing Branch. The letter came from an overseas Agency language trainee and is dated September 1, 1958. It thanked the office for its help in arranging his return. The letter is a small sign of the Registrar's hand in the daily movement of trainees.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300110035-4:
A survey report gathers the opinions of DD/P supervisors on the Agency's new training evaluation report used for Operations Course number 6, scales and Eyes Only section together. Seven supervisors had very favorable impressions of the whole report. One singled out the Eyes Only section for praise. Two said that the more information the report contained, the better they liked it.

One supervisor called the Eyes Only section the most important part, because it held good, serious judgments. For him the heart of it was the instructor's choice of the individual he would, or would not, like to go overseas with. Three more supervisors replied favorably but with qualifications, including a view on which case officer qualities mattered most. The report thus measures how a new, franker form of student reporting landed with its readers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400060028-4:
Weekly Activity Report number 4 comes from the Agency's Instructional Services Branch. It covers January 22 to 28, 1958. A film script had been transcribed from the sound tape of the finished show. Fifty copies were being dittoed. At a special showing the previous Friday, a member of the SI Staff raised an objection. It was a minor technical point. It had to be settled before the film could be released for use. The branch hoped to clear it that week.

Editing continued on another film. Effort went into hiding one fact. Its on-screen speaker had plainly been reading his lines from a teleprompter. A treatment and a first draft script for a further film were in preparation. Scenes for the Intelligence Process Film were shot on January 27.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000100100061-4:
A November weekly summary report of the Office of Training records a new program under way. The Chief of the Management Training Division had begun the CIA Human Resources Program on November 10 with a group of division chiefs, deputy chiefs, and staff personnel. The response was excellent, and group meetings would continue the following week. A new advanced program was also about to be announced to offices across the Agency.

That program would cover business policies, administrative practices, business in American society, cost and financial administration, marketing and management, and problems in labor relations, over three months. Course starts are listed ahead: Communist Party Operations Course number 10 on December 1, and Clandestine Psychological Warfare Course number 13 on December 15. The Director of Training had also joined a November 13 briefing on the value of a career service.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000300010008-4:
A letter from Philip W. Thayer looks back to 1952. Thayer was dean of the School of Advanced International Studies of Johns Hopkins University. He wrote to Matthew Baird, the Agency's Director of Training. In 1952 the school sponsored a summer session and conference on Southeast Asia. Its theme was Southeast Asia in the coming world. It meant to focus attention on the problems of the passage from colonialism to sovereignty. That area was critical. The letter judges the aim well met. The interest shown supports the judgment. So does the warm reception of the book that followed.

Thayer now proposes a successor conference, to be held in Rangoon. Papers from both meetings could appear in a single published volume. It would treat nationalism alongside political and social factors. Rangoon, he adds, would more easily draw important personalities. They could not make the longer journey to Washington.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400070010-4:
A paper titled Personnel Problems lays out the Office of Training's staffing troubles in plain figures. The office carries twenty-eight instructor vacancies. They are to be filled by experienced intelligence officers. Most would be drawn from the DD/P. Smaller numbers would come from the other directorates. Efforts to pull enough eligible candidates from the rest of the Agency have failed. They failed for the empty posts. They failed to replace borrowed instructors whose thirty-six-month tours have expired.

Rotation cuts the other way as well. The office's own career instructors need their operational experience refreshed. Some have been unrotated since 1950. Refreshing keeps a proper balance between theory and practice in the classroom. A processing complaint closes the paper. Putting costly security processing early in hiring risks wasting thousands of dollars. A cheap later step may then reject the man.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400130013-4:
A memorandum dated August 24, 1952, comes from the Chief of the Management Training Division. It describes the division's Executive, Administrative, and Supervisory Training Branch. The division's mission is stated first. It is to plan, initiate, conduct, and supervise training programs. Those programs will sharpen how work is managed, at every level of the Agency. The branch in question builds programs of its own. They strengthen the craft of management. They run from the Director's level down to the first-line supervisor.

Staffing follows. Three posts were proposed for the branch, at grades GS-14, GS-13, and GS-12. They differed only in the degree of skill and the depth of experience required. A sister Clerical Training Branch, the paper notes, would handle the rest. It would run the programs meant to raise clerical work across the Agency.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100080005-4:
A statement of mission and functions defines the Technical Branch. It is the Office of Security's audio arm. The branch is responsible for Agency-wide defensive audio surveillance security programs. They run in the United States and abroad. It does other work in the audio field that supports the Agency's security programs. It develops security systems that use technical methods.

Its listed functions run from the field to the desk. They include technical inspections to detect hostile listening devices against Agency activities. They include the development of audio countermeasures. They include worldwide reporting procedures in the defensive audio field. They include analysis of the inspection reports that flow in from around the world. The branch also builds training programs in the audio technical field. It gives special technical support on sensitive security work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100220009-4:
A staff paper on the Real Estate and Construction Division of the Logistics Office opens with its organization chart. The chart shows the chief's office and four units: construction engineering, acquisition and utilities, engineering, a safe house branch, and a facilities branch. No significant change is needed, the paper says. One exception sits inside the Space, Maintenance and Facilities Branch, which would be divided into four sections.

Three of those sections are geographic, shaped to match the Public Buildings Service, so the two bodies can work together smoothly. The work itself is the Agency's physical footprint. It includes colored plans showing exactly which component occupies what space. It includes records and reports on the status and use of space, for Agency heads, the Bureau of the Budget, and the General Services Administration. It includes arrangements, through the GSA and the owners of leased buildings, for their upkeep, alteration, and repair.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200010010-4:
An Agency memorandum for the record describes the career boards of the Department of State, drawn from interviews with Fred Darnell, chief of the department's Performance Evaluation Branch. The Board of the Foreign Service sits at the top. The organization chart shows it reporting directly to the Secretary of State; in practice its chairman is the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration, and its reports reach the Secretary through him.

Its duties are policy: recommendations on the functions, policies, and procedures governing the selection, assignment, rating, and promotion of Foreign Service Officers, and the administration of the Service itself. Its composition is prescribed by the Foreign Service Act of 1946. The memorandum also covers the Foreign Service Institute, whose director and faculty the Secretary appoints, and which keeps the training records of the employees it teaches.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200100001-4:
A proposed reorganization of the Office of Research and Reports starts from a changed world. As the relative weight of its tasks shifts, the office and its staffs have to be reshaped with them. Large levels of intelligence support once expected will probably not be required in the future. Defense intelligence support activities are falling away. The same research and reporting work, the paper argues, can then be done acceptably. It would take considerably less of the manpower now devoted to it.

The proposal works through the office's divisions. They include the Industrial Division and its guided missile branch. It also restates what Agency regulations demand of the office's chief. He must produce intelligence on the Sino-Soviet Bloc. He must support the Office of Current Intelligence with all-source current economic intelligence. He must screen incoming material promptly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200110028-4:
Appendix A to a production review report, marked Restricted, gathers the basic papers that defined the mission of the Office of Reports and Estimates. The papers listed are the National Security Act of 1947 and National Security Council directives from 1947 and 1948. Director of Central Intelligence directives from 1948 follow. The list ends with the office's own statement of functions of 15 July 1948, confirmed in a 1949 Agency organization manual. Discussion follows each source in turn.

The Act charged CIA with matching and judging material tied to national security and with services of common concern. Later directives spoke of national material, yet the appendix notes that this broad charge gave planners at working level little firm guide. The office's own statement filled the gap, defining it as the main Agency unit for judging, analysis, and production, science aside.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200150006-4:
Finance Division Operating Procedure 20-6, dated 13 January 1958 in revised form, governs personnel clearances when staff leave the CIA or change status. It replaces all earlier Finance releases on the subject. The cases covered are resignations, leave without pay over sixty days, military staff returning to their parent service or taking civilian status, and moves between unvouchered and covert posts. Summer temporary staff are excluded.

The Finance Division must make sure a person's debts to the Agency are recovered before departure or before final pay, leave, travel, or other payments are settled. Where needed, debts could be met from retirement credit or other means. Branch steps follow in detail, including checks on tax standing for staff who file covert returns. Worksheets record whether a person is current or owes a stated sum.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200180003-4:
A request seeks higher grades for two Reproduction Specialist posts in the Office of Logistics, backed by a chain of memos from September 1956 onward. Logistics officials, including the Chief of the Printing Services Division, strongly endorse the upgrade. Their case is that duties and responsibility have grown much since the posts were last graded, and that close review and supervision are not in fact available to the holders.

Because of that, the two staff must plan and run their own work with only broad guidance from above. The posts also carry a special duty: to set up and run a complete printing and reproduction service in support of Agency emergency operations. Later pages set out the knowledge the work demands, covering printing, photographic, and related methods, and the deadlines and priorities the holders must meet.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300030009-4:
A prepared statement by Maurice H. Stans, Director of the Bureau of the Budget, was marked for release on delivery on a Friday morning in August 1959. Stans addressed the House Committee on Post Office and Civil Service on S. 2162, the federal employee health insurance bill. He said he would stick to the main points of the Administration line, leaving detail to the Civil Service Commission report and to earlier testimony.

The Administration, he said, favored pay and benefit systems for federal staff that matched, in shape and level, those of good private employers. A 1954 presidential statement on personnel bills is cited for that view. Later he faults the bill's organization, naming three points needing change. They are the planned Advisory Council, a planned reshaping of the Civil Service Commission, and the way contracts and rules would be sent in.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300030036-4:
A statement dated Tuesday, 21 July 1959, was given to the House Committee on Post Office and Civil Service by the Hospitalization Committee of the Government Employes Council, AFL-CIO. The speakers said they spoke for 600,000 members of groups tied to the council. A long list of those groups opens the statement, running from government employee and municipal worker unions to machinists, firefighters, iron workers, and printing trades unions.

The case rests in part on what other plans pay. Tables in the statement count plans by the share of cost borne by the employer. The committee argues that practice in government and industry points to the government paying at least half. Major medical cover draws much discussion, with the need for it weighed against plan design. The statement is a union-side brief for a strong federal health program.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300190011-4:
Secretary of State John Foster Dulles addressed the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Wednesday, 14 January 1959, in a numbered statement of United States aims. The opening goals are a stable world order at a time when war carries risks no side can accept. Wider respect for human dignity and responsible freedom follows. Faster economic growth among free nations, so their independence stays secure, completes the list. The threat section follows.

The Soviet Union and Communist China, he says, are building economic and industrial power fast through state control of labor and imposed austerity, which speeds capital growth. Soviet quality is also stressed, with a recent space probe as proof, and he concedes the United States is still catching up in that field. Later pages argue that free world change is steady but rarely news, unlike Communist probing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100020130-4:
June 1958 fills this monthly report for the Cartography Division, though several figures are softened by poor OCR. Requests accepted ran above one hundred maps and charts, most for the CIA and a smaller share for the Department of State, with the research and scientific offices the largest sources. The division completed 134 maps and charts during the month, seven of them for State.

The survey map coordinator received twenty-five requests, split between final printing and color proofing, and receipts from reproduction came back higher than jobs sent out. Nineteen maps remained in process at month's end. The division held 460 maps and charts in all, spread among branches led by the USSR and Satellites branch. Notes add that a new procedure in one branch had run a full month with very good results, saving time and effort.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100180016-4:
Marked IAC-D-103/8 and labeled a first draft, a Fourth Semi-Annual Report of the Ad Hoc Committee on Exchanges covers 1 February to 31 July 1958. The committee was set up on 28 February 1956 to gain the most intelligence value from East-West delegation exchanges, and its field later grew to include materiel. Paper IAC-D-103 served as its guide and general terms of reference throughout the period.

Membership is spelled out: the State Department, Army, Navy, Air Force, the Joint Staff, CIA, and the Atomic Energy Commission, with the information agency attending regularly. CIA supplies both chairman and secretariat, and the committee has no standing subcommittees, turning instead to existing groups or ad hoc teams. The draft notes a rising tempo of exchange activity and detailed negotiation during the half year, and the care needed where a target, a private sponsor, and security concerns meet.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100180025-4:
An ad hoc subcommittee reviews the intelligence side of a proposed exchange with the USSR in the field of permafrost, permanently frozen ground. Background pages stress Soviet strength: over twenty years of organized permafrost research had made the USSR highly capable in its far north, and work was expanding under the International Geophysical Year. Skill in handling frozen ground aided building across the Soviet north.

That skill carried military, economic, and farming weight, the review notes, through better airstrips, possible missile sites, roads, railroads, mining, and water power structures in cold regions. The question put to the subcommittee is the balance of gain: what the United States might learn against what the Soviets might gain. Later pages survey how permafrost study is organized as a separate science, with its own institutes, teaching, journals, and field work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00442a000100050029-4:
Weekly Activities Report No. 10 from the Chief of Headquarters Training, dated 12 March 1959, covers 4 to 10 March and goes to the Director of Training through the Chief of the Operations School. Under significant items, security comes first: two papers on security, one for Headquarters Training staff and one for students, were finished and circulated to all personnel. A named officer was also made Headquarters Training Security Officer, with orders to run occasional surprise checks and report violations.

Syllabus work follows. Production of a syllabus for the Counterintelligence Familiarization Course was completed. Later notes track a course contribution of two and a half days, including a day for cases and problems, and approval of an outline of operational methods. A staff member's draft paper on nuclear energy had been edited, typed, and reproduced during the period covered.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000100110009-4:
A second copy of the Fifth Annual Progress Report of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee covers the same period, 1 July 1956 to 30 June 1957, with the same contents and tabs. The program headings again are planning for economic warfare, an edited transcript of a propellants seminar from June 1956, and other activities. Tabs list completed committee reports, documents distributed to members, and cases pending and completed, with page numbers differing slightly from the companion copy. Its control number also differs slightly from the other copy in the file.

The body argues the same central point. Operational need was pushing the economic defense community to deal direct with individual intelligence parts. At the same time, a government review of multilateral trade controls and coming negotiations made committee coordination valuable. Cover notes record State review completed and Commerce release instructions on file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200080002-4:
A memorandum from the Office of National Estimates, dated 17 May 1957, warns of an Egyptian-Soviet threat in the Yemen. While world attention sat on Jordan and the Suez Canal, the memo argues, Egypt and the USSR had steadily pushed to grow their influence in the Yemen. Set back in Jordan and facing a harder line from King Saud, both had special reason to firm up their Yemen position before it was too late.

The Imam's present coolness toward the United States and Britain gave them a favorable opening, in the memo's judgment. If the trend ran on unchecked, Cairo and Moscow would likely gain a beachhead on the Arabian Peninsula threatening the British position in Aden and giving a flanking position against Saud. A later passage notes the Imam was still smarting over an American aid offer of only one percent of the sum authorized for the Middle East.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200080011-4:
A memorandum dated 1 March 1957, for the Director, opens a two-part account of the situation in Indonesia. President Sukarno was trying to make major changes in the nature and makeup of the Indonesian government. He sought to arrest a fast-worsening political and economic position and to raise his own prestige and power. Under his plan, still in general terms, the role of parties and parliament would be sharply cut back.

Sukarno would chair a new advisory council drawn from non-party groups such as youth, veterans, labor, women, religious bodies, and the military. That council would take a large share of policy decisions from the cabinet. A new cabinet would include all parties holding seats in parliament, Communists among them. Many officers, the memo notes, opposed drift, waste, and corruption. They disliked bringing Communists into government, though army reshuffles may have raised Sukarno's support in Java.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300070002-4:
Paper IAC-D-130, dated 28 August 1958, forwards agreed procedures for United States participation in the NATO Standing Group Intelligence Estimate, sent for information. Tab A holds a letter from Allen W. Dulles to Deputy Secretary of Defense Donald A. Quarles, thanking him for a letter of 15 August that sent the agreed procedures over. Dulles writes that he has approved the statement of understanding, and returns it with the letter.

Tab B carries the Secretary of Defense side of the exchange, and Tab C gives the agreed procedures themselves. They govern, in preparing that estimate, the relations between the Department of Defense and the Joint Chiefs of Staff on one side and the Director of Central Intelligence on the other. Defense review notes on the cover record completed reviews by the defense and joint staffs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000100020143-4:
A materiel annex, organized by tabs, supports a proposed reorganization of Agency air support, though its OCR is rough. Tabs cover a proposed support procedure, and the functions of a materiel branch. They also cover the functions of supply station, maintenance, depot supply, and installations engineering sections. Assigned aircraft lists for a project and for an air division complete the tabs. The mission statement can be read in the opening tab.

That mission is to merge the work of the Aircraft Maintenance and Support Division in the Office of Logistics with Project CHALICE materiel work. The merged functions would be named the Materiel Branch of the Development Projects Division. A second aim is more effective support of Agency air assets. Phases follow: a third phase would push aircraft maintenance and support responsibility out to the field, through an Air Force relationship like the one Project CHALICE enjoyed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000200020043-4:
A United States Air Force service contract, negotiated and dated in 1959, is made with the Lockheed Aircraft Corporation of Burbank, California. Under Article I, the contractor shall furnish, as the government requests from time to time during the contract period, the services of fully qualified airplane contract service technicians. The estimated maximum at any one time is fifteen such technicians, paid at a rate per technician per day of work, plus a monthly administrative charge.

That charge reimburses the contractor for direct costs, indirect costs, and fees tied to the technicians' work; the rate figures themselves are removed in this copy. A termination passage allows the contracting officer to end the contract where he judges that step in the government's best interest, with fair compensation for work performed. A later article bars stated conduct in connection with performance of the work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000200050059-4:
An untitled contract fragment opens with a notice that original pages are missing, then gives clause text on data rights. The contractor may hold a right to grant a license without becoming liable to pay compensation to others solely because of that grant. The same right covers any person employed or assigned by the contractor to originate and prepare data under the contract. The contractor must use all reasonable effort to tell the contracting officer, when subject data is delivered, of any limits on the right of first use in it.

Limits also include portions of data copied from work not composed or produced under the contract. Copies of any license granted to the government under a patent are included too. A ban on affixing restrictive markings follows. A transport passage provides reimbursement of actual cost where commercial transport is available. Where it is not, government transport is free.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300020033-4: A machine-printed account transcript dated 31 July 1956 lists balances and year-to-date figures for project accounts, in columns partly garbled in the scan. Account codes in the rows center on the 6-100410001 group, with sub-accounts and credit entries marked CR. Totals for issues appear in small sums at the head of the visible table, and voucher-style rows follow. The sheet is a raw allotment transcript for the project accounts named in its codes, with no narrative text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300060002-4:
Allotment ledger sheets on Standard Form 1015B carry a printed notice. The postings are furnished as a means for reconciling the reader's records with the accounting office's account. Prompt notice of any discrepancy will be appreciated. One sheet is headed for fiscal 1958, with an account in the 6-1004-40 group marked Other and 01.

An entry on that sheet cancels a fiscal 1956 item by a memorandum dated 16 July 1958, in the amount of 43,469.75 dollars, shown as a transfer figure. Other sheets in the file repeat the form for further accounts, with previous balance, disbursement voucher, and balance columns in the standard layout. The ledger is a working reconciliation tool between offices, not a report.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080046-4: An allotment ledger headed August 1957 covers Aquatone accounts for fiscal 1957. The lead account, 7-1004-10-001, shows 933,369.20 dollars in one column and obligation figures carrying its total to 5,021,167 dollars, while a 7-1004-10-004 account shows 676,479.97 dollars. Column heads sort the figures into expenditure issue, unliquidated and total obligations, allotment authority, and unobligated balance. The sheet is a raw ledger print with no narrative text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080055-4: An allotment ledger headed March 1957 covers Aquatone accounts for fiscal 1957. A small 7-1004-10-000 account shows 124.79 dollars, while the 7-1004-10-001 account shows 333,631.12 dollars in one row and a combined 808,424.76 dollars in another. Column heads cover expenditure issue, unliquidated and total obligation requests, allotment authority, and unobligated balance. The file is a raw ledger print with no narrative text and partly garbled digits.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080064-4: An allotment ledger headed December 1956 covers Aquatone accounts for fiscal 1957 across the 7-1004 series. The lead account shows an expenditure issue of 327,432.65 dollars with 20,225.33 dollars carried forward, closing at 347,658.18 dollars, and the same structure repeats for the 10-004, 30-010, and 50-group accounts. Column heads cover expenditure issue, unliquidated and total obligations, allotment authority, and unobligated balance. The file is a raw ledger print.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080073-4:
September reconciliation sheet for fiscal year 1957 covers allotment account 7-1004-50-012, the same account named in the evidence title. Handwritten figures fill the page in columns, working through the balances that had to agree before the month could close. The scan is faint, and many of the handwritten numbers cannot be read with confidence.

What survives clearly is the form of the work itself. A clerk checked the account line by line, entered corrections, and carried totals forward in pencil or ink. The sheet shows routine Agency bookkeeping at its most basic level, where a monthly account was proved against its own entries rather than simply filed away.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080082-4:
Short Agency accounting sheet headed Adjustments to Be Made to Monthly Report sets out allotment symbol corrections as paired debit and credit entries. Account strings such as 886-600.1-1004-10-001 and 887-600.1-1004-50-011 appear again and again, with small amounts posted between them. The sheet is marked Secret and dated September in the scan.

Each line moves a charge from one allotment symbol to another, so the monthly report would show costs under the right account. Amounts are mostly small, in the tens and low hundreds of dollars. The page is a plain record of bookkeeping repair work, fixing symbols after the original entries had already been made.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00900a000100020005-4:
Agency Comptroller Instruction No. 58, dated 25 June 1958, sets interim steps for collecting data on duty performed by staff employees outside the United States. Its stated aim is to pull the facts from Comptroller records for service on and after 1 July 1958 and place verified data in Office of Personnel files.

All overseas tours and temporary duty trips were to be reported, and United States territories and possessions counted as outside the country. Form 1451a was prepared from travel vouchers after a trip ended, using departure and return dates as actually travelled. Source documents were named by type, so each entry could be traced back and checked again later.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00901a000200020003-4: This declassified CIA document has no surviving title. The untitled pages wait. Their story is kept. The archive holds the file. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00901a000300030001-4:
Confidential Agency list dated December 1959 ranks the Machine Division, OCR, top ten programs for 1 March to 30 September 1959 by machine hours used. The ten are Intellofax, IR ICF, Minicard, Book Orders, GR Spot Index, Gazetteer, Microfilm work, GR Film Index, and the ORR Time Study, with one entry partly redacted in the scan.

Notes on each program follow the ranking. Intellofax volume was falling as requests dropped between the quarters ending June and September 1959. Minicard detail cards were destroyed after summary cards were made, and that test was due to end early in 1960. Book Orders had levelled off and supplied allottees with cost centre data, though Comptroller deadlines were hard to meet on current equipment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00137a000100050001-4:
Revised ORR Machinery Index is a long paper of figures from the Agency's Office of Research and Reports. It gives much wider output indexes for Soviet machine work and fields close to it. The new index is built straight from output data for a great many items. Notes under the tables mark the basis used for each line. The shipping index rests on one set of estimate figures. The electronics index rests on radio and battery data that the branch in charge accepts.

Output of machines for home and farm use is cut down in the new index. The paper itself calls the cut a large one. The drops fall in farm gear, power gear, and goods for the home. A table lists index values branch by branch. Power gear, farm machines, motor vehicles, and railway machine building all appear in it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00137a000100160126-4:
Agency memo dated 22 October 1954 from the Chief, D/I, sends an attached list of top industrial targets in East Germany. Its heading is Selection of Industrial Targets in East Germany. A location and a reason are given for each site on the list. The targets are set out in goods groups, not in order of importance. Copies went to the addressee, to the Chief, D/I, and to branch files.

The attached table is hard to read in the scan. Plant names and figures are badly broken by the poor copy. The covering note is clear, though. The file is a target selection record. It fixes which East German industrial sites one branch rated highest at that date. It also keeps the reasons recorded for each choice.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100020047-4:
Revision dated 15 November, year not shown in the head, updates Section 31, Railways, of the Agency's country questionnaire for Rumania. Chief gaps are named at the start: data on investment and on locomotive and freight car holdings, plus technical facts such as gradients, curvature, rail weight, and length of block sections. Full data of that kind come only from official records, the paper notes, but much can be drawn from observation.

Progress reports are wanted on new line building, double tracking, line repair and improvement, electrification, and new signalling equipment. Question items then call for traffic and operating data, passenger and ton-kilometre figures, and financial and staffing facts for the railway system as a whole.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100030037-4:
Submission dated 29 October 1957 gives economic needs for the Agency's OCI Periodic Requirements List. The list runs from 1 December 1957 to 31 March 1958. Argentina opens the list. A new item asks, in respect of GATT, for facts on reported money troubles. It also asks about member discontent in that body. Reports of Bloc goods and gear of poor quality are asked for as well. Several Argentine items are kept as they stand.

Fresh questions ask for the number of Bloc technicians in Argentina. They ask where those men are and what projects they work on. They ask the status of a Hungarian credit offer to fund imports of rail gear. Brazil items follow in the later pages. They include possible Czech interest in factory growth in Rio Grande do Sul. They include Soviet interest in land growth in northeast Brazil, with investment near 600 million named in the scan.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100160015-4:
Tab A outline sets out an Agency study of Eastern Europe. Section I covers first data on the region. It covers goods and people, and prewar uneven growth. It covers population and factory jobs, and the weight of the region's trades. It covers farming, with land shares and output per acre. It covers bids to build up factories, and chances of saving for growth. It covers state action in the economy. Closing remarks end the section.

Section II covers shifts brought by war and liberation. Land shifts come first. Allied and former enemy countries are then taken in turn. For each, the heads are war damage, status of property, and new duties such as payments for war harm. Later sections treat factory methods made leaner, and how managers are chosen. They treat output per worker and social layers. A last survey sets national income side by side.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180040-4:
Minutes in the Agency's files, ED/EC M-253, record a meeting at 2:00 p.m. on 10 July 1957. The meeting sat in Room 1213, Maiatico. The minutes were issued on 17 July 1957. Mr. William I. Cargo, former United States delegate to COCOM and CHINCOM, attended. The chairman voiced the committee's deep thanks for his work. That thanks went beyond the formal commendation EDAC had already given him. Main items are List II quotas for China. Talk on paragraphs 9 and 21 of the policy paper follows.

Quota talk weighed two ways of setting the sums. One way was item by item. The other was a single lump sum. The lump sum idea rested on a point of fact. Communist China's import needs would not run at one fifth of Soviet needs. They might be far higher, set against a lower national product. So a single sum could suit both sides better.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180167-4:
Statement kept in the Agency's files was prepared for delivery by Vice Admiral Walter S. DeLany, Deputy Director for Mutual Defense Assistance Control. He was to speak before the Subcommittee on Foreign Economic Policy of the Joint Committee on the Economic Report. The talk was set for 2 p.m. on 16 November 1955. Its subject is East-West trade controls. The International Cooperation Administration in Washington issued the text.

DeLany opens by calling the timing apt, since recent efforts had tried to tie security controls to the low level of East-West trade. The items controlled, he argues, are very few. Beside them stands the wide range of goods the Soviet Union and its European satellites could buy from the free world if they wished and could pay. Later passages describe the International Lists and the Battle Act duty to list controlled items, after hearing State, Defense, and Commerce.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200080022-4:
Debriefing summary, with information dated May 1958, records a lecture by a redacted source. The source was questioned by the Agency's ORR staff after a long Soviet trip. The route ran by rail from Helsinki to Moscow and on to Irkutsk. It ran then to Odessa and Kiev. From Kiev it went by air through Chop and Prague, and by rail again. The source took many photographs on the trip. He met only four minor objections, which he neatly avoided.

Rail notes fill the summary. A Finnish steam locomotive hauled the Leningrad to Moscow train eight miles into Soviet territory. An electric locomotive of 5,700 horsepower was seen stored near Leningrad. Subway headways are given as four minutes in Leningrad and two in Moscow. In question and answer, the source saw no reason to doubt the announced Soviet rail figures. He called the railroads extremely active, with vast tonnages moving.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200130026-4:
Selected intelligence compilation dated 17 May 1957 gives data on USSR inland waterways. It is held in the Agency's files. A cargo table compares 1955 and 1956 volumes by goods type. Petroleum rose from 16.5 to 17.9 between the two years. Rafted timber rose from 64 to 68, and lumber carried by ship from 17 to 19. Grain rose from 8.5 to 9.3, and coal and building materials rose as well. A total of 150 is shown for one year on a plan basis. Tons originated and terminated are then tabled by waterway system. The table covers the RSFSR in 1955, about 92 percent of the Soviet total.

A second part lists seasons of use river by river. In the European USSR, seasons run from about late March or early May. They run into October or late November. The Baltic and White Sea waterways are covered on that pattern.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200140025-4:
Study in the Agency's files covers Soviet Bloc and Latin American trade from 1948 to 1958. It describes a flow that stayed small beside Latin America's total trade, however fast it grew from a low base. Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay account for most of the movement. A sharp drop in 1957 is treated in part as the result of set policy by Latin American governments. They had restricted exports on purpose. Exchange rules made trade with Bloc countries harder to run as well.

Latin American motives are set out plainly. Exporters wanted wider markets to raise export earnings. Imports from the Bloc could replace goods hard to import from the West for lack of hard currency. Nationalist feeling reinforced the trend. It pressed for trade ties with all parts of the world. It pressed for greater economic freedom from the United States. The USSR used those openings to expand its trade.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100090051-4:
Top Secret letter dated 8 November 1952 opens with the words Dear Park. It is signed by Allan W. Dulles, Deputy Director of Central Intelligence. It is addressed to W. Park Armstrong Jr., Special Assistant for Intelligence at the Department of State. It encloses a copy of a letter from Fred Andersen, dated 27 October 1952. The writer had a good talk with Andersen the day before about the subject of his letter. Andersen would call on Armstrong before returning to Paris on Tuesday, 11 November.

Andersen's enclosed letter follows up a conversation about intelligence interests and activities in Paris, in partly garbled text. Later pages concern a planned Washington visit in December by another named man, and his consultations with Armstrong and State staff. One subject was use of State channels for transmission, already discussed between the parties.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000200030056-4: A declassified CIA file also on coordination of requirements. The needs, aligned again. The document holds this version. The file remains. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000200050081-4:
Minutes ARC-M-36, handled via the TALENT Control System as TCS-990-57, record a meeting of the Ad Hoc Requirements Committee on Project Aquatone. It met at 2:00 p.m. on 26 February 1957 in Room 214, Administration Building, CIA, James Q. Reber in the chair. Present were Colonels William A. Dodds and Quintin S. Dander, Lieutenant Colonel Byrd Sargent, and Donald Conroy, USMC, with James H. Macia Jr. and Paul J. Nelson of AFOIN.

One item is an Army query from an ACSI memo of 18 February 1957. It asks about receiving available information on reactions of the PS early warning system to Aquatone test flights over this continent. Later business sets an agreed format for the target listing: an introductory statement, category explanations, and a list of Soviet Union targets in alphabetical order. Each target carries its name, coordinate, BE number, and category of primary interest, and the column for agency interest is dropped.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000200080015-4:
Draft dated 26 August 1957 in the Agency's files opens with the word Gentlemen. It is a briefing text on coverage of Soviet targets. One line is drawn at the start of it. Coverage of SAC-type targets, and preparation of folders on them, is not the objective of the briefing. Three areas are named as the critical fields instead. They are the Soviet guided missile system, the long range bomber force, and the Soviet nuclear energy production system.

Present intelligence on all three is stressed as weak: much of the information is fragmentary, and estimates carry significant margins of error. Kapustin Yar is given as an example of the gaps. Perhaps a couple of hundred firings were known. Nothing was known of launching pads, erection and handling equipment, guidance installations, test stands, or fuel storage there. Developments at Tyura Tam are shown against that background.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000500030134-4:
A top secret target list for the Far East fills the file, marked TS-164205. Entries are grouped by country code and then by place name. Each entry names an installation and gives its coordinates, a category code, and a level of interest. Soviet places dominate the early pages, from Alekseyevskoye and Anadyr to Bratsk, Chita, and Irkutsk. Airfields, complexes, and ports make up most entries, with cross references between alternate place names.

Chinese places appear as the list goes on. Entries cover Canton, with a government control centre, Dairen and Port Arthur, Harbin, Hangchow, Hankow, and Peiping. Sakhalin and Pacific coast sites also appear, including Dolinsk, Olga submarine base, and Okhotsk. Like its western companion, the list is a planning reference. It records which Far Eastern sites mattered, where each one sat, and how interest in each was graded for collection purposes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000500080049-4:
Rosters of Talent billets in the Joint Chiefs of Staff make up the file, marked for handling through the Talent control system only. Each entry pairs a post with the officer who held it. The first roster covers the Office of the Chairman, listing the Chairman, his special assistant, executive officer, and military assistant. It continues through the Secretary of the Joint Staff, the Joint Strategic Survey Council, and staff for National Security Council affairs.

A second roster covers J-2, the intelligence directorate. It names the director and deputy director, then officers in plans and policies, estimates, technical intelligence, and collection and dissemination work. Branch teams carry colour names such as Rainbow, Gold, and Red. Asterisks mark new billets. The lists show which senior posts were cleared into the Talent system and who filled them at the time.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700070011-4:
A planning book entry dated 19 December 1952 covers outside research. Staff notes come first, with names withheld in the release. One officer has taken full charge of the office's outside research role. A leadership study for the current intelligence office will be run inside, not farmed out. Staff from the deputy directorate and the clandestine side have roughly agreed a way to start and steer such projects, bound for approval.

Approved work for the rest of fiscal 1953 is then listed by sponsor. Titles include studies of Soviet takeover patterns and control, forced labour in the USSR, machine indexing, and the Manchurian railroad. Sums are withheld. A pending Chinese vulnerabilities study has passed to the clandestine side, which will sound out State and the Psychological Strategy Board. Requests also went out for fiscal 1954 project ideas, for talks in early January.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700070048-4:
Terms of reference for the Watch Committee are sent round in an Army G-2 memorandum dated 20 December 1950. It goes to the heads of State, Navy, Air Force, Joint Staff, Atomic Energy, and FBI intelligence. On 7 December the Intelligence Advisory Committee had agreed the government needed one watch body, run with full member part. The body already working as the Joint Intelligence Indications Committee would fill that role.

Director W B Smith had asked G-2 chief Alexander Bolling to share the terms and arrange any changes needed.
