The memo notes the committee grew over nearly two years from a G-2 file group set up in May 1949. Its agreed terms then follow in full. Name and mission head the list: to gather, weigh, study, and report signs of Soviet-Communist hostile intent. Membership covers all committee agencies. Each may send as many cleared staff as it sees fit.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700080001-4:
A State Department guide, revised on 9 June 1955, reshapes the National Intelligence Survey standard guide for psychological warfare needs. Army, Navy, Air Force, and USIA ideas fed the rewrite. The guide runs very long. Its Chapter IV sections tell writers what a survey of a country's society must cover.

Section 40 asks for a short portrait of the society as a whole. Writers must show its character, stability, and power to bend under change. Class, race, faith, nationality, and language groups all need weighing. So do land, weather, and place. Later sections press on work and jobs. Joblessness and part-time work need causes, trades hit hardest, and groups with spare hands, such as migrants and displaced people. The aim is survey text that planners of persuasion can use.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100110019-4:
Minutes dated 17 January 1957 record a meeting of EDAC Working Group I, on international export control systems. The group met on 9 January in Room 509, Maiatico. Members came from the mutual defence office, State, Commerce, Defense, the aid agency, and CIA. Seven agenda items, plus a cloth item, fill the front page.

Ship sales control heads the list. The group agreed to study the whole ships problem afresh, using two past papers as its base. Tungsten wire cases follow: a German sale to Rumania, and a Dutch sale to Poland. On the Dutch case, Commerce read a fresh technical view. Very low stretch in the wire would bar redrawing it, which opened the way to a kind finding. Other items cover the 1957 List II review, a British China exception for tires, Italian mercury for Poland, fused aluminum oxide powder, and nylon parachute cloth.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470010-4:
Minutes of the seventeenth meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee are dated 31 October 1956. The group met on 11 October. Lieutenant Colonel Richards chaired, with members from the defence, air, Army, naval, commerce, aid, and State sides. First business reached back to June: Commerce asked the group to rethink killing a subcommittee on trade in freed goods.

State raised no bar, and the subcommittee was restored. Next, a paper on Soviet bloc gold sales in free markets won approval. Its case was closed, since the facts did not merit regular reports; big moves would get special papers instead. Ship deliveries to the bloc in 1955, with forecasts to 1958, drew talk. CIA warned that 1958 figures were not yet ready. A last item covered a propellants seminar held in June. Its summary would go out once formally written up, with a working group report to follow.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100490009-4:
A draft copy of the minutes of the tenth meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee fills the file. The meeting ran on 2 June 1955. Pending cases lead, as in the final copy. A paper on bloc exports of capital goods drew promises of more material from Commerce and the aid agency. Work on makers of deleted items moved ahead in Defence, with G-2 to follow through.

Fresh ground in this copy centres on borax. A trade cable of 14 February 1955 had raised questions the group now worked through. Findings were stark: the bloc matched the United States in research on military uses of this goods group. Little was known of real Soviet military use, though. The United States had moved from research into full output in the field. An item on swapping facts with a foreign service, raised in that same cable, sits beside the borax debate.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100490081-4:
A survey report dated 25 January 1955 sets out findings on lowering the grading of allied control papers. It was built to judge which papers could drop from secret to confidential. Tests were fixed with a research chief. Papers hold secret rank, the report states, if they show bloc demand or supply for set goods. Papers on a good's strategic weight, East-West trade, or sources and methods also stay high.

Lower rank fits narrower stuff. Papers sunk in goods definitions, quota calls, or broad allied views on control problems can drop. Trade figures giving only amounts and values can drop too, as can pure process and office matter. The report then sorts the series by kind. One set holds policy debate. Control body records hold talks on figures, enforcement, exceptions, ships, and ratings of single list items.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100500007-4:
Minutes of the sixty-seventh meeting of the Intelligence Working Group cover a session held on 21 October 1954. They are dated 26 October. First came views on a State research staffing plan for economic defence. The defence member cited a directive on what that office owed the parent body. A second item weighed a lasting record of goods intelligence.

At the prior meeting, the defence aid member had offered to spec out such a record. It would log goods facts fed to the joint body during security list reviews. He now withdrew the idea: the hours it would eat beat the gain. CIA noted that its own grading of past list review help sat in one central file, open to all as a reference. The acting chairman then floated a wider tool: a rolling stock list of economic defence projects across the whole community.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100510015-4:
A CIA study of the petrochemical industry in the USSR goes out under a memo dated 27 July 1958. Commerce opened the case. Members had till 1 August to call for debate, or the study would stand approved. Its summary sets the scale of the task. Building up petrochemical output is one of the chief jobs facing the Soviet chemical trade.

Plan language is quoted to prove the point. The now dead Sixth Five-Year Plan called for a drastic rise in the use of oil, natural gas, and oil products. From them would come synthetic rubber and alcohol, detergents, and more. The gain would cut spending of grain and other food stocks. Later pages weigh single products. Fibres for tire cord, aircraft tires, and parachute cloth get close study. Output of two such types is put at about 8,500 tons in 1955, too small for much civil use.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100510060-4:
A letter dated 20 November 1956 forwards the minutes of a committee meeting to a sister group. The acting chairman of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee wrote it. His readers are the chair of the working group on emergency plans. The minutes cover the eighteenth meeting, held on 18 October 1956, as amended on 15 November.

One passage carries the point of the letter. The committee told its chairman to seek help and guidance from the Office of Defense Mobilization. The topic is planning for wartime running of economic warfare. That ask stands only if the emergency plans group finds it fitting. In the minutes, talk opens with a ruling from above: each subcommittee must draft a wartime plan of work. Members were urged to keep debate tight. On one broad point they agreed at once: war would demand joined handling of economic warfare intelligence, much as with censorship material.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100510097-4:
A working group paper dated 2 November 1955 marks up a draft Foreign Service reporting rule. The rule covers economic ties with the Sino-Soviet bloc. It may sit in the Foreign Service Manual as a secret add-on, coded ERC 34. CIA views are given section by section. Some sections win no comment. Others draw one sharp fix: write Sino-Soviet Bloc where the draft says Soviet Bloc.

Several sections get full rewrites, supplied as attachments. The first attachment restates who uses these reports and why. Commerce, Defense, State, and Treasury hold the chief policy and working stakes. Commerce and Treasury run American export and money control laws in the main. Later guidance tells posts to mine allied control papers and delegation cables. East-West trade reporting must also tie closely to control work already in train.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200010051-4:
A short letter from Lawrence Houston, the Agency's general counsel, confirms a deal on patent help. It goes to the chief of the Army's Patents Division. Agency patent traffic has been light, Houston writes, and will stay so. Its staff and rooms for such work are most modest. The Army's offer to lend its skilled staff is thus warmly valued.

With the letter go the papers on one live case. It is the same deadbolt re-locking device for combination locks, built by an Agency employee. A patent board has ruled that no transfer of title to the government is required. Yet the device will likely serve the public interest, so the man has been asked to grant the government a lasting, royalty-free licence. Two papers are listed as needed: a certificate that the improvement fits the public interest test in law, and the signed licence agreement itself.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200090008-4:
A legal memo dated 10 March 1959 takes apart two bills on the National Security Agency. It goes to the Legislative Counsel. Senate bill 421, of 17 January 1959, comes first. Its first section frees that agency from the Classification Act of 1949, with a cap: pay may not top the rate for like work under that Act. Its second section lets the agency's director set higher pay for scarce research staff.

That higher pay is capped at 19,000 dollars a year, the rate set in Title 10. Further sections cover hardship payments for staff abroad, and a tidying cut of an older power to set fifty such posts. A secrecy section bars forced spread of the agency's structure, work, or staff names. House bill 4599, of 17 February, is then set beside it. It would itself grant the fifty research posts at the same pay cap. Its secrecy clause matches the Senate bill in substance.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200100006-4:
Correspondence dated January 1958 links CIA's counsel to a hearing on atomic law. A letter of 29 January from Lawrence Houston thanks James Ramey, executive director of the Joint Committee on Atomic Energy. Houston is frank: the Agency's stake in the planned changes to the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 is narrow.

The Agency will have little to add on the points in that letter, he writes. Still, a witness will attend the subcommittee hearing and give such testimony as members wish. Ramey's own letter of 28 January rides in the file. It carries Senator John Pastore's letter to Lewis Strauss, who chairs the atomic commission. Pastore chairs the subcommittee on agreements for cooperation. His letter sets a hearing for the next day at two in the afternoon. It asks for firm answers to listed questions, starting with how the plans change the swapping of atomic information with other lands.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300070009-4:
A memo on an Inspector General survey of the Office of Personnel adds one officer's own views. The writer starts with a legal fact: CIA stands exempt from the Classification Act. It must thus build its own stand-in for the career shelter the civil service gives by law.

The present program, he argues, is only a small step that way. The heart of any career system is holding staff safe from the whim of an agency head or from political winds. Law gives that shelter to the civil service, the Foreign Service, and the armed forces. CIA tried to give it by inside orders alone. That shelter has never faced a hard test: a deep cut in force, or a change of Director. A congressional panel, the Kilday Subcommittee is named, might doubt the Agency can stay above politics if no worker holds a retention right in law.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300070018-4:
Memos for the record from January 1956 log the legal birth of language training awards. The first, dated 25 January, notes a talk with John Moore of the Comptroller General's legal staff. The program was not yet fully built out, counsel told him. Moore saw no need for a fine account of how award rights would be set. 

An earlier note, dated 17 January, catches a task force at work. On 10 January it held the third in a run of meetings, set up by the deputy director for support. Counsel's stake was one slice of the plan: cash awards for staff who reach set levels of skill in a foreign tongue. A statement of principles for building the Agency's language store rides in the file. It demands skill in reading, writing, and speaking the tongues that matter to national security, held ready at all times.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400030002-4:
A memo dated 29 October 1958 flags a court case for the Director's eye. The Supreme Court has just taken up Greene v. McElroy. At stake: the law of a security clearance pulled from a contractor's man. If the Court backs Greene on rights grounds, the Defense Department's plant security scheme will need some change. CIA's own way, the memo judges, should stand near untouched.

Greene ran a firm, ERCO, whose trade was defense work. When the Navy pulled his clearance, he lost a post paid at eighteen thousand a year. He fell to drafting work at forty-four hundred. The trial court held for the state: no true court point arose. A man who takes a pact takes its terms, security terms in the count. The appeals court backed that view. Both low courts dodged the rights point. The high court may not.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100080068-4:
Dated 6 March 1959 and marked LAS/TR, a course outline presents Personal Effectiveness Abroad, a seminar on cultural and personal factors in the work of Agency staff overseas. Staff gain the understandings and skills needed to deal with people of other cultures and to live well in a foreign society. An American's home habits are compared with those of foreign nationals in their own settings.

A day-by-day schedule follows, running through April sessions in 1959. Topics move from basic concepts for grasping personal effectiveness abroad to surveys of the individual in his society, then to specific problems of dealing with foreign nationals. The outline shows how each session builds on the last, mixing talks, discussion, and study of accepted behaviour abroad.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00939a000100080018-4:
Language study at the Foreign Service Institute is put on a set schedule in a 15 October 1949 memorandum to division and staff chiefs. Requests for most languages could be made simply by a note on the training request form, with the training office handling arrangements and approval. Chiefs were urged to file requests as far ahead as possible.

Popular languages would run as close to their enrolment ceilings as staffing allowed, to cut the present cost per student. Exceptions to the schedule would be rare, granted only for extreme and unforeseen emergencies. Special languages not in usual demand needed long-range planning because staff, rooms, and budget were limited. An attached schedule lists the courses, including weekly seminars on geographic areas meant to accompany intensive language classes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000400080012-4:
Comments on an Inspector General survey of the Office of Communications are forwarded to the Director of Central Intelligence on 22 February 1956 by L. K. White, Deputy Director for Support. The comments of the Director of Communications are attached, and White states his general agreement with them. Several points, though, needed more study before a firm conclusion could be reached.

That further study would involve coordination with activities inside and outside the Agency, and a follow-up report was promised for about 1 May 1956 if the Director approved. A second attachment carries a proposed commendation for the communications office, drawn up at the Inspector General's suggestion and sent onward for the Director's signature.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200030006-4:
Handling the flood of intelligence expected from Project AQUATONE is planned in a 1 November 1955 memorandum from the Deputy Director for Intelligence to the Air Force intelligence director. A new Agency office would screen, interpret, index, and file the project's information. Photography was expected to start flowing in April 1956, small at first, then rising sharply to a peak that October.

The case for the office rests on value. High-quality aerial photographs would cover parts of the Soviet Union that had stayed out of reach, and the sums spent gathering them demanded full use. Filing systems are weighed in detail. A large MINICARD installation is judged premature, since the system was untested and delivery dates unsure, though a move toward it later is recommended.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200110016-4:
A trip to ITEK on 2 and 3 December 1958 is reported in memorandum COR-0270, dated 9 December 1958. Two visitors went to settle a dispute over film processing and printing equipment for CORONA photography. ITEK's processors and printers were being compared with those made by Eastman Kodak, and ITEK's general manager, Walter Levison, had raised two concerns.

Levison held, first, that Eastman's processors and printers would not keep the fine detail the camera captured. Second, he charged that Eastman's Mr. Green was not giving the ITEK equipment a fair trial and was not cooperating with ITEK staff. The visitors spent the two days working through each charge, walking Levison through the Eastman equipment and the test results. Untangling a mix-up over who had barred repairs to an electronic unit.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200110098-4:
Duties for research, development, and test work inside the Development Projects Staff are clarified in a 24 October 1958 memorandum, DPS-4898. New technical staff at headquarters and a full rotation of senior people at Edwards Air Force Base had unsettled old habits and procedures. Whether a major new program would be launched was still unsure, but the writer judged an informal clearing of roles useful at once.

Primary responsibility for all new development work rests with the Director of Development and Procurement. He was to be free to concentrate on technical matters, with negotiation and expediting kept off his desk as much as possible. Later passages cover how headquarters decisions reach the field, noting that most are priority calls between rival test activities, and that local staff must coax contractors through a multitude of small matters.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200200034-4:
Two linked decisions are framed in a paper on AQUATONE and the Soviet note of 10 July. Within days, choices must be made on the project's future and on the answer to the Soviet protest, Soviet Note No. 23. Any reply has to reckon with whether overflight operations continue, and should leave the United States well placed against further Soviet moves.

The main risk of continuing is political: the cost if overflights were convincingly pinned on the United States government in world opinion, perhaps through Soviet action in the Security Council. To judge that risk, the paper asks what Soviet reaction may follow and how a damaging political offensive could be discouraged. One proposal shapes the reply as both a denial of the alleged crossings and a counter-attack built on documented Soviet clandestine activity.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100040006-4:
Objectives for an electronics conference session on economic intelligence are stated in a revised paper numbered EIC/JTSC-D-3, dated 7 November 1957. The first day's session treats telecommunications facilities. Its theme asks why the Soviet electronics industry's broad postwar progress does not show up in the quality and quantity of electronics used in basic telecommunications operations.

If that observation holds, the paper argues, Soviet telecommunications facilities still suffer from low priority. Judged against present plant and future need, those facilities lag five to ten years behind other priority electronics achievements. Papers and discussion for the session are meant to answer the general question of the state of Soviet telecommunications facilities and services, treating specific aspects one by one.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100050078-4:
Soviet sites known or suspected of association with ballistic missile development and production are listed in Attachment A, with installation names, places, and short descriptions. Bolshevo, Chirchik, Dnepropetrovsk, Dzerzhinsk, Gorkiy, and Irkutsk open the list. Plant numbers appear where the site is a factory, such as Plant 96 at Gorkiy and Plant 39 near Irkutsk, south of that city's airfield.

Moscow entries reach into research and teaching. They include the All-Union Institute of Aviation Materials, the Artillery Engineering Academy, the Central Institute of Aviation Engines, and the Central Institute of Aircraft Fuels and Lubricants, each with a street address. One Dnepropetrovsk plant is placed south of the town, beside a main road with a double-track tramway running from the town to a crossroads at the works' southeast corner.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100120016-4:
A senior planning and review board for the Economic Research Area is proposed in a paper dated 12 November 1959, sent to all recipients with a request for their caveats. The board would sit directly under the chief of the area and consist of its division chiefs. Its first duty would be review before publication of all major products from every branch in the area.

National estimate contributions and area-wide projects fall in that duty, while survey and current intelligence pieces are left out. The board would receive products straight from the branches, pass them on with a group recommendation, discuss coordinated reports with the responsible branch early. Help set the terms of reference for estimate work. A further aim is judgment of worth: not only whether products are correct, but whether they are worth doing at all.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100120052-4:
Notes on Project 30.2043 pick through a draft on China page by page. One correction is factual and sharp. A table cited for a claim shows only percentages. The proper table shows that complete plants made up about one-fourth of Soviet machinery and equipment exports to China in 1950 and 1951. Is more than the 'insignificant' share the draft asserted.

Style and judgment are pressed elsewhere. A passage on cultural services such as bus stations, schools, and hospitals is called overly didactic and in need of shortening. Later, the reviewer asks who cheap electric fans are meant for, when copper is scarce and electric power both scarce and costly. The closing notes ask whether choices about building items for home production and about surplus labour were first made in terms of Chinese objectives, before effects are measured by outside standards.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100130079-4:
A gaps statement on the aircraft industry of East Germany is forwarded for review on 9 March 1959. Knowledge of that industry's scope, performance. Progress matters strategically and economically, the statement says, since East German aircraft effort can signal East German and Soviet intentions in military matters and in free-world economic penetration.

Performance is judged quite well known in outline. At Dresden-Klotzsche, output of Il-14 Crate piston-engine transports is described, with production of the type to stop late in 1959 when series production of '152' jet transports is scheduled to start. Other aircraft are considered for eventual production at Dresden. Sub-assembly work, overhaul of aircraft. Series production of large piston and turbojet engines elsewhere in East Germany are also noted, with better knowledge of investment and production costs named as a need.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100170011-4:
Project 30.2043, a study of the development of the machine building industry in Communist China from 1949 to 1962, is reviewed on 26 January 1959. The reviewer calls it a comprehensive and penetrating analysis of the industry's status and problems, unusually discerning and essentially sound. In his opinion it will make a valuable contribution and should be submitted for publication.

One major obstacle stands in the way: length. At almost three hundred pages, much of the good analysis is buried in detail, and the organisation repeats itself. Problems are treated separately under investment, production, and theory of development, so conclusions diffuse and weaken. Detailed comments are attached, down to an overworked phrase about types of motors that China can and does produce, used three times in one paragraph.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100170039-4:
A service contract with an outside scholar is proposed to fill a research gap. The scholar's name is blacked out. The study wanted deals with small-scale plants in Communist China. It asks what weight such plants carry in machine making. No sound study exists on the point. None weighs the small plants plan as a path to fast gains. None weighs its problems and limits either.

Branch staff are fully used on secret facts. Their field is machine building and light trade in the Sino-Soviet bloc. So the work must go outside. The scholar would use Chinese-language books at Stanford. The Library of Congress would serve as well. Work would be full time in summer and part time after. That equals about four to six months of full time in all. The study is judged fit to print outside the government when done.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00346a000100110038-4:
Solidified gasoline is the subject of a paper dated 26 February 1958. A process had been developed by which a solid fuel is prepared from a chemical derivative, an ester. Gasoline, and an Italian process of similar kind is named as inferior to it. In the processes described, the gasoline can be returned from the solid to the liquid state by mechanical means.

A contract to produce solid gasoline had been negotiated, with a named company taking part. United States interest, though, had cooled long before. The original American project was abandoned in 1948 after a study was analysed by a committee drawn from the petroleum industry, Columbia University. The National Research Council, and American industry is described as indifferent to the process. Fresh foreign activity in late 1957 is what brings the subject back onto the desk.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100040080-4:
A memorandum from the Director of the Office of Civil and Defense Mobilization on Soviet civil defence, dated 17 November 1959, is corrected point by point. Soviet claims that eighty-nine percent of the population had completed a ten-hour course. That a more advanced twenty-two-hour course had reached twenty-nine percent, are repeated in that memorandum without evaluation, the comments note.

Research in the Central Intelligence Agency leads to a smaller shelter figure. Only about twenty-eight percent of the city population of the Soviet Union could be accommodated in existing shelters. Most of those shelters are of the relatively light basement type, which afford little protection against blast effects. The outside report, the comments add, speaks of the urban population, not the total population. On training, available intelligence suggests only about half the total population has completed the longer course.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090003-4:
Soviet goals, capabilities, and limits from 1959 to 1975 form the second lecture in the Army War College series. The series deals with the Soviet economic system. The goals set by the Kremlin leaders reflect the goals of world Communism itself, the speaker argues. In the broadest sense, that goal is the end of the free society of the West. A Sovietised world order would take its place.

A harder tone in Soviet foreign policy over the past year is traced to one belief. The leaders think the bloc's power has grown while the West's has declined. The lecture then turns to the Seven Year Plan and the Soviet consumer. In consumer goods output, the Soviet citizen will see slower gains through 1965. The same holds for likely rises in real wages. The pace will fall below that of the past seven years. Strength is weighed against those limits for the years ahead.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090012-4:
Comments on the draft of the Director's address to a Joint Economic Committee group are sent on 2 November 1959. The sender is the Chief of the Analysis Division. The comments follow the draft page by page. They propose cuts and swaps. One note gives page references to the best estimates of Soviet economic growth then at hand.

A swap paragraph is offered for the part on Soviet factory output. It restates output as a share of the American level, on a normal base year. It warns that the national income estimate carries a larger margin of error. Other notes tighten single sentences. One strikes a long passage on transport. The file shows the economic research staff vetting the Director's public figures line by line before delivery.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090049-4:
America's human resources to meet the world scientific challenge are considered at a Yale conference on 3 February 1958, where Allen W. Dulles speaks on the Soviet challenge. His share of the task is the challenge posed by Soviet scientific and technical advances, which is not easy, he says, to divide into tidy compartments.

Science pervades the Soviet military threat. It pervades its industrial and economic progress too. Much Soviet aid to newly developing countries includes technical help, and even Soviet subversive work shows great skill in the technical training of agent personnel. The challenge calls for united action: Dulles urges pooling the scientific assets of the United States with those of the free world, for the common good and mutual defence. On the immediate issues, he sees no evidence that the Soviet Union now intends a policy involving serious risk of nuclear war, given its healthy respect for American military strength.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090085-4:
Soviet Economic Development is a declassified Agency briefing text on the pace and shape of Soviet growth. It states that Soviet gross national product was growing nearly twice as fast as that of the United States. Soviet output stood at about 40 percent of the United States level, while what consumers received stood near 25 percent.

Heavy industry and military readiness kept first claim on resources. A newer consumer program added housing and farm output to that list. The text gives military spending at about 170 to 180 billion rubles a year. It closes with Bloc trade and aid in poorer regions, and with Soviet oil output as a coming source of exports.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090094-4:
The Soviet Civil Defense Program is a declassified Agency paper dated January 1958. It judges the Soviet civil defense effort to be long standing rather than new. Spending on building, gear, and training had grown over many years, with no sign of a sudden surge since 1950 or 1951.

Training ran through small groups in factories and club rooms, with little public notice. Shelter signs, the paper notes, would be posted only under stated doctrine at a set time. It also reports guard type units formed in main cities since 1956, sirens in place, and duty officers on watch. Stocks of emergency supplies are noted, though their exact size is left unknown.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090148-4:
An untitled Agency text, partly hard to read in its scan, weighs the Soviet Union's place in world trade and aid. Legible parts state that Moscow had declared its aim to build a first class commercial fleet. They also note that Soviet trade rested on a state monopoly system unlike Western practice.

Clearer later pages compare aid given by each side. Western help to poorer nations over about two and a half years is put near twelve billion dollars. That total covers private investment and loans from world bodies as well as state aid. Aid from the whole Sino-Soviet Bloc in the same span is put at under two billion dollars.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100010-4:
The Economic Front is a lecture given on 17 July 1959 to the National Strategy Seminar for Reserve Officers, kept in declassified Agency files. The speaker warns that the Soviet challenge is military, political, and subversive as well as economic. He states the Communist aim as the end of free society and a Sovietized world order.

Aid terms form a large part of the lecture. United States aid had rested mainly on grants, while Bloc loans are put at two and a half percent interest. Repayment came in goods, starting the year after a project such as a cement plant began to produce. Yearly talks on repayment prices let Moscow be tough or lenient at will.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100038-4:
Ponomarev on International Workers Solidarity is a declassified Agency file holding an excerpt from the Moscow newspaper Pravda of March 6, 1959. The piece argues that the Soviet seven-year plan would lift the strength of the whole socialist camp. It predicts a rising pull for the ideas of Marxism-Leninism across the world.

It also predicts new strength for national liberation movements in colonial and dependent lands. Soviet aid is praised as help given without military or political conditions. The Bhilai metallurgical plant in India, built with Soviet aid, is held up as a plain result of that help. Western charges of pressure on aid recipients are rejected as slander.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s01099r000100010009-4:
Inspector General's Recommendation, Page 111 is a declassified Agency attachment that records a review point and the replies to it. The recommendation asks the DD/P to review budget and fiscal arrangements between Division D and the area divisions. Projects supervised by one side were budgeted by the other, and a clear policy statement was wanted.

The DD/P reply concurs and notes that a revised directive was being readied. Area divisions would fund and support projects aimed at collecting special intelligence. Policy and technical guidance would stay with Division D. A later attachment, on pages 146 and 147, takes up machine methods for other COMINT files under the same chief.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s01099r000100030007-4:
Inspector General's Recommendation, Page 51 opens a thick set of declassified Agency attachments, each pairing a recommendation with office replies. The first asks that help with housing, furniture, and furnishings for personnel be allowed within safe limits. The chief of station on the spot would judge how far such help could safely go.

Both the DD/P and DP/S replies concur, with action to start once the Director approved. Attachments run on through page 353, with most replies marked concur or defer. Many of the statements themselves are blacked out in the released copy. What remains shows the review machinery at work: a finding, a named action, and a signed reply.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100020019-4:
Alternative Possibilities in Trade Control Policy is a section of a declassified Agency staff study on how to control trade with the Soviet Bloc. Its first choice is stark: a complete embargo, or selective denial under a set standard. The aims of the program, it argues, should decide which system is used.

A full embargo is granted real strengths. It is clear, easy to defend, and denies all help to a possible future enemy. It might even draw less protest from exporters than a partial system. Price ratio tables in the study, covering goods such as aluminum and cobalt, supply the cost data behind the argument.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100040008-4:
Foreign Attitudes Toward Economic Defense is Staff Study No. 3 in the CFEP Drafting Group's Economic Defense Policy Review, draft of June 6, 1955. Its abstract states the core point plainly. The United States by itself had almost no direct control over what the Soviet Bloc imported, since United States exports formed so small a share.

Allied views thus decide what controls can do. The Italy section credits a forceful recent chairman of COCOM for part of that nation's role. It also notes Italian traders who gained from illegal trade in strategic goods. Heavy United States economic and military aid is given as a reason Italy might follow the United States lead more closely. The paper rests in the Agency's CREST release.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100080004-4:
Comments on CFEP Staff Study #7 form a declassified Agency office memorandum dated 12 June 1955. The study under review dealt with uniformity of free world trade controls. The writer finds it generally sound and backs its conclusion, while granting that deeper analysis in spots would improve it.

Two edits are urged. The words or danger should come out of the conclusion on page 10, the writer argues. A new sentence should warn that repeated grants of special latitude carry their own risk. Later notes ask whether agreed tests for special latitude could be set, then doubt that the effort would pay.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100160005-4:
U.S. Policies on Enforcement of Controls is Staff Study No. 16 of the CFEP Drafting Group, draft of June 7, 1955. It treats enforcement as one problem with two faces. One face is joint action with allies, and the other is what the United States does alone or with a single partner.

The study warns that the two faces cannot truly be split. Acts taken alone still shape how allies judge the shared program. On the joint side, progress came only after long talks and delays. Five months of added bargaining followed the deal that tied new transactions controls to the August 1954 list reduction. The paper rests in the Agency's CREST release.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100190002-4:
Note on the Balance of Payments of the European Soviet Bloc with the Free World is Staff Study No. 19 of the CFEP Drafting Group, draft of June 15, 1955. The study runs to six pages. It tries to set Bloc earnings and spending with the free world into one balance.

Its tables carry frank gaps. Some franc figures and clearing accounts are left out for lack of data, though the authors judge the broad picture safe. When all items are added, a leftover of errors and omissions remains. That leftover, put at about 50 million dollars in 1948-49 and 100 to 125 million in 1950-53, marks Bloc exchange earnings whose use could not be traced. The study survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000100040053-4:
Final Course Report, Instructional Techniques Course No. 44, dated 2 June 1960, closes out a forty hour course run from 23 to 27 May 1960. Eight students took it, all from the Office of Communications, at grades GS-9 through GS-12. Their own work called on them to lecture and to run demonstrations.

Seven films from the training film library supported the teaching, covering learning rules, lesson planning, and speech methods. Practice teaching filled much of the week. After each student's presentation, classmates and the instructor gave an oral critique at once. That instant feedback is named as the course's core device for fixing lessons in mind. The report survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200020126-4:
Foreign Service Institute Training names a Congressional Record appendix item kept in Agency files: an extension of remarks by Hon. Francis P. Bolton of Ohio in the House on Tuesday, April 12, 1960. The appendix pages around it range widely, as such pages do. Health bill debate under the Forand bill fills part of the text.

The training matter that gives the item its title weighs how the Foreign Service Institute teaches. Poor maintenance of class strength, the text warns, cuts the value of teaching and raises costs. A second question follows: how far other agencies should use FSI facilities. Such use fills standby staff time, but it may also work against the State Department's own best interests.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200060005-4:
Extracts from Executives for Government, a Brookings Institution study of federal personnel administration by Paul T. David and Ross Pollock, dated October 1957 and December 1958, were kept in Agency files. The extracts set two staffing patterns side by side in a plain table. Each row contrasts how the two systems hire, judge, and advance their people.

The program system recruits for a lifetime career, young and before deep work experience. It judges long range promise over quick output, and it grows staff by training and assignment. The job system, by contrast, hires people already fit for set posts. Advancement there turns on open posts and job fitness, not on service merit or seniority.
cicero-letters-shuckburgh-vol-4:
Murder and revenge close Cicero's correspondence in the fourth volume of Shuckburgh's 1899 version. Caesar falls on the Ides of March, and Antony rises in his place. Cicero thunders against him in the Philippics and pays with his life.

Private letters sit beside public fury in this most dramatic volume. Hope after the tyrant's death curdles into fresh terror and proscription lists. The Republic's last great voice is hunted down and silenced. Few ancient books end so darkly or so well, with the writer's own death as the final, grim proof of all he had warned against.
cinq-mars-volume-4:
Alfred de Vigny leaps two years forward in Cinq-Mars, Volume 4 of the English edition. His narrator borrows Shakespeare's privilege, he jokes, and jumps across time and space at will. Paris and the dark old palace of the Louvre come back into view. Two years, he warns, can change men and fortunes past knowing.

Cinq-Mars returns hardened, his favor curdled into open rivalry with Richelieu. The conspiracy that was talk in earlier volumes now gathers names, money, and foreign promises. De Thou still follows his friend, though dread grows with each secret meeting. Court ceremony hides the plotting like silk over a blade. Marie de Gonzague's marriage prospects shift the hero's hopes as politics shifts his plans. Readers feel the pace change here: youth and pageantry give way to whispers, couriers, and the first shape of a treaty that France will call treason when it surfaces.
clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of-a-you:
Clarissa Harlowe — Volume 4 of Richardson's novel in letters finds Clarissa in lodgings, fighting over a single question: whether she and Lovelace are privately married. He offers matrimony, the contents note, but in such a manner that she could not close with the offer. Her caution extends to doors, windows, and the seals of letters.

Miss Howe devises a way for the two friends to write every day. Lovelace hunts for a house, Mrs. Fretchville's, and presses Clarissa to attend a collation with four of his select friends and a Miss Partington. His own letters, with their stage directions for his friends' behavior before the lady, expose the delay as studied, not chance.
conscience-volume-4:
Hector Malot lets success rot from inside in Conscience, Volume 4 of the English edition. Saniel, now an established doctor, finds his sleep broken after Madame Dammauville's death. Until then he had slept in tranquility, even after Caffie. Now he wakes suffocating and startled, with hallucinations crowding the dark.

Caffie, long effaced from memory, returns in dreams dragged back by the second dead woman. Long workdays fail to buy him hours of the sleep Shakespeare called sore labor's bath. Saniel diagnoses his own case with calm and private terror. Phillis and her brother Florentin's case press new choices on his success. Malot makes the haunting clinical: nerves, habit, and memory do the punishing. Readers in the final volume watch conscience collect its debt in the one currency the murderer cannot refuse, his rest.
cosmopolis-volume-4:
Paul Bourget closes his Roman novel in Cosmopolis, Volume 4 of the English edition. Count Boleslas Gorka lies wounded after his duel, beaten by the man he meant to punish. Dorsenne, the friend he struck at as a traitor, has humiliated him instead. His seconds, Cibo and Pietrapertosa, arrive from the Tor di Quinto races with careful, lying reports.

Madame Steno and her daughter were at the races, and Madame Maitland came triumphantly with her husband. The engagement of young Ardea to Fanny Hafner is public, and a cardinal has baptized the girl. Lydia Maitland's infamy stands discovered at last, yet she glitters on unpunished. Gorka counts his wrongs from his bed: rival, mistress, and false friend all happy in May sunshine. Bourget ends on that contrast rather than a tidy settling. Readers finishing Cosmopolis find its moral plain: modern society wounds faith and honor, then hurries smiling to the races.
curtius-history-greece-vol-4:
Athens crowns the fourth volume of Curtius's History of Greece, in Ward's 1868 version. Pericles leads, the Parthenon rises, and bold new thinkers question all things. Then the Peloponnesian War breaks out and shadows the glory.

Curtius writes the golden age with feeling for both its shine and its cost. Drama, sculpture, and debate flourish beside plague and ambition. Athens gains an empire and begins to lose its soul. The volume holds his history's brightest and saddest turn in one. A city stands at its height, already sowing the strife that would bring it down in time.
dialstone-lane-part-4:
Chapters fourteen to seventeen of W. W. Jacobs's novel fill this fourth part of Dialstone Lane. Mrs Chalk sits on the turf and watches the schooner shrink to a white speck, half hoping it will own its error and come back for her. It does not, and she denounces husbands in general and her own in chief.

Mrs Stobell finds the plot plain at last: that is why no yachting costume was allowed her, and why the house was never shut up. Her husband's morning kiss, she now sees, meant goodbye. Fried bacon, Brisket holds, will finish any man disposed to be queer at sea, and Tredgold lays it to imagination. This file holds part four only.
diana-of-the-crossways-volume-4:
The fourth volume of George Meredith's Diana of the Crossways covers chapters twenty-seven to thirty-five. Matter for a subsequent explosion is laid quietly in place. A dialogue around a portrait shows Diana as adviser to Percy Dacier, the young minister of state. Political and domestic crises approach in company.

A little dinner leaves an aftertaste of danger. Diana's enemies whisper that she sells political secrets, and the charge gathers force. Meredith darkly hints that the criminal's judge may be love's own appointee. The true heroine of romance comes at last to her time of trial. These chapters tighten the net around a woman whose wit made her famous and vulnerable. Talk itself becomes evidence against her, in a novel built from conversation.
dio-cassius-roman-history-cary-vol-4:
Books forty-one through forty-five of Dio Cassius cover the civil war of Caesar and Pompey and what came after. They appear here in Earnest Cary's Loeb English, the fourth volume of his set. Dio wrote around 230 CE, drawing on records and tales that have since been lost.

Caesar crosses the Rubicon, wins at Pharsalus, and takes sole power in Rome. Dio follows his reforms, his rule, and the daggers of the Ides of March. Speeches and omens fill out the story. No Roman writer gives a fuller run of these years, and Dio's books form the spine of the set's middle.
dionysius-halicarnassus-roman-antiquitie:
The fourth volume of Edward Spelman's 1758 English Dionysius holds books nine through eleven of the Roman Antiquities, with an index. Dionysius wrote around 7 BCE, and his huge history of early Rome ends, as far as it survives, in the early fourth century BCE.

These books give the decemvirs, the ten men whose rule turned harsh and shook the state, and the wars that followed. Dionysius wrote with a Greek reader in mind, keen to prove Rome Greek in its roots. His work stays our fullest source for the regal age and the early republic. Later books are lost past this point.
donovan-pasha-and-some-people-of-egypt-v:
Donovan Pasha and Some People of Egypt, Volume 4, by Gilbert Parker, opens above Cairo at Ramadan. In A Young Lion of Dedan, two men look out from a minaret. The Pyramids of Ghizeh and Sakkara stand far off. Nearer lie the tombs of the Caliphs and the Khedive's palace. Below them the city spreads its roof gardens and minarets. Housewives lounge on the housetops. Harem women watch through carved panels.

The two watchers are Dicky Donovan and Captain Renshaw of the American Consulate. Donovan is now English Secretary to the Khedive. Parker says no man in Egypt held more importance. It could neither be bought nor sold. He Would Not Be Denied, The Flower of the Flock, and The Light of Other Days complete this final volume. The cycle ends where it lived, between palace and bazaar, with reputation as the only real currency.
elson-grammar-school-literature-book-4:
William H. Elson and Christine Keck's Elson Grammar School Literature, Book Four, is a school reader for grammar-school pupils. Elson, superintendent of schools in Cleveland, joined with Keck, principal of the Sigsbee School in Grand Rapids, to assemble it.

The first part offers famous rides, from Longfellow's Paul Revere's Ride to Tennyson's Charge of the Light Brigade, with selections from Shakespeare and other poets and studies in rhythm. Later parts add nature poems, stories and patriotic pieces by Bryant, Shelley, Byron, Poe and others. Teachers and collectors of schoolbooks will find it a rich, old-fashioned anthology, built to teach reading through great verse.
ethics-part-4:
Benedict de Spinoza calls part four of his Ethics, in Elwes's translation, Of Human Bondage, or the Strength of the Emotions. His preface defines bondage plainly: a man prey to his emotions is not his own master and often follows the worse course while seeing the better. Perfection, good, and evil are first redefined as useful notions, not facts of nature.

The propositions show why reason counsels cooperation, honesty, and the state, whose laws settle by common consent what belongs to each man. Justice and sin, he notes, are ideas from outside, not attributes of the mind itself. Part four is Spinoza's ethics in the everyday sense: how people can live together with less fear.
euripides-plays-way-loeb-1912-vol-4:
The fourth Way volume of Euripides, first printed in 1912, holds Ion, Hippolytus, Medea, and Alcestis. The scan staged here is a 1928 reprint. Medea, the most famous of the four, gives the foreign wife who murders her own children to wound the husband who discarded her.

Hippolytus shows a queen's false charge destroying the stepson who scorned love. Alcestis opens the set's lighter side: a wife dies for her husband, and Heracles wrestles Death to bring her back. Ion traces a temple foundling to his royal, god-touched birth. With this volume Way's Loeb Euripides stands complete in nineteen plays. English readers gained the whole poet in verse at last.
evan-harrington-volume-4:
The fourth volume of George Meredith's Evan Harrington runs from chapter nineteen to chapter twenty-five. Letters from the Countess de Saldar, Evan's managing sister, drive much of this stretch. She reports a runaway wife sheltered by Lady Jocelyn and manoeuvres around the scandal. Her despatches mix high comedy with cool calculation.

A break-neck leap gives the volume its physical climax. The daughters of the great Mel must digest their father's memory at a grand dinner. Evan's double life, gentleman abroad and tailor's son at home, strains every relation. Rose Jocelyn's family watches him with growing suspicion. Meredith ends the portion with a stream flowing muddy and clear, an image for reputations in doubt. Courtship, family pride, and the fear of the shop counter fill these chapters.
fairy-gold-ship-s-company-part-4:
Jacobs's Fairy Gold is the fourth part of his Ship's Company story set. W. W. Jacobs wrote these comic tales of working men and sharp talk. This part opens in talk between Mr. Augustus Teak and his friend Mr. Chase. Teak presses Chase to come for a pint and talk things over.

Teak wants Chase as a lodger in his house of thirteen years' standing. His former lodger, Mr. Dunn, left the week before. Mrs. Teak insists on honest folk under her roof, for a reason she guards. Teak whispers that she is a rich woman, then breaks off. The bar of the Ship and Anchor frames the bargaining. Jacobs builds the humor from hint, greed, and wary friendship.
falkland-book-4:
Lytton's Falkland, Book 4 opens with a letter from Mrs. St. John to Erasmus Falkland. Edward Bulwer-Lytton's tale here speaks through a blunt family friend. Emily is out of danger at last, the letter reports. Her health and reputation suffered from Falkland's forced visit to her room.

Mrs. St. John hopes the next meeting will be the last. Emily's happiness is injured for life, though her virtue stands spared. The writer then answers Falkland's charge of bitterness head on. Emily is soft and susceptible, she says, while he is fickle and wayward. No change in him would pass unnoticed by such a wife. Book 4 judges the lover in plain terms seldom used to his face.
famous-affinities-of-history-the-romance:
Lyndon Orr's Famous Affinities of History, complete in four volumes, gathers thirty-two famous love stories. The set opens with Antony and Cleopatra, whom Orr calls the most remarkable lovers of nineteen centuries. Abelard and Heloise, Elizabeth and Leicester, and Mary Queen of Scots follow. Courts, camps, and battlefields supply the early settings.

Later volumes move through Catharine and Potemkin, Napoleon and Marie Walewska, and Aaron Burr. The wives of General Houston bring the survey to America. Writers dominate the final volume: Swift, Shelley, the Carlyles, Dickens, and Balzac. Orr's subtitle, The Romance of Devotion, states his measure throughout. He asks what each great figure gave up for love. The result is popular history as a gallery of grand attachments, readable and romantic rather than critical.
following-the-equator-a-journey-around-t:
Following the Equator, Part 4, by Mark Twain, lands in New Zealand at Bluff, at the bottom of the middle island. Twain notes that Bluff sits nearly forty seven degrees below the equator. That is as far south as Quebec lies north of it. Yet the climate refuses the comparison. Winters are moderate, summers are moderate, and the temperature difference between seasons stays remarkably small.

Chapter XXX then takes up the rabbit question. New Zealand's rabbit plague began at Bluff, Twain reports. The man who introduced the animal was banqueted. They would hang him now, he adds. Around that joke Twain builds a small essay on natural enemies and colonial introduction. Poachers check rabbits in England. In Bluff the work falls to imported stoats, weasels, ferrets, cats, and mongooses, none of them native. Travel writing becomes environmental history here.
freeman-norman-conquest-vol-4:
William's reign and the settlement of England fill the fourth volume of Freeman's Norman Conquest, from 1867. The Domesday survey counts every hide and plow team in the realm. A feudal order is imposed from above on a conquered people.

Freeman traces how conquest remade laws, language, and landholding for good. Norman lords take English acres, and a new England takes shape. His learning maps the change parish by parish, almost hide by hide. The volume turns from battle to the slower, deeper work of rule, showing how a kingdom is remade after the swords are sheathed.
fromont-and-risler-volume-4:
Alphonse Daudet brings his factory novel to its crisis in Fromont and Risler, Volume 4 of the English edition. Risler walks home through snow, dreaming of profits and the house's good name. Carriages line the street for Sidonie's ball, which she excused him from attending. He pauses to admire her shadow behind the curtains.

Another shadow tells the reader what the husband cannot see. Sidonie's treachery with Georges Fromont moves toward discovery in this volume. Risler's worship curdles as accounts and signs align against his happiness. Daudet stages the fall inside the world Risler built: ballroom, factory, and counting house under one roof. The honest Swiss engineer must choose between shame, revenge, and self-destruction. Readers closing the volumes get Daudet's saddest design: a good man's trust spent as fuel for two people's ruinous affair.
froude-history-england-vol-4:
Two short reigns tear England apart in the fourth volume of Froude's History, from 1858. Edward the Sixth, a boy king, backs a bold Protestant experiment. Mary then restores Rome's faith and burns heretics in her Catholic reaction.

Froude tells the religious seesaw with pace and strong feeling. Prayer books change, altars rise and fall, and subjects pay in blood. Each reign undoes the other's work within a few short years. The volume sets the stage for Elizabeth's settlement, showing a nation weary of swings in faith and hungry for a steady hand on the throne at last.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-4:
Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 17, 1945, take up the military side of Japan's surrender formula. The top secret extracts are an unnumbered item following document 710 in volume two of the Potsdam papers. The paper before the chiefs had been drafted by the State, War, and Navy departments.

Admiral Leahy said the Joint Strategic Survey Committee backed that draft, with one change in its closing part. General Marshall then gave the military view in plain terms. Nothing should be done before fighting ends that would signal the Emperor's removal. His staying in office, Marshall argued, might sway the ending of hostilities in areas outside Japan itself. An Emperor's order could stop distant garrisons that no Allied force could quickly reach. The minutes catch the chiefs treating the throne as a tool for ending the war, not as a prize of it.
frus-1952-1954-american-republics-vol-4:
Volume four of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1952 to 1954 covers the American republics: United States policy toward Latin America in the early Eisenhower years. The Office of the Historian compiled it from declassified records. The Cold War had come to the hemisphere, and Washington read local reform as communist advance.

The volume's centerpiece is Guatemala: the documentary record of PBSUCCESS, the 1954 CIA operation that overthrew President Jacobo Arbenz. Around it stand the era's aid programs, arms deals, and anti-communist diplomacy across the region. The papers show how one covert success became a template used for a generation. The records are public government documents.
gao-gaoreports-b-293435-4:
The matter of Career Quest, a division of Syllan Careers, Inc., is decided in GAO file B-293435.4, dated March 31, 2005. Career Quest protested a General Services Administration cost study under Circular A-76. The study compared keeping help desk work in-house against contracting it out. The work served users of the Federal Supply Schedule. GAO denied the protest. The record showed that the agency's in-house plan, and the scoring of it, were sound. Both fit the work statement and the A-76 guidance.

The firm had argued that the study was run in ways that skewed the result. GAO found the flaws alleged were not borne out.
gao-gaoreports-b-294605-4:
Yang Enterprises, Inc., and Santa Barbara Applied Research, Inc., are the protesters in companion GAO files B-294605.4 through B-294605.6, dated April 1, 2005. The Air Force had awarded Call Henry, Inc., the launch operations support contract at Vandenberg Air Force Base. GAO denied the protests on each ground raised. The scoring of the winner's technical offer and past performance was sound. Talks with offerors gave them a fair chance to meet the agency's concerns.

A third point takes up price. Even where cost counts least, an agency may pick the cheaper, lower-rated offer. It must only judge fairly that the premium for the higher-rated offer is too great.
gao-gaoreports-b-294722-4:
GAO ruled in file B-294722.4 on July 28, 2005, in the protest brought by SGT, Inc. The Space and Naval Warfare Systems Command had awarded Systems Integration and Management, Inc., a support services contract at its New Orleans technology center. The work covered business, operations, and administrative support. SGT attacked the scoring of both its cost offer and its technical offer. GAO denied the protest. This copy is a redacted version cleared for release.

Two short digest points carry the ruling. The agency's cost realism adjustments were fair. The record also supported its view of the technical offers. With both points held, the award stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-294974-4:
Envirosolve LLC's second fight with the Drug Enforcement Administration is decided in GAO file B-294974.4, dated June 8, 2005. The agency had set up blanket purchase agreements for hazardous waste cleanup services. Envirosolve's first protest was dismissed as academic when the agency promised corrective action. The firm then protested that the promised fix never came. GAO sustained the new protest. This copy is a redacted version cleared for release.

The record showed that the agency had failed to carry out its own promised remedy on points that were clearly meritorious. The firm had thus been put to the cost of protesting twice on the same ground.
gao-gaoreports-b-295126-4:
GAO file B-295126.4, dated June 14, 2007, names Engineered Electric Company, doing business as DRS Fermont, as the protester. The firm attacked the terms of an Army solicitation for tactical quiet generator sets and standard generator sets. It said the Army had wrongly relaxed the fuel efficiency standard. GAO denied the protest. No offeror had been able to meet the stricter standard. The relaxed one met the Army's needs and widened the field.

The firm's claim that it could now meet the old standard changed nothing. An agency need not keep a term that shuts out all rivals when a looser term serves its purpose.
gao-gaoreports-b-295529-4:
Johnson Controls World Services sought its protest costs in GAO file B-295529.4, dated August 19, 2005. The costs arose from the Walter Reed A-76 fight, over base operations support at the medical center. GAO granted the request. The first protest filing had clearly flagged flaws in the Army's cost judgment. The agency admitted it never probed those detailed claims. It also held back relevant papers for more than 70 days, until a hearing forced them out.

On those facts, the agency had let a clearly sound protest drag. The delay in corrective action, undue in GAO's word, is what opens the door to repayment.
gao-gaoreports-b-295582-4:
Dated October 5, 2005, GAO file B-295582.4 records Brewbaker White Sands JV as the protester. The Air Force had awarded NASCENT Group JV a contract for base engineering services at Holloman Air Force Base, New Mexico. The winner's offer was rated slightly lower but priced lower too. Past performance was the top factor, and the protester's rating there was slightly higher. GAO denied the protest. This copy is a redacted version cleared for release.

The selection official had weighed the offers in an integrated way. Both firms' past performance posed much the same risk, the official found. The premium for the protester's edge in rating was not worth paying.
gao-gaoreports-b-295952-4:
LENS, JV, sought its protest costs in GAO file B-295952.4, dated December 12, 2005. The Navy had run a utility privatization program at Marine Corps Base Hawaii, at Kaneohe Bay. The firm lost and protested the agency's should cost method for running the electric system. The agency then took corrective action. GAO denied the cost request. This copy is a redacted version cleared for release. Corrective action alone does not earn repayment of protest costs.

The protest must also be shown clearly meritorious on the record. That showing, GAO held, was not made here. The firm's challenge to the cost method stayed unproven.
gao-gaoreports-b-295990-4:
Cogent Systems protested an Army award for a fingerprint system for Iraq in GAO decision B-295990.4, dated October 6, 2005. The winner was Motorola. The system was an Automated Fingerprint Identification System. Cogent attacked the tech marks, the price review, and the final pick. Its low price bid had been ruled not fit for award.

GAO sustained the protest. A key flaw on a flatbed scanner was not well founded. GAO also found the agency gave no real talks on that point. With that flaw gone, the bar to award fell. Readers can use the case for how a weak flaw and thin talks can undo a pick.
gao-gaoreports-b-296090-4:
Kola Nut Travel again protested Army travel service awards in GAO decision B-296090.4, dated August 25, 2005. This time the winners were Alamo Travel Group and Wingate Travel. The firm said its tech bid was marked too low. It also said fee deals tied to the winners were improper.

GAO denied the protest. The review notes backed a mark of just acceptable for the firm's bid. On fees, GAO saw no proof of undue sway. The winners won on lower prices and higher marks. The case pairs with the firm's first protest. It shows the same fee claim fail on a fuller record.
gao-gaoreports-b-296194-4:
Foster-Miller protested its cut from the same Army CREW jammer contest in GAO decision B-296194.4, dated August 31, 2005. The system helps stop roadside bomb blasts. The firm was barred from field tests. It had sought to swap its program load for the field test.

GAO denied the protest. The test plans barred a new load after the first test round. GAO said that read of the plans was sound. The firm also failed to show its low mark on a key point was wrong. The cut from the field thus stood. The ruling shows test rules bind both sides once set.
gao-gaoreports-b-296435-4:
Port-A-Pit Catering protested its loss in the same Forest Service food contest in GAO decision B-296435.4, dated September 15, 2005. The work was hot and cold meals at 27 field sites. The firm hit how bids were scored. Price review was the core flaw it named. Other firms won at some sites.

GAO sustained the protest. The price review used unit prices alone. That base was too thin to match the true cost of rival bids. With no sound way to match costs, the call that prices were not fair fell. Price review must give a real base to match bids. Unit prices alone failed that test here.
gao-gaoreports-b-296628-4:
Ystueta protested the axing of an Agriculture call for build work in GAO decision B-296628.4, dated February 27, 2006. The site was a research center in Stoneville, Mississippi. The call had been set aside for small firms. That bar was then lifted and the call was axed. The firm said the acts dodged an award to it.

GAO denied the protest. Lack of funds is a clear cause to axe a call. An agency cannot award a deal past its funds. That cause needs just a sound base. The fund gap gave that base here. Claims of dodge did not beat the fund facts. The axing thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-296783-4:
ITT Federal Services sought protest costs after its win in the Europe logistics case in GAO decision B-296783.4, dated April 26, 2006. The Army fought sums for lawyers and a hired expert. GAO had backed the firm in the first fight. The winner there was Kellogg, Brown and Root. Rate caps were the core fight now.

GAO set the rates by law. A plea for a rate above the 150 dollar cap must use the broad price index for all goods. The index for legal work alone does not count. Pay for a hired expert was capped at the top federal pay rate. That cap held even when the expert billed more.
gao-gaoreports-b-297022-4:
Alion Science again protested the spectrum design award in GAO decision B-297022.4, dated September 26, 2006. The winner was again the ITT unit. The agency had done fix work after the first loss. It read the goods of the winner, its rivals, and its buyers. It weighed how the job could sway those stakes.

GAO denied this protest. The fix work met the flaw from the first case. Notes now showed a full clash check. The winner would use walled-off sub firms for clash parts of the work. That wall was judged fit to block the clash. Harm to work grade was small. A sound fix can cure a clash flaw.
gao-gaoreports-b-297053-4:
Haworth protested a General Services award for office furniture in GAO decision B-297053.4, dated June 7, 2006. The winner was Herman Miller. The site was a new federal block in San Francisco. All bid goods had to sit on the firm's schedule deal by a set date. The firm's quote was cut for a miss on that date.

GAO denied the protest. The agency had told firms of the date rule in clear terms. The firm failed to make sure all its goods were on the deal in time. That miss was its own. A fresh claim raised late in briefs was cut as late. Facts for it were known at the first filing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297534-4:
CHE Consulting protested the terms of a Defense call for gear upkeep in GAO decision B-297534.4, dated May 17, 2006. The gear was StorageTek kit at sites round the land. The call asked firms to show how they would get maker help. That help was a back-up if a fix failed in the set time. The firm said that term asked too much.

GAO denied the protest. The record gave a sound base for the term. The work was key upkeep with a tight fix clock. A back-up path to the maker is a fair need in that case. Terms that track a real risk can stand, even if they narrow the field.
gao-gaoreports-b-297790-4:
T Square Logistics sought protest costs in GAO decision B-297790.4, dated April 26, 2006. The first fight hit an Air Force award for base support. The site was Grissom Air Reserve Base in Indiana. The winner was Data Monitor Systems. Talks in the first case had flaws. The agency fixed the buy late, after a GAO talks track.

GAO backed pay of the costs. The claims were clearly strong, as the talks track showed. The agency was slow to fix the buy. Talks had cut the firm's past work mark to low trust for gaps in skill. That flaw drove the high price pick. Talks never named that gap to the firm.
gao-gaoreports-b-298033-4:
American Systems Consulting protested a Defense award in GAO decision B-298033.4, dated March 28, 2007. The winner was ManTech Security Technologies. The work was systems and software help. The user was the Defense Commissary Agency. The firm hit tech and cost marks. It also sought costs for past protests on this call.

GAO denied the protest and the cost plea. The record backed the agency finds on marks. The winner was higher rated on tech and lower on price. That mix is a strong win base. Past protest costs were not backed on this record. A firm that loses on marks and shows no cost base will get no costs.
gao-gaoreports-b-298099-4:
Overlook Systems again protested the GPS center award in GAO decision B-298099.4, dated November 28, 2006. The winner was again LinQuest. The agency had done a fresh clash check. It took a full plan to curb clash risk from the winner. It also added more watch steps of its own. The firm said the plan was too thin and talks were unfair.

GAO denied the protest. The clash risk was found to be not great. That find was sound on a deep check. The plan, as honed, plus more watch, was fit to guard the state. Talks on clash go to fitness to win. They need not be held with all firms. The pick thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-298443-4:
Partnership for Response and Recovery protested corrective action by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. The case grew from a prior protest of awards for housing inspection services. Those services send inspectors to homes after a disaster. GAO ruled in B-298443.4 on December 18, 2006.

FEMA chose to reopen talks and seek fully revised proposals. The protester said that broad fix unfairly favored its rival. GAO disagreed. The agency had found its first talks and scoring weak. New needs had also been added to the work. An agency may widen a fix to match such flaws. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298489-4:
Compunetix, Inc. protested a NASA award to Frequentis USA, Inc. The Goddard Space Flight Center ran the buy. The contract covered Mission Operations Voice Enhancement systems. The work spans design, build, test, and upkeep of voice gear. GAO ruled in B-298489.4 and B-298489.5 on January 12, 2007.

Compunetix held a lower-rated, higher-priced proposal. It attacked nearly every step of the scoring. It also said the awardee was not a small firm fit for this set-aside. GAO reviewed the full record. It found the agency's calls fair and in line with the stated scheme. The broad attack did not hold up. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298575-4:
Alaska Structures, Inc. asked GAO to back payment of its protest costs. The plea grew from an Army buy for a mobile field hospital system. The Army Medical Research Acquisition Activity ran that buy. GAO acted in B-298575.4, a costs ruling, on January 22, 2007.

The agency had taken corrective action after the protest. It pledged to cancel and reissue the request. Cost payment turns on a protest being clearly sound. GAO found no such clear merit here. It also saw no proof for a linked claim from an earlier protest round. A weak protest earns no cost award. GAO denied the request.
gao-gaoreports-b-298833-4:
IBM Global Business Services protested an Air Force task order to Computer Sciences Corporation. The order named a system integrator for the Expeditionary Combat Support System. The work deploys shelf software and change management methods. GAO ruled in B-298833.4 and B-298833.5 on March 1, 2007.

The agency scored IBM's offer as high risk. Its plan used too few government staff in the change work. Key change tasks needed more agency hands than the plan gave. IBM's ratio of staff to consultants fell well below trade norms. That gap backed the risk mark. The terms attack also failed. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298918-4:
EBSCO Publishing, Inc. sought payment of its protest costs from the Department of Defense Education Activity. The agency had taken a fix after the firm's protest. That protest fought its removal from a buy for online information services. GAO acted in B-298918.4, a costs ruling, on May 7, 2007.

GAO backed payment of $20,945.95 in costs. It also took up the cap on lawyer fees. That cap sits at $150 per hour by statute. GAO urged that the cap be raised to match cost-of-living growth. The agency did not fight the raise or the sum claimed. The full claim could go forward.
gao-gaoreports-b-299145-4:
The Air Force sought a fresh look at a prior ruling in the combat search and rescue aircraft case. That ruling had backed protests by Sikorsky and Lockheed Martin Systems Integration-Owego. The award to The Boeing Company sat at the core. GAO acted in B-299145.4 on March 29, 2007.

The agency asked GAO to rule on points left open before. One point was a past performance mark for one protester. GAO found the mark of little confidence fair. Recent, badly flawed work on a like aircraft drove that mark. Strong work on a second like deal did not erase it. One grave lapse on close work can shape the score.
gao-gaoreports-b-299229-4:
MELE Associates, Inc. protested the rejection of its proposal by the Department of Energy. The buy sought services to find, remove, and guard nuclear and radiological materials. Those stocks sit at sites at risk of theft or misuse. GAO ruled in B-299229.4 on July 25, 2007.

The agency scored the bid under technical approach and firm experience. The bid pledged to meet the terms. But it did not show how it would do so. GAO found that gap showed a weak grasp of the work. The bid also failed to prove past work on like tasks. Thin claims in place of proof can sink a bid. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299260-4:
Swales Aerospace sought payment of its protest costs from NASA. The plea grew from protests of an award to SGT, Inc. That deal covered mechanical systems engineering services at Goddard Space Flight Center. GAO acted in B-299260.4, a costs ruling, on April 30, 2007.

Cost payment needs a strong protest plus slow agency action. The agency here had taken a fix in reply to the protests. GAO asked if that fix came with undue delay. It found no such delay on the record. Nor did the protests stand as clearly sound from the start. A plea built on those grounds fails. GAO denied the request.
gao-gaoreports-b-299307-4:
Panacea Consulting, Inc. protested Labor Department task orders to Systems Integration and Development, Inc. The orders covered project management support and core research support services. Both ran through a federal supply schedule deal. GAO ruled in B-299307.4 and B-299308.4 on July 27, 2007.

The record, GAO found, was too thin to back the award. Scores sat on the page with no real account of why. The pick memo likewise gave no sound logic. An agency must show the sense behind its marks. A bare score sheet leaves rivals and reviewers in the dark. Such a void cannot support a source selection. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299317-4:
The Department of the Army asked GAO to revisit its ruling in the Iraq linguist services case. That ruling had backed a protest by L-3 Communications Titan Corporation. The award to Global Linguist Solutions, LLC was at stake. GAO acted in B-299317.4 on June 8, 2007.

A fresh look needs more than a wish to reargue the case. GAO held to its prior call. The scoring flaws it found before stood on the record. The fill-rate and benchmark points had been weighed with care. The agency's plea gave no sound base to flip the result. GAO denied the reconsideration request. The prior ruling stayed in place.
gao-gaoreports-b-299582-4:
Korrect Optical protested a Veterans Affairs award to Safe-Lite Optical Company. The contract covered eyeglasses for veterans at medical centers in one network. The firm said the winner's bid missed a key term. GAO ruled in B-299582.4 and B-299582.5 on September 7, 2007.

The claimed gap was the count of frame styles on offer. The record showed the winner did meet that count. With that claim gone, the pick came down to price. The agency found the bids near equal on non-price points. A lower price can then break the tie. That path fit the best-value terms. No flaw in the firm's own score was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299721-4:
The Mangi Environmental Group protested an Agriculture Department award to Geo Marine. The contract covered programmatic environmental assessments. The work grew from a settlement on haying and grazing lands in 20 states. GAO ruled in B-299721.4 on January 24, 2008.

The firm attacked the technical review and the pick. GAO found the agency's dim view of its bid fair. The bid read as muddled on key points. It held many flaws and gaps across its pages. A muddled bid gives a panel little to credit. The flaws were the firm's to cure at draft time. No breach of the stated tests was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-310372-4:
Pemco Aeroplex, Inc. saw its protest thrown out. GAO ruled in B-310372.4 on May 2, 2008. The case ties to the Air Force KC-135 depot care race. Pemco claimed the Air Force's true needs had shifted in a big way. It said the call no longer matched those needs. It asked for a fresh race on new terms.

GAO dismissed the protest. The agency aide who turns needs into deal terms swore a key fact. The agency has made no call yet on shifts to the deal's terms. A claim built on a shift not yet made has no base. The race terms stand for now.
gao-gaoreports-b-310398-4:
Protest costs are backed in this GAO decision, B-310398.4, dated January 16, 2008. World Communications Center, Inc. had fought a sole-source award for satellite trackers.
